file: 1998/1998-06-19_top executives_locked_conference room_starved to death_call help_phone_trouble_deciosns_get outside line.gif
title: Executives Starve Over Decimal Phone Number

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I just heard that all our top executives got locked in a conference room and starved to death.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why didn't they use the phone to call for help?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: One week ago...

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: It's agreed: we dial 8.3 to get an outside line.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Uh-oh. This one doesn't do decimals.

setting: Office cubicle area and a conference room (flashback)
situation: Alice tells Dilbert that the company's top executives were locked in a conference room and starved to death. Dilbert asks why they didn't phone for help. A flashback shows the executives agreeing to dial 8.3 for an outside line, only to discover the phone keypad has no decimal point.
punchline: The executives' incompetence was so profound that they decided on an impossible phone number, which doomed them to starve in a room with a working phone.
summary: A flashback reveals that the doomed executives were undone by their own absurd instruction to dial a number containing a decimal point.

file: 1998/1998-06-17_drug treatment program_registration form_objective_battering ram_use head.gif
title: Alice's Turnip-Head Battering Ram Plan

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Drug treatment program

transcript.speaker: Counselor
transcript.text: Alice, I'd like to talk to you about your registration form.

transcript.speaker: Counselor
transcript.text: Under "objective," you said you want to use my "turnip-shaped head as a battering ram to break out of here."

transcript.speaker: Counselor
transcript.text: Alice, drop the duct tape.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stay tense; that will help.

setting: Counselor's office at a drug treatment program
situation: A counselor at a drug treatment program reviews Alice's registration form and reads aloud her stated objective, which is to use his turnip-shaped head as a battering ram to escape. Alice, her hair looming large in the foreground, then produces a roll of duct tape and calmly advises him to stay tense.
punchline: Alice is not remotely reformed; she cheerfully proceeds with her violent escape plan and casually tells her victim to tense up because it will make the head-battering easier.
summary: A rehab counselor confronts Alice about her alarming escape plan, only to find she is already prepared to carry it out with his own head.

file: 1998/1998-04-01_catbert_evil hr directorm not enjoying job_powerful anti depressant_prescribe drugs_illegal.gif
tags: evil hr directorm not enjoying job
title: Catbert Prescribes Lifelong Antidepressants

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'm not enjoying my job.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Take this powerful anti-depressant drug for the rest of your life.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I didn't know H.R. could prescribe drugs.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'd hate to live in a world where that was illegal.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: "Boss-proof cap."

situation: A worried employee with big hair tells Catbert, the evil H.R. director, that she is not enjoying her job. Instead of fixing the job, Catbert hands her a powerful antidepressant to take for life. She questions whether H.R. can prescribe drugs, and he shrugs off the legality while she examines the pill bottle.
punchline: Rather than address why employees are miserable, evil H.R. simply medicates them into tolerating it, dismissing the illegality of prescribing drugs; the 'boss-proof cap' on the bottle is a pun on child-proof caps.
summary: Faced with an unhappy worker, the feline human resources chief offers a lifelong pill instead of any improvement to her working conditions.

file: 1998/1998-10-14_don't know cobol_elbonia_imaginary keyboard_no computers_teach cobol.gif
title: Teaching COBOL Without Computers or Knowledge

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Somewhere in Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been sent to teach you COBOL.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: We don't have any computers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's okay. I don't know COBOL.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And if you had a keyboard, you would do this.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Oops...How do I delete?

situation: Dilbert arrives in Elbonia to teach the locals COBOL, only to learn they have no computers. He admits he doesn't know COBOL either, so he mimes typing on an imaginary keyboard. The Elbonians play along and mime making a typing mistake.
punchline: A training session with no computers and an instructor who doesn't know the language is a complete sham, yet everyone carries on as if it were a real class, even pretending to hit delete on an imaginary keyboard.
summary: A traveling instructor and his imaginary-keyboard students go through the motions of a programming class that has neither computers nor expertise.

file: 1998/1998-02-02_dilbert_harmful to workers_demonstrate danger_controlled experimnet_rebellion_sarcasm_complacency_going bald.gif
title: Dilbert Strip Declared Harmful to Workers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: WARNING!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Author Norman Solomon has determined that the Dilbert comic strip is harmful to workers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I will demonstrate the danger with this carefully controlled experiment.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Have your plans for rebellion been replaced by sarcasm and complacency?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And I think I'm going bald!

setting: A conference table in an office
situation: Dogbert announces that an author has concluded the Dilbert strip harms workers, then conducts a quick 'experiment' on Wally, who sits across the table. Dogbert hands Wally a paper and asks whether his rebellious plans have been replaced by sarcasm and complacency. Wally agrees and adds that he thinks he's going bald.
punchline: The 'controlled experiment' is a sloppy one-subject test in which Wally, a worker already known for apathy, confirms the accusation while also complaining about something unrelated, mocking the claim that a comic strip could sap workers' will to rebel.
summary: Dogbert stages a mock scientific test to check a critic's claim that this very comic numbs workers into passivity, with a hapless coworker as his only subject.

file: 1998/1998-07-16_son-of-a-boss_complete lack_knowledge_vice president_amrketing_gift_piano.gif
title: Promoted For Knowing Nothing, Wants Piano

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Son-of-a-Boss

transcript.speaker: Son of the Boss
transcript.text: My complete lack of knowledge has not gone unnoticed.

transcript.speaker: Son of the Boss
transcript.text: I've been promoted to Vice President of Marketing!

transcript.speaker: Son of the Boss
transcript.text: If you feel the need to buy me a gift, I'd love a piano.

situation: The Boss's son, who has the same horn-like hair as his father, tells Dilbert and a coworker at a meeting table that he has been promoted to Vice President of Marketing. He credits his total ignorance for the promotion, then hints that he'd like a piano as a gift from them.
punchline: He is promoted precisely because of his incompetence, and he immediately expects his subordinates to shower him with an extravagant gift.
summary: A clueless manager's heir cheerfully announces a vice presidency earned by ignorance and then angles for a pricey present from his new underlings.

file: 1998/1998-07-17_project plan_strategy_leadership_radiates_boss ego_proud_strategy is plan.gif
title: Strategy Means Making You Plan

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is your project plan done?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't do a plan until you tell me the strategy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My strategy is to make you do a plan.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sometimes the leadership just radiates from my body.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert whether his project plan is finished. Dilbert replies that he needs a strategy from the Boss first, and the Boss declares that his strategy is simply to make Dilbert write the plan. The Boss then smugly thinks about how his leadership radiates from him.
punchline: The Boss's 'strategy' is just delegating his own job back to the employee, yet he congratulates himself on being a brilliant leader.
summary: A manager passes the buck on strategy to his subordinate and then basks in his own imagined brilliance.

file: 1998/1998-08-19_catbert_evil hr director_contract employee_regular employee_pay less_motivated_other than money_stupidity.gif
title: Contract Employee Offered Permanent Pay Cut

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You've been a good contract employee. We'd like to make you a regular employee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You mean you want to pay me less?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We want you to be motivated by something other than money.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Like... stupidity?

situation: Catbert, acting as the evil H.R. director, tells Dilbert that his good work as a contract employee has earned him an offer to become a regular employee. Dilbert correctly guesses that this means a pay cut. Catbert says the company wants him motivated by something other than money, and Dilbert sarcastically suggests stupidity.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that the only thing left to motivate an employee who is paid less is his own foolishness in accepting the deal.
summary: A cat in charge of personnel presents a promotion to staff status that is really a downgrade in earnings, and the worker sees right through it.

file: 1998/1998-05-16_optimistic assumptions_revenue target_visited by alien_our new pordcut_autopsy video_technology.gif
title: Alien Autopsy Video Revenue Plan

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I had to make some optimistic assumptions to meet the revenue target.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In week three, we're visited by an alien named D'Utox Inag who offers to share his advanced technology.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then do we use his technology to design our new product?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, we kill him and sell the autopsy video.

setting: Conference room during a business presentation
situation: Dilbert presents a revenue projection chart and admits he made optimistic assumptions to hit the target. He describes an assumed event in which a friendly alien offers advanced technology. When the Boss asks if they'll use it for the new product, Dilbert says they'll kill the alien and sell the autopsy video instead.
punchline: The financial forecast only works by assuming an absurdly lucky windfall, and the cynical way of cashing in on it (murdering the alien and selling the video) shows how far-fetched and unethical the 'optimistic assumptions' really are.
summary: To justify a rosy sales forecast, an engineer invents a fantasy scenario involving a generous alien visitor and a gruesome money-making scheme.

file: 1998/1998-07-13_technology development group_boss's son_college_hid in attic_no college_smart_education.gif
title: Boss's Son Hid in Attic

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired my son to manage our technology development group.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's young, but I'm almost positive he went to college.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where did you go to college?

transcript.speaker: The Boss's Son
transcript.text: Actually, I hid in our attic for four years.

situation: The Boss introduces his young son to Dilbert as the new manager of the technology development group. The Boss admits he is only almost sure his son went to college. When Dilbert asks the son where he studied, the son reveals he actually spent four years hiding in the family attic.
punchline: The boss's unqualified son was hired through nepotism and has no education or qualifications, having spent the college years hiding in an attic, yet he is placed in charge of technology development.
summary: A manager installs his barely qualified son as head of a technical team, and the young man cheerfully admits he skipped college by lurking in the attic.

file: 1998/1998-10-23_new hire_not working_no head_headless man_made mistake hiring_fired_insubordination.gif
title: Headless New Hire Fired Insubordination

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The new guy isn't working out.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why not?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe because he has no head.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, you think I made a mistake hiring him?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... no. But the new guy thinks so.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then he's fired for insubordination!

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that the new employee isn't working out because he has no head, which is visible as an empty shirt and tie standing beside them. The Boss asks whether Dilbert thinks he made a hiring mistake. Dilbert tries to deflect by saying the new guy thinks so, and the Boss immediately decides to fire the new hire for insubordination.
punchline: The Boss, unable to accept that his hiring decision might be flawed, fires the headless employee for supposedly criticizing him, ignoring the obvious problem that the hire has no head.
summary: An obviously unqualified headless recruit gets dismissed for disagreeing with the manager's judgment rather than the manager admitting his error.

file: 1998/1998-03-24_personal habitats_cubicles_hellhole junior_pictures.gif
title: Cubicles Renamed Personal Habitats

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can replace your cubicles with "personal habitats."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They look exactly like cubicles, but we've made huge advances in what they're called.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is it expensive?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If money is an issue, you could start with the "Hellhole Junior" model and upgrade later.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you have pictures?

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, stands on the Boss's desk and offers to replace the office cubicles with "personal habitats." He admits they look identical and only the name has changed. The Boss asks about cost and then asks to see pictures of the budget "Hellhole Junior" model.
punchline: Dogbert is selling a rebranded product with no real improvement, and the gullible Boss is eager to buy it, even asking for pictures of a model whose name openly admits it's awful.
summary: A consultant dog sells a boss on identical cubicles that have simply been given a fancier name, and the boss happily asks for brochures.

file: 1998/1998-09-03_receipts_look fake_notorized_dna evidence_process voucher_difficult secretary_annoying procedures_formal_not neccessary_red tape.gif
title: Receipts Mistaken for Forgeries

transcript.speaker: Accounting Clerk
transcript.text: I can't process your voucher because these receipts look fake to me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: They aren't fake!

transcript.speaker: Accounting Clerk
transcript.text: Then why aren't they notarized?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because they're just receipts!

transcript.speaker: Accounting Clerk
transcript.text: And now you'll tell me there's no DNA evidence either.

setting: Accounting clerk's desk in an office
situation: Dilbert submits an expense voucher with receipts to an accounting clerk, who refuses to process it because the receipts look fake. When Dilbert insists they are genuine, the clerk demands they be notarized, then treats his frustrated protest as suspicious, sarcastically demanding DNA evidence too.
punchline: The clerk's absurd paranoia and impossible standards of proof turn a routine expense claim into a criminal investigation, making Dilbert's honest explanations sound like guilt.
summary: A suspicious bureaucrat treats a simple expense report like a forgery case and demands increasingly ridiculous verification.

file: 1998/1998-12-15_power of cute ears_abuse banking industry_dogbert_large withdrawl_other peoples accounts.gif
title: Dogbert Robs Bank With Cute Ears

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I will now use my power of cute ears to abuse the banking industry.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd like to make a large withdrawal from other peoples' accounts.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It was funny when I made her count it twice.

setting: Outside a bank, at the teller window inside, and then on the sidewalk
situation: Dogbert walks up to a bank announcing that he will exploit his cute ears to abuse the banking industry. At the teller window he openly asks to withdraw a large sum from other people's accounts, and the teller complies. He then drags a heavy money sack down the street, amused that he made her count the cash twice.
punchline: Dogbert brazenly requests to steal other people's money and gets it simply because he looks cute, showing how shallow appearance-based trust can be exploited.
summary: A charming little dog strolls into a bank, openly demands money from strangers' accounts, and walks out with a sack of cash thanks to his adorable looks.

file: 1998/1998-04-30_overpaid_do bad work_funny_think about it_terrible job_job security.gif
title: Consultant Overpaid, Engineer Underpaid

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As a consultant, I'm overpaid even if I do bad work.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Whereas you're underpaid even if you do good work.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's funny if you think about it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I might have a terrible job, but at least I don't have any job security.

situation: Dogbert, working as a consultant, sits beside Dilbert at his desk and points out that he gets overpaid even for bad work, while Dilbert is underpaid even for good work. Dilbert, typing at his computer, responds with a bleak attempt to find a silver lining.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt at optimism is sarcastic: lacking job security is not a benefit, so he has no real upside to offer.
summary: A smug consultant dog contrasts his lavish pay with his friend's meager wages, and the friend's only consolation turns out to be another drawback.
keywords: funny if you think about it

file: 1998/1998-09-13_annual inspirational talk_work hard_competition_feel afraid_quality of lives_too afraid_management incompetetnce.gif
title: Boss's Fear-Based Inspirational Talk Backfires

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's time for my annual inspirational talk!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We must work twice as hard, or the competition will crush us!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to feel afraid twenty-four hours a day!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: Wouldn't that lower the quality of our lives?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Seems like it might.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm too afraid to work here now. I wonder if our competitors are hiring.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Question: Should we continue to be afraid of our own management's incompetence?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's compromise. I'll cut the meeting short if you'll all agree to feel worse in some way.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now I remember why I only inspire them once a year.

setting: Conference room during a company meeting
situation: The Boss gives his annual inspirational talk, telling employees to work twice as hard and to feel afraid all day, every day. Dilbert, Wally and Alice ask pointed questions about quality of life and about fearing management's own incompetence. The Boss offers a pointless compromise and then privately regrets the whole exercise.
punchline: The Boss's attempt to motivate through fear only makes employees want to quit or fear him, and he concludes the real problem is the inspiring itself, not his bad message.
summary: A manager tries to motivate his staff by terrifying them, and they respond by questioning his competence and considering leaving for rivals.

file: 1998/1998-01-25_document_on desk_overdue_last minute_going home_boss to dilbert_wait until tomorrow_sociopath_spookily accurate.gif
title: Boss Corners Dilbert at Quitting Time

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's time to go home. That means...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hi

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Right on schedule.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait. Let me guess why you're here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You want to discuss a document that's been on your desk for a month.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's something that could easily wait until tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But you'll insist that I handle it now because you're a sociopath.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wrong. I majored in anthropology.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But that was a spookily accurate guess about the document.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle at the end of the workday
situation: As Dilbert prepares to leave for the day, the Boss shows up with a document right on schedule. Dilbert predicts the whole conversation, including that the Boss will demand immediate action and is a sociopath. The Boss corrects only the claim about his psychology, not the prediction about the document.
punchline: The Boss denies being a sociopath on a technicality about his college major while confirming everything else Dilbert accurately predicted about his last-minute, inconsiderate behavior.
summary: Dilbert correctly predicts his boss's quitting-time ambush down to the details, and the boss only quibbles with the diagnosis.

file: 1998/1998-11-04_barger_closed dorr_curse_intense enrgy_new hire_not a knocker_pushes.gif
title: Alice Barges Into Boss's Office

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Get out of my way, weaklings!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This closed door can't stop me! I'll curse it off its #@%!!* hinges!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You could have knocked.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm a barger, not a knocker.

setting: Office hallway and the Boss's office
situation: Alice storms down the corridor shoving coworkers aside and shouting that a closed door won't stop her. She then bursts into the Boss's office, where the door has been knocked flat on the floor with a person's legs sticking out from under it. The Boss mildly points out she could have knocked, and she proudly declares she is a barger.
punchline: Alice's aggressive style is so extreme that she treats barging in as a personality type, and she has no remorse for flattening the door and a bystander.
summary: Alice plows through the office, flattening a door and whoever was behind it, then shrugs off the Boss's suggestion of simple politeness.

file: 1998/1998-10-11_must delight customoers_stop price gauging_stop selling defective products_talking about customers_delighting customers_empathy.gif
title: Delighting Customers Without Changing Anything

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's not enough to "serve" our customers...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We must delight them!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You mean we have to stop price-gouging?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I think we can still do that.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ooh ooh! I know!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We could stop selling products with known defects.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm talking about customers, not products!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you feel like delighting customers?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I barely have the empathy to pity them.

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: The Boss announces that the company must go beyond serving customers and actually delight them. Alice and Wally suggest practical ways to do this, such as ending price-gouging and no longer selling defective products, but the Boss rejects both ideas. Dilbert admits he has no real empathy for customers.
punchline: The Boss wants customers to be delighted without making any real change to how they are treated, such as fair pricing or working products, which exposes the empty nature of corporate customer-service slogans.
summary: A manager demands delighted customers but dismisses every concrete improvement his staff proposes, leaving the team with nothing but cynicism.

file: 1998/1998-11-02_%#!!_asoks ears_curse at work_ears fell off_like to curse_vulgarity_warm up.gif
title: Cursing Warm-Up Blows Ears Off

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I must warn you, I'm one of those women who like to curse at work.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: That was a warm-up.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My ears fell off!!

situation: A new woman at a meeting politely warns her colleagues that she likes to curse at work. She then unleashes a furious burst of profanity, shown as comic-strip symbols, while Asok sits stunned across the table. She calmly says that was only a warm-up, and Asok exclaims that his ears fell off.
punchline: Her outburst was so intense that it was merely a warm-up, leaving Asok so shocked he claims his ears fell off.
summary: A colleague gives fair warning about her love of swearing, then delivers a blistering tirade that leaves a young coworker reeling.

file: 1998/1998-02-05_clothes defective_going to kitchen_maintain discipline_telecommute_throry_wearing work clothes_clothes.gif
title: Work Clothes Fail Telecommuting Discipline Test

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm wearing my work clothes while I telecommute, to maintain discipline.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is it working?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll test the theory by seeing if my clothes stop me from going to the kitchen.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently my clothes are defective.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Haven't I been saying that?

setting: Dilbert's home, at his computer and then in his kitchen
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he is wearing his work clothes while telecommuting so he will stay disciplined. He then tests the theory by walking to the kitchen, and ends up at the table surrounded by chips, cookies and soda. He concludes that his clothes must be defective.
punchline: Dilbert blames his clothes rather than himself for his lack of willpower, and Dogbert's reply cheekily suggests Dilbert's clothes have always been defective, a dig at his fashion sense.
summary: A telecommuter's dress-for-work trick fails to keep him away from the snacks, so he decides the outfit itself must be faulty.

file: 1998/1998-10-31_cubicle walls_improve communication_worst ideas_noblest reasons_leashed and branded_improve morale.gif
title: Terrible Ideas With Noble Excuses

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Cubicle walls will be removed "in order to improve communication."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do the worst ideas always have the noblest sounding reasons?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Employees will be leashed and branded "in order to improve morale."

setting: Conference room during a management meeting
situation: The Boss reads an announcement at a meeting that cubicle walls will be removed to improve communication. Dilbert wonders aloud why bad ideas always come with such noble-sounding justifications. The Boss, apparently missing the point, reads the next announcement: employees will be leashed and branded to improve morale.
punchline: Dilbert's complaint is proven right when the Boss immediately announces an absurdly cruel policy and dresses it up with a noble reason, showing he missed the sarcasm entirely.
summary: A manager cheerfully announces a string of awful workplace policies, each justified with lofty goals, and cannot see why an employee finds that suspicious.

file: 1998/1998-03-22_catbert_evil hr dircetor_vacation policy_more vacation days_restroom breaks_count as vacation_porcelain cruise.gif
title: Restroom Breaks Count as Vacation

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: There's been a slight change in the vacation policy.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Are we getting more vacation days?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You must be new here.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: As you know, all vacation time must be used in the year it is earned.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I realize this is not always convenient. So I've decided to be flexible.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: From now on, any time you spend in the restroom will count as vacation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We should complain.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: If you need me, I'll be taking a porcelain cruise.

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, announces a change to the vacation policy at a meeting. An employee hopefully asks if they are getting more vacation days, and Catbert mocks his naivety, reminds them of the use-it-or-lose-it rule, and then 'flexibly' declares that restroom time counts as vacation. Dilbert suggests complaining, while a coworker heads off to the restroom.
punchline: Catbert's 'flexibility' is a policy that deducts bathroom breaks from vacation days, effectively cutting employees' time off while pretending to help them use it.
summary: The malicious personnel chief 'generously' lets staff burn their expiring leave by charging their toilet visits against it.

file: 1998/1998-12-03_sabotaged_global conspiracy_plant misspelled work_spell checker_webster.gif
title: Blaming Webster for Misspelling

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: What the...? I've been sabotaged!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, I am not part of a global conspiracy to plant a misspelled word in your "spell checker."

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Gasp! They got to Webster too!!!

situation: Tina sits at her computer and accuses someone of sabotaging her after her spell checker flags or contains a misspelling. Wally calmly denies being part of any global conspiracy to plant a misspelled word. Tina then checks a dictionary and, finding it agrees with the spell checker, concludes that the conspiracy has corrupted Webster too.
punchline: Tina is so paranoid that when the dictionary confirms the spell checker, she assumes the dictionary has been sabotaged rather than accepting she misspelled the word.
summary: A paranoid coworker refuses to believe she made a spelling error and decides even the dictionary has been compromised.

file: 1998/1998-11-10_project plan_justify resources_change software_software changes_plan.gif
title: Plan Needed After Work Is Done

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll need a project plan to justify the resources we need to change our software.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can make those software changes in ten seconds.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Done.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now all we need is that plan.

setting: The Boss's office, at a desk
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert for a project plan to justify the resources needed to change the software. Dilbert points out he can make the changes in ten seconds and does so immediately. The Boss praises the work but still insists on getting the project plan.
punchline: Bureaucratic process takes priority over results, so the plan is demanded even after the work it was meant to justify has already been completed.
summary: A manager still wants a paperwork justification for a task his employee has just finished in seconds.

file: 1998/1998-12-06_vast wisdom_evil sadistic_obstructionists_trust no one_except the lazy.gif
title: Trust No One But the Lazy

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wally, may I tap in to your vast wisdom?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Okay, but make sure you pull out before your head explodes.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I've noticed that many employees are evil, sadistic obstructionists.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Do all the nuts work here by some strange coincidence?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Or are most employees evil?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Don't focus on the evil, Asok.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Focus on the few employees who seem good.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: They're the ones who will stab you when you're sleeping!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Trust no one but the lazy!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Ow! Ow! Ow!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I warned you to pull out!

situation: Asok asks Wally for career wisdom and wonders whether most employees are evil. Wally advises him to distrust the seemingly good employees and trust only the lazy. Asok's head begins to hurt from the cynical logic, and Wally reminds him he was warned.
punchline: Wally's cynical advice is so twisted that it literally hurts Asok's head, just as Wally warned, and the 'trust only the lazy' philosophy reflects Wally's own self-serving slacker worldview.
summary: A naive young intern seeks guidance from the office slacker and ends up with a headache from his upside-down view of coworkers.

file: 1998/1998-10-04_bell_improve moral_achieve goal_ring bell_yell accomplishment_bell works_alice_resisted killing boss.gif
title: Morale Bell Tempts Alice's Rage

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This bell will improve your morale.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You ring the bell whenever you achieve a goal.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then yell your accomplishment to the rest of the office

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I know it sounds corny, but the bell has worked at other companies.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does your information come from the bosses of those other companies?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No. It comes from a magazine that interviewed those bosses.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'll go first.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Clang clang

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I resisted killing my boss with a stupid bell!!

situation: The Boss introduces a morale-boosting bell that employees must ring and then shout out their accomplishments. Dilbert points out that the bell's success stories come only from other bosses, as reported by a magazine. Alice then grabs the bell, rings it, and announces her accomplishment.
punchline: Alice's 'accomplishment' is that she restrained herself from murdering her boss with the bell, showing how much the morale scheme actually irritates employees.
summary: A manager's gimmicky achievement bell backfires when an employee proudly celebrates not attacking him with it.

file: 1998/1998-04-29_declare martial law_jailing ombudsmen_personal phone calls_recommend changes_shoot emplyees_shoot employees.gif
title: Consultant Recommends Martial Law Changes

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Although your company is very profitable, I wouldn't be much of a consultant if I didn't recommend changes.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You recommend jailing our ombudsman and declaring martial law... makes sense.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Then could I shoot employees who make personal phone calls?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's okay with me.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, presents a report to the Boss, insisting he must recommend changes despite the company's profitability. His recommendations are to jail the ombudsman and declare martial law, which the Boss accepts as sensible. The Boss then asks whether he can shoot employees who make personal phone calls, and Dogbert approves.
punchline: The Boss uncritically accepts absurdly authoritarian consulting advice and eagerly escalates it to murdering employees, while the consultant cares only about justifying his own fee.
summary: A consultant with a ridiculous report convinces a gullible executive that tyranny is a sound business strategy, and the executive happily proposes executing staff.

file: 1998/1998-04-21_airport_gold stories_change seat_six hour flight.gif
title: Seatmate Eager to Share Golf Stories

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: At the airport

transcript.speaker: Golfer
transcript.text: Hey, Dilbert! We must be taking the same flight!

transcript.speaker: Golfer
transcript.text: I'll change my seat assignment so we can talk for six hours.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, no! That's okay!

transcript.speaker: Golfer
transcript.text: These flights can be very long if you don't have someone to listen to your golf stories.

situation: At the airport, an acquaintance greets Dilbert and realizes they are on the same flight. He offers to change his seat so they can talk for the whole trip, and Dilbert politely declines. The man sits next to him anyway and explains that long flights are tedious without a captive audience for his golf stories.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to politely avoid the conversation fails, and the man openly admits he wants a seatmate as a captive audience for his boring golf stories.
summary: A chatty traveler spots Dilbert at the airport and ends up seated beside him, eager to bore him with golf tales for the whole flight.

file: 1998/1998-02-24_gullible fool_sens anonymous letter_curse of dogbert_future senders_chain letters_wally flinch.gif
title: Dogbert Curses Chain Letter Senders

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've been hired to find the gullible fool who continues to send anonymous chain letters to everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I place the "Curse of Dogbert" on all past and future senders of chain letters.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I think I saw Wally flinch.

situation: Dogbert, wearing a mummy-style wrapped headdress with a crescent moon, announces he has been hired as a consultant to find whoever keeps sending anonymous chain letters. He then places a curse on all past and future senders. The Boss, seated at the table, remarks that he saw Wally flinch, implicating him as the culprit.
punchline: Wally's involuntary flinch at the mention of the curse gives away that he is the anonymous chain letter sender, and the Boss notices.
summary: A consultant dog threatens a mystical curse on chain letter senders and an unintended reaction exposes the guilty coworker.

file: 1998/1998-11-16_legalese_totally incomprehensible_legal rights_involuntary biological testing.gif
title: Signing Incomprehensible Legal Documents Without Reading

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You expect me to sign this? The legalese is totally incomprehensible.

transcript.speaker: Woman at desk
transcript.text: You will.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you expect me to give up legal rights just because it's too hard to figure out what any of it means?

transcript.speaker: Woman at desk
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Woman at desk
transcript.text: And initial the "involuntary biological testing" box.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, okay!

setting: Office desk with a computer, likely an HR or administrative office
situation: Dilbert is handed a legal document to sign and objects that the legalese is incomprehensible. The woman at the desk flatly insists he will sign it, confirms that she expects him to give up his rights, and then tells him to initial the involuntary biological testing box. Dilbert gives in and complies.
punchline: The company openly admits it expects employees to surrender their legal rights simply because the contract is too confusing to understand, and Dilbert caves immediately when the sinister clause is mentioned.
summary: A bureaucrat bluntly bulldozes a reluctant employee into signing away his rights, sneaking in a creepy testing clause he meekly accepts.

file: 1998/1998-02-07_email monitoring system_personal message_unpaid overtime_cluelessness in vicinity_manipulating emplyee.gif
title: Alice Monitors the Boss's Monitoring

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new e-mail monitoring system shows that you sent a personal message last week.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Coincidentally, the new Alice monitoring system detects twenty hours of unpaid overtime.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: According to the manual, productivity will soar now.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Beep... beep... boop... now detecting cluelessness in the vicinity.

situation: The Boss confronts Alice because the company's new e-mail monitoring system caught her sending one personal message. Alice retorts that her own monitoring system shows she worked twenty hours of unpaid overtime. The Boss misses the point and thinks productivity will soar, while Alice mockingly announces she detects cluelessness nearby.
punchline: Alice turns the surveillance back on the company by tallying her unpaid overtime, but the oblivious Boss ignores the rebuke and thinks the monitoring will boost productivity.
summary: When the boss reprimands her for one private e-mail, Alice counters with her own tally of free extra hours worked, which sails right over his head.

file: 1998/1998-07-19_goal to motivate_build global satellite netwrok_feel sdifferent_right_energetic feeling_pinned_burning couch_dizzy_budget cuts.gif
title: Impossible Goal Provides Burning Motivation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's the goal that will motivate you for the next year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "Build a global satellite network. Budget: $12,000."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Motivation feels much different from what I imagined.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was expecting a light, energetic feeling.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But it's more like being pinned under a burning couch.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Whoo! I'm getting dizzy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd better lie down until the motivation wears off.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He's going to be trouble during the next round of budget cuts.

situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a goal meant to motivate him for the year: build a global satellite network on a $12,000 budget. Dilbert describes the resulting feeling as being pinned under a burning couch rather than energized, gets dizzy, and lies down. The Boss, with his feet up on his desk, decides Dilbert will be a problem when budget cuts come.
punchline: Dilbert's honest reaction to an absurdly impossible goal is treated by the Boss as a reason to target him for layoffs, showing that management punishes candor rather than fixing unrealistic expectations.
summary: A manager assigns a ridiculous year-long objective and then marks the employee for cuts when he reacts with dismay instead of enthusiasm.

file: 1998/1998-06-15_drug treatment program_drug problem_childproof container.gif
title: Boss Demands Drug Problems For Statistics

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one in my division is using the company drug treatment program. This is very embarrassing.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My boss will think I'm not managing the drug problem. Don't ANY of you have a drug problem?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: #!*% childproof "Midol" container!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hmm...

situation: The Boss complains in a meeting that nobody in his division is using the company drug treatment program, which makes him look bad to his own boss. He asks if anyone has a drug problem, and Alice, struggling to open a childproof Midol bottle, curses loudly. The Boss thinks he may have found a candidate.
punchline: Alice's frustrated swearing at a childproof pill bottle gives the Boss a chance to misread an ordinary headache remedy as a drug problem so he can fill his treatment program quota.
summary: A manager desperate to show his program is being used hunts for an addict among his staff and zeroes in on a coworker wrestling with a pill bottle.

file: 1998/1998-08-11_launch sequence_lift off_cubicle in space_near moon.gif
title: Cubicle Rocket Heads for Moon

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Initiate launch sequence.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We have liftoff.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I keep waiting for this to seem like a bad idea.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle, which becomes a rocket flying through space
situation: Dogbert, strapped in with a seat belt on Dilbert's desk, orders the launch sequence while Dilbert types at his computer. The whole cubicle blasts off on rocket thrusters through clouds and then drifts through space toward a cratered moon. Dilbert remarks that he keeps waiting for the situation to feel like a bad idea.
punchline: Dilbert is so willing to go along with Dogbert's schemes that even flying his cubicle toward the moon hasn't made him doubt the plan, which implies he usually ignores obvious warning signs.
summary: Dogbert launches Dilbert's whole office cubicle into space, and Dilbert calmly notes he's still waiting to regret it.

file: 1998/1998-11-06_big fat guy_blob_condescending_creative director_foster innovation_new hire.gif
title: Humorless Creative Director Fears Ideas

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I'd like you to meet the humorless Blob I hired.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Blob is our new creative director. His job is to foster innovation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have some ideas.

transcript.speaker: Blob
transcript.text: Whoa, loose cannon.

situation: The Boss introduces Dilbert to Blob, a bald, stern new hire he has made creative director, whose job is to foster innovation. When Dilbert says he has some ideas, Blob recoils and calls him a loose cannon.
punchline: The person hired to encourage innovation treats an employee's offer of ideas as dangerous, showing the company's creative director is hostile to creativity.
summary: A newly hired innovation chief reacts to an engineer's willingness to share ideas as though he were a reckless threat.

file: 1998/1998-05-28_fertility drugs_coffee_tabloids_million dollars_doctor_agent_advice_medical.gif
title: Dog's Fertility Drugs Become Tabloid Story

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My dog put fertility drugs in my coffee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At first I was mad. Then the tabloids offered me a million dollars for my story.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Have you seen a doctor?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My agent advises against that.

situation: Dilbert, whose midsection has swollen dramatically, tells Wally that his dog secretly slipped fertility drugs into his coffee. He explains that tabloids have offered him a million dollars for his story. When Wally asks whether he has seen a doctor, Dilbert says his agent advises against it.
punchline: Dilbert is so focused on cashing in on his bizarre story that he ignores his own medical condition, taking business advice from his agent over basic health care.
summary: A man with a mysteriously enlarged belly shrugs off a doctor visit because a lucrative media deal matters more to him than his health.

file: 1998/1998-01-22_huge risk_entrepreneur_denail_archival_ceo_humane_bonuses.gif
title: Acquired By Archrival, Hoping For Bonuses

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd quit and become an entrepreneur, but I don't know how they handle such huge risks.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Denial, probably.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We got bought by our archrival this morning.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Their CEO says he plans to be as "humane" as possible.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He sounds nice.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Maybe we'll get bonuses!

situation: Dilbert and Wally are eating lunch when Dilbert muses about quitting to become an entrepreneur but fears the risk. Alice arrives with her tray and announces the company has just been bought by its archrival. The acquiring CEO promises to be 'humane', and Dilbert and Wally naively respond with optimism about niceness and bonuses.
punchline: Employees facing a hostile takeover and likely layoffs cling to the absurdly naive hope that a 'humane' new CEO means bonuses, just as Wally says entrepreneurs cope with risk through denial.
summary: Over lunch, the coworkers learn their firm has been swallowed by a rival and respond with wishful thinking instead of worry.

file: 1998/1998-08-16_evil hr director_post prey_vacation request form_lose vacation_exist_shadows_cubicle wall_philosophy os useless.gif
title: Catbert Philosophizes Wally Into Despair

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The evil Director of Human Resources spots his prey.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wally, you haven't filled out a vacation request form yet.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: If we don't get it by tomorrow, you lose your vacation.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Where do I get a form?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We're all out.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Did they ever exist?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wally, does anything really exist, or is it all just shadows on a cubicle wall?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I leave you with that thought.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Bonk bonk

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Who says philosophy is useless?

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells Wally he will lose his vacation unless he turns in a request form by tomorrow, then admits HR has run out of forms. Wally spirals into doubt about whether the forms ever existed, and Catbert deepens it with a philosophical question about whether anything exists. Wally ends up banging his head on his desk while Catbert gloats.
punchline: Catbert uses a bit of philosophy as a weapon, tormenting Wally into an existential crisis so severe he bangs his head on his desk.
summary: A malicious HR cat threatens an employee with losing his vacation, then drives him to despair by questioning the nature of reality.

file: 1998/1998-09-28_broken binder award_once in a lifetime award_peers_dumping trash.gif
title: Broken Binder Award Is Trash

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Asok, you're the winner of the prestigious "Broken Binder Award."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a once-in-a-lifetime award that is voted on by your peers.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How long have you been dumping your trash here?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Since my can got full.

situation: Dilbert presents Asok with a blue binder, calling it a prestigious, peer-voted once-in-a-lifetime award. Asok accepts it politely. Wally, holding a coffee mug, then asks how long Dilbert has been dumping his trash in Asok's cubicle, revealing the award was just a broken binder Dilbert was throwing away.
punchline: The so-called prestigious award is really just Dilbert disguising his garbage as an honor to offload a broken binder onto Asok.
summary: Dilbert dresses up his discarded broken binder as a prestigious honor so he can unload it on a gullible coworker.

file: 1998/1998-08-23_combined birthdays_birthdays last year_fake cake_one cake_all birthdays_sing happy birthday.gif
title: Boss Forgets Wally's Combined Birthday Party

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Happy combined birthdays.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Today we honor the employees who had birthdays within the past year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's Dilbert... Alice... Asok... Did I miss anyone?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Um... you missed me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You too? That's spooky.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd cut the cake but it's a plastic prop.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's sing. Does anyone know the words to "Happy Birthday"?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll bet those weren't the real words.

situation: The Boss holds a single combined birthday celebration for everyone who had a birthday in the past year, with a single cake. He lists the employees but overlooks Wally, then acts surprised that Wally had a birthday too. The cake turns out to be a plastic prop, and the Boss doesn't even know the words to the birthday song.
punchline: The Boss's lazy, cheap celebration shows how little he cares, and after the botched singing he stubbornly insists the real lyrics must be different rather than admit his own ignorance.
summary: A cut-rate group birthday party falls apart when the manager overlooks an employee, serves a fake cake, and can't recall the birthday song.

file: 1998/1998-12-10_complex financial model_lindbergh_inventing light bulb_boss is dumb.gif
title: Boss Misattributes Inventions to Dismiss Warning

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I created a complex financial model for our company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's see.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's dangerous if you don't understand it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's what they told Lindbergh...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But that didn't stop him from inventing the lightbulb.

situation: Dilbert hands the Boss a floppy disk containing a complex financial model he built for the company and warns that it is dangerous if not understood. The Boss brushes off the warning by comparing himself to Lindbergh, then Dilbert sarcastically notes that Lindbergh went on to invent the lightbulb, which is wrong since Lindbergh was an aviator.
punchline: The Boss's muddled historical analogy shows he ignores warnings without understanding anything, and Dilbert's deadpan 'lightbulb' remark mocks the Boss's ignorance while confirming he'll run the dangerous model anyway.
summary: A manager waves off an engineer's caution about a risky spreadsheet by invoking a famous aviator, and the engineer sarcastically goes along with the muddled comparison.

file: 1998/1998-12-13_justin_job interview_medical research_hydroelectric dam_sound of idealism dying_fabric covered boxes.gif
title: Interview Idealism Dies in Cubicles

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... Justin, tell me why you want to work here.

transcript.speaker: Justin
transcript.text: I want to find a cure for asthma!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We don't do medical research here.

transcript.speaker: Justin
transcript.text: Oh.

transcript.speaker: Justin
transcript.text: Then I want to build the biggest hydroelectric dam in the world!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We don't do that either.

transcript.speaker: Justin
transcript.text: What do you do?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We sit in fabric-covered boxes.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Shrivel crinkle ack!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That was the sound of your idealism dying.

transcript.speaker: Justin
transcript.text: Show me to my box.

setting: Dilbert's office during a job interview
situation: Dilbert interviews a young job candidate named Justin, who eagerly says he wants to cure asthma and then build the world's biggest hydroelectric dam. Dilbert tells him the company does neither and that employees just sit in fabric-covered boxes. Justin's hopeful attitude visibly collapses and he resigns himself to the job.
punchline: The candidate's lofty ambitions are crushed by the reality that the job is just sitting in a cubicle, and he accepts it anyway, showing how workplaces drain idealism.
summary: A starry-eyed applicant's grand dreams shrivel the moment he learns the job consists of sitting in a cubicle, and he gives in immediately.

file: 1998/1998-01-18_bill for freindship_giving freeliy_trust_sharing_face of deadbeat_reaching.gif
title: Dogbert Bills Dilbert for Friendship

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Here's my bill.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's for all the time we've spent together when I didn't enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If it wasn't fun, it must have been work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert, let me explain what friendship is all about.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Friendship is about giving freely of oneself. It's about trust and sharing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now, I expect you'll want this back.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I need to round it up to the next hour.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No checks. You have the face of a deadbeat.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't think I'm reaching you.

situation: Dogbert presents Dilbert with a bill for all the time they spent together that he didn't enjoy, reasoning that anything not fun counts as work. Dilbert delivers a heartfelt lecture on friendship, then hands the bill back, and Dogbert simply agrees and rounds the charge up to the next hour and refuses to accept a check.
punchline: Dogbert is immune to any appeal to friendship and responds to a sincere speech about trust and sharing by padding the invoice and insulting Dilbert's creditworthiness.
summary: A self-serving dog invoices his human companion for the less enjoyable hours of their friendship and brushes off a sincere lecture by inflating the charge.

file: 1998/1998-05-24_new customer_top 5 compnaies_low price_high margins.gif
title: Selling to a Clueless Customer

transcript.speaker: Salesman's Boss
transcript.text: I'd like you to meet our newest customer.

transcript.speaker: Salesman's Boss
transcript.text: You won't be sorry; we're one of the top five companies in this field.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I thought you said no one else makes this kind of product.

transcript.speaker: Salesman's Boss
transcript.text: No one else makes one with so few features.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: So... your strategy is low price, right?

transcript.speaker: Salesman's Boss
transcript.text: No, high margins!

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: You!

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I'd better ask someone what a "margin" is.

situation: A sales manager brings a salesman to meet the pointy-haired customer and pitches the company's product. The pitch unravels as the manager admits it has few features and is expensive, so the salesman is left looking bewildered. The salesman gets grabbed and shaken while the customer, who is the boss, ends up putting his feet on the desk and admitting he doesn't understand the basic business terms.
punchline: The clueless buyer is about to purchase an overpriced, feature-poor product and then admits he doesn't even know what a profit margin is, showing how uninformed purchasing decisions get made.
summary: A seller's pitch for a bare-bones, pricey product falls apart, but the ignorant buyer is too confused about business basics to notice.

file: 1998/1998-07-11_stellar week_accomplishments_data bits_disaster recovery_back up facility_copy a file_diskette_resume.gif
title: Resume Backup Counts as Accomplishment

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I'm pleased to report another stellar week of accomplishments!

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I moved more than 800,000 bits of data to a disaster recovery back-up facility!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you just take credit for copying a file to a diskette?

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: It was my résumé.

setting: Conference room during a team status meeting
situation: At a status meeting, a bald coworker proudly reports a stellar week, claiming he moved over 800,000 bits of data to a disaster recovery back-up facility. Dilbert sees through the inflated wording and asks if he just took credit for copying a file to a diskette. The coworker admits the file was his résumé.
punchline: The coworker's grand-sounding accomplishment was just saving his own résumé to a floppy disk, implying he is preparing to leave the company.
summary: A colleague dresses up the trivial act of saving a file to a floppy as a major data-protection achievement, then reveals it was his job-hunting document.

file: 1998/1998-07-06_eliminate privacy_dignity_share hotel rooms_business trips_tandem showering policy.gif
title: Catbert's Escalating Privacy Elimination Policies

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: "Consistent with our effort to eliminate privacy and dignity..."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: "...Employees must share hotel rooms on all business trips."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: After they get used to this, I'll introduce the tandem showering policy.

setting: Office, Catbert's H.R. desk and Dilbert's cubicle
situation: Catbert, as H.R. Director, types a memo announcing a policy meant to eliminate employee privacy and dignity, requiring employees to share hotel rooms on business trips. Dilbert reads the memo at his computer. Catbert then privately thinks about following up with an even worse policy once staff have adjusted.
punchline: Catbert is deliberately easing employees into worse and worse indignities, planning to make people share showers once they accept sharing hotel rooms.
summary: An evil H.R. cat rolls out a humiliating travel rule while secretly planning an even more invasive one as the follow-up.

file: 1998/1998-11-29_mandatory class_windows_training_teacher doesn't know_no computers_uses box_teeth as keyboard.gif
title: Clueless Trainer Teaches Windows NT

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Welcome to the mandatory Windows NT class.

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Personally, I've only been using a computer for... how long? Anyone?

transcript.speaker: Whiteboard
transcript.text: 2 weeks

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: But a good trainer can teach any subject.

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Okay, everyone stand up and stretch!

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: Or sit there and glare at me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's good too.

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: I forgot to reserve the room with the computers, so I'll use this box.

transcript.speaker: Trainer
transcript.text: ...And let's say this eraser is the moose.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I left when he told us to use our teeth as a keyboard.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ooh-yah.

setting: A corporate training room, then Dilbert's living room
situation: A trainer leads a mandatory Windows NT class despite having used a computer for only two weeks. He has no computers for the class, so he demonstrates with a cardboard box and an eraser as a mouse. Dilbert ends up at home, having walked out when told to type with his teeth.
punchline: The trainer is so unqualified and unprepared that the training is absurd, and Dilbert's boredom turns to leaving the class entirely.
summary: A newbie instructor tries to teach computer skills using a cardboard box and an eraser, driving Dilbert out of the session.

file: 1998/1998-04-25_cubicle_returned from trip_boss says hi.gif
title: Cubicle Womb Interrupted by Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ahh ... sweet cubicle, I have returned from my trip.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's just like being in a womb.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just wanted to poke my head in and say hi.

situation: Dilbert returns from a business trip carrying a briefcase and happily settles into his cubicle. He thinks to himself that the enclosed space feels like a womb. His boss then peeks his head around the cubicle wall to say hi, interrupting the cozy moment.
punchline: Dilbert compares his cubicle to a womb, and the boss immediately pokes his head in, which makes the womb comparison uncomfortably literal.
summary: A traveler glad to be back in his cozy cubicle compares it to a womb just as his manager's head appears around the partition.

file: 1998/1998-09-25_ratbert_rat_says whats on mind_silent_quiet_nothing_eye opener_surprised himself.gif
title: Dilbert's Blunt Honesty Experiment Fails

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've decided to be one of those guys who says whatever is on his mind.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Still nothing?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Boy, this is a real eye-opener.

situation: Dilbert, getting dressed in his bedroom, announces that he will start saying whatever is on his mind. Ratbert sits on the bed while the second panel shows the empty room. When Dilbert returns with his briefcase and asks 'Still nothing?', Ratbert admits the quiet has been a real eye-opener.
punchline: Ratbert's remark reveals that Dilbert's mind is empty, so the plan to speak his mind leaves him with nothing to say at all.
summary: A man vows to speak every thought aloud, only to produce complete silence all day, which his pet finds revealing.

file: 1998/1998-01-13_psychic ability_flip coin_called_edge_coincidence_coin toss_ratbert.gif
title: Ratbert Calls Edge Every Time

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I will debunk your ludicrous claim of psychic ability with one hundred flips of this coin.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Call it.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Edge.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That is just a coincidence.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I call edge for the next 99 too.

situation: Dilbert sets out to disprove Ratbert's claim of psychic ability by flipping a coin a hundred times and having him call each result. Ratbert calls 'edge' on the first flip, and the coin lands standing on its edge. When Dilbert dismisses it as coincidence, Ratbert announces he will call edge for the remaining 99 flips too.
punchline: Ratbert's absurdly improbable prediction of the coin landing on its edge comes true, and his promise to repeat it 99 more times shows he is confident in his psychic power, making Dilbert's skepticism look foolish.
summary: A skeptical engineer's coin-flip test of a small pet's psychic powers backfires when the coin lands on its edge exactly as predicted.

file: 1998/1998-01-11_bred_work in cubicle_personal life_stealing_good square meal_square head.gif
title: Square-Headed Employee Bred For Cubicles

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, this is Rex Tangle, our newest employee.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Rex was specially bred to work in a cubicle.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He looks like he'll fit right in.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ask him about his personal life.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Rex, how's your personal life going?

transcript.speaker: Rex
transcript.text: I don't have one. That would be like stealing from the company.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you eat lunch?

transcript.speaker: Rex
transcript.text: I would enjoy a good square meal.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Meet the future.

transcript.speaker: Rex
transcript.text: Hello, you round pegs!

situation: The Boss introduces Wally to Rex Tangle, a new employee with a perfectly square head who was supposedly bred to work in a cubicle. Rex says he has no personal life because that would be stealing from the company, and later says he'd like a good square meal. At lunch Wally introduces him to Dilbert and Alice as the future, and Rex greets them as round pegs.
punchline: The new hire is the ideal corporate drone, literally a square peg who fits the box-like cubicle, and he mocks the ordinary round-peg employees as obsolete because he gives the company his entire life.
summary: A manager proudly presents a boxy-headed new hire engineered for cubicle life, who devotes himself so completely to work that he looks down on his coworkers.

file: 1998/1998-01-30_quit_work from home_human contact_testing email_miss humans.gif
title: Missing Human Contact, Same as Now

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I should quit and work for myself from home.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I would miss all the human contact.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Same as now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm testing my e-mail. Did you get the "E" I sent?

situation: Dilbert walks through the office thinking about quitting to work for himself from home, but worries he would miss human contact. He then realizes his current job offers no more human contact than working at home would. The Boss walks up and asks whether Dilbert received the single letter 'E' he emailed while testing his email.
punchline: Dilbert's only workplace human contact is with a clueless boss who communicates through absurd email tests, so working from home would cost him nothing.
summary: Dilbert muses that home-based self-employment would be lonely, then concludes the office is just as isolating, as his boss interrupts with a nonsensical email query.

file: 1998/1998-06-21_fast email_boss confused_priorities_program compiling_weasel_dilbert_ignore email_winning argument important.gif
title: Boss Punishes Dilbert's Fast Email Replies

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What the...?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You respond too quickly to my e-mail.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Obviously you aren't focusing on priorities.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I do e-mail while my program is compiling.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can't weasel out of this with your technical mumbo jumbo.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You win. I'll ignore your e-mail from now on.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The important thing is that I win.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wonder if my programs ever compile.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and the Boss's office
situation: The Boss is startled at his computer by how quickly Dilbert answered his e-mail, then accuses Dilbert of ignoring priorities. Dilbert explains he reads e-mail while his program compiles, but the Boss dismisses this as technical jargon. Dilbert concedes and promises to ignore the Boss's e-mail, and the Boss only cares that he won the argument.
punchline: The Boss cares only about winning the argument, not about getting what he wants, and he ends up with a worse outcome (ignored e-mail) while idly wondering whether his own programs ever compile.
summary: A manager scolds an employee for answering messages too promptly, wins the dispute by default, and gets exactly the unresponsiveness he provoked.

file: 1998/1998-11-24_magnets_big impact_erased hard drive_feeling healthy_boss with magnets_joints.gif
title: Boss's Magnets Erase Wally's Hard Drive

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm feeling much healthier since I strapped all of these magnets to my body.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's fascinating. You should show them to Wally. It would have a big impact on him.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You erased my #%!!* hard drive!!

situation: The Boss proudly tells Dilbert he feels healthier since strapping magnets to his body. Dilbert, wanting revenge on Wally, suggests the Boss go show them to Wally, and the Boss agrees. In the last panel an off-panel Wally angrily shouts that his hard drive has been erased.
punchline: Dilbert deliberately sends the magnet-covered Boss to Wally's computer, knowing the magnets will wipe his hard drive, and the 'big impact' he promised is data loss.
summary: Dilbert tricks his magnet-wearing boss into visiting a coworker, and the resulting damage to that coworker's computer is heard from offstage.

file: 1998/1998-08-04_vendor_vast tagalongs_prodcut_didn't bring guy.gif
title: Vendor Brings Clueless Tag-Alongs

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Meeting with a vendor

transcript.speaker: Larry
transcript.text: I'm Larry.

transcript.speaker: Larry
transcript.text: And these people are my vast array of unnecessary tag-alongs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What does your product do?

transcript.speaker: Larry
transcript.text: We didn't bring the guy who knows that.

setting: Conference room during a vendor sales meeting
situation: Dilbert meets a vendor named Larry, who introduces the group of people he brought as his unnecessary tag-alongs. When Dilbert asks what the vendor's product actually does, Larry admits they left behind the one person who knows the answer.
punchline: The vendor's entourage is large but useless, because nobody present understands the product they are trying to sell.
summary: A salesman arrives with a crowd of colleagues yet no one who can explain what his company's product does.

file: 1998/1998-03-26_rag man_project luser_budget cuts_beg for resources_pencil shavings_coffee.gif
title: Rag Man Begs for Pencil Shavings

transcript.speaker: Rag Man
transcript.text: I'm the rag man from Project Luser.

transcript.speaker: Rag Man
transcript.text: Budget cuts have hit our project hard. I'm forced to beg for resources.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can spare some pencil shavings.

transcript.speaker: Rag Man
transcript.text: Excellent! We make coffee out of that.

situation: A ragged, tattered man wearing a blue headband arrives at Dilbert's desk and introduces himself as a beggar from another project, Project Luser. He explains that budget cuts have forced him to beg for resources. Dilbert offers pencil shavings, and the rag man happily accepts, saying his team makes coffee out of them.
punchline: Budget cuts have left the project so destitute that its team is grateful for pencil shavings, which they turn into coffee, exaggerating how severe resource starvation can be.
summary: A tattered beggar from a budget-starved project asks Dilbert for supplies and cheerfully accepts scraps that his team brews into coffee.

file: 1998/1998-08-05_catbert_evil hr director_grossly underpaid_type of work_current duities_compensation review_true story_not qualified_subordinate is qualified.gif
title: Pay Review Exposes Unqualified Employee

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I'm grossly underpaid for the type of work I do now.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Write a description of your current duties. I'll be happy to do a compensation review.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Based on a true story

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Sadly, it appears you're not qualified for your own job. But one of your subordinates is.

situation: An employee complains to Catbert, the evil H.R. director, that they are grossly underpaid for their work. Catbert offers a compensation review and asks for a written description of the employee's duties. After reviewing it, Catbert announces the employee is not qualified for their own job, but one of their subordinates is.
punchline: Asking H.R. for a raise backfires when the job review reveals the employee is unqualified and a subordinate would be better suited to the position.
summary: A worker seeking a raise from the devious H.R. cat ends up with a job analysis that puts their own position in jeopardy.

file: 1998/1998-04-26_research dept_study_value of research_just lie_no research_industry salaries_two oclock_quitting time_role model.gif
title: Research Department Decides to Lie

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our special guest is Tod, from our research department.

transcript.speaker: Tod
transcript.text: We recently did a study to assess the value of our previous research.

transcript.speaker: Tod
transcript.text: Sadly, all of our past work was either ignored or totally misinterpreted by idiots...

transcript.speaker: Tod
transcript.text: ... such as yourselves.

transcript.speaker: Tod
transcript.text: So from now on, rather than do research, we'll just lie.

transcript.speaker: Tod
transcript.text: Play along and we'll make sure the "industry salaries" study goes your way.

transcript.speaker: Tod
transcript.text: Well, it's two o'clock, and that's quitting time in the research department.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You're not my role model anymore... I've found another.

situation: Tod from the research department tells the assembled managers and staff that their past research was ignored or misinterpreted by idiots like them. He announces that research will be replaced by lying, offers to rig the industry salaries study in their favor, then declares it quitting time at two o'clock. Wally, who has always idolized slacking, says Tod has displaced him as his role model.
punchline: Tod outdoes even Wally in laziness and cynicism, since admitting that research is pointless and leaving at two o'clock makes him Wally's new role model.
summary: A researcher insults his audience, promises to fabricate findings in exchange for cooperation, and knocks off early, earning the admiration of the office's laziest employee.

file: 1998/1998-05-23_catbert_evil hr director_eyes_computer_sore_typing with fingers_restful on eyes_use as bed_alice_technology.gif
title: Catbert Dismisses Employee's Sore Eyes

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: My eyes are sore from using the computer.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Try typing with your fingers, the way everyone else does.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Personally, I find computers very restful on my eyes.

situation: An employee with big brown hair tells Catbert, the evil H.R. director, that her eyes are sore from using the computer.
