Catbert sarcastically suggests she type with her fingers like everyone else. In the last panel, his thought bubble shows him lounging on top of a computer monitor, napping on it.
punchline: Catbert gives a useless, insulting answer to a health complaint, then reveals he finds computers restful because he uses one as a bed.
summary: A worker's eyestrain complaint is brushed off by a smug H.R. cat who secretly treats a computer as his personal cushion.

file: 1998/1998-10-18_delegate tasks_cash flow estimate_urgent_boss must wait_dilbert_assignment request_wait a few days.gif
title: Boss Asks, Dilbert Stalls Him

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's time to delegate.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I want you to give me a new cash flow estimate for your project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, fine.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When will I get it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When do you need it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: As soon as possible!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And when do you think that will be?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I usually wait a few days to see if you change your mind.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then I'll give you last year's cash flow as a test to see if you read it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The more experience they get, the worse they are.

situation: The Boss decides to delegate and asks Dilbert for a new cash flow estimate for his project. When the Boss tries to pin down a deadline, Dilbert turns the questions back on him. Dilbert then reveals his routine of waiting for the Boss to change his mind and handing over last year's numbers to test whether anyone reads the report.
punchline: Dilbert has learned to game his boss's whims, so the Boss concludes that experienced employees get worse, when really they are just getting better at coping with him.
summary: An employee who has seen it all explains how he manages a fickle manager's requests with delay tactics and a recycled report.

file: 1998/1998-11-08_wally and boss_no actual work_excellent reviews_make job helll_moved cucbicle_bathroom stall_cubicle with door_calls mother.gif
title: Wally Outlasts Boss's Hellish Plan

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, you haven't done any actual work for years, yet we continue to pay you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Have I said thanks?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd fire you, but your performance reviews are all "excellents."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, my plan is to make your job a living hell until you quit.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You'll never win! My standards are lower than you can imagine!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll start by moving you to a smaller cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is that the best you got? Ha ha ha!!!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Mom, guess who got an office with a door!

setting: Boss's office, then a restroom with toilet stalls
situation: The Boss complains that Wally hasn't done real work in years but can't fire him because his performance reviews are all excellent. He announces a plan to make Wally's job miserable until he quits, starting with a smaller cubicle. Wally gleefully taunts him, then phones his mother from a bathroom stall, delighted with his new 'office'.
punchline: The Boss's punishment of moving Wally to a smaller workspace backfires because Wally's standards are so low that a toilet stall with a door counts as a promotion.
summary: A manager tries to drive a lazy employee to resign by downgrading his workspace, only to see him cheerfully accept a restroom stall as a private office.

file: 1998/1998-04-09_new computer_dispose of old computer_engineering solution.gif
title: Catapult Solves Computer Disposal Problem

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm not allowed to get a new computer until I get rid of this old one.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The janitor won't allow it in the trash; union rules won't let me carry it to storage. So I built this catapult.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Like I always say, every problem has an engineering solution.

situation: Wally explains to Dilbert that he can't get a new computer until he disposes of his old one. The janitor won't take it as trash and union rules prevent Wally from carrying it to storage, so he built a catapult. In the last panel the catapult swings up over the cubicle wall while Dilbert comments that every problem has an engineering solution.
punchline: Rather than follow the rules he can't satisfy, Wally engineers a catapult to fling the old computer away, a ridiculous but technically rule-compliant workaround that Dilbert cheerfully endorses.
summary: Stuck between a janitor's refusal and union rules, a coworker builds a catapult to launch his obsolete computer out of the way.

file: 1998/1998-07-29_momentum alighns_value added distribution_babble_points_meeting_alice_business.gif
title: Babbling to Fill the Meeting

transcript.speaker: Woman (Carol-style coworker)
transcript.text: Blah blah.

transcript.speaker: Man with slicked hair (thought)
transcript.text: I haven't talked yet, but all the good points have been taken.

transcript.speaker: Balding coworker
transcript.text: Blah blah.

transcript.speaker: Man with slicked hair
transcript.text: We must make sure our momentum aligns with our value-added distribution!

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: That was just babble, right?

transcript.speaker: Man with slicked hair
transcript.text: All the good ones were taken.

situation: At a meeting, coworkers talk in turn while one man silently worries that all the good points have already been made. When his turn comes he blurts out an impressive-sounding but meaningless sentence about momentum and value-added distribution. A colleague asks if that was just babble, and he admits the good points were all used up.
punchline: When people feel pressured to contribute in meetings, they fall back on empty buzzword babble because the meaningful things have already been said.
summary: A man with nothing left to say fills his turn in a meeting with meaningless jargon and cheerfully admits it.
keywords: talking for the sake of talking

file: 1998/1998-03-19_user manual_typo_technical calls_phone sex place_complaints are down_customers.gif
title: Manual Typo Sends Support Calls Astray

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our user manual has a typo. Our technical support calls are going to a phone sex place.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Complaints are way down.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Well, okay, but... has that ever worked?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Customer's house

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: No complaints yet.

setting: Office cubicle area, then a customer's house
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that a typo in the user manual is sending customers' technical support calls to a phone sex line. The Boss only notices that complaints have dropped sharply. Meanwhile a customer at home, on the phone beside his computer, has apparently been misdirected and is oddly unbothered, commenting that no complaints have been made yet.
punchline: The Boss treats a embarrassing error as a success because the complaint numbers fell, while the misdirected customers are evidently getting something other than tech support and aren't complaining.
summary: A printing mistake reroutes help-desk callers to an adult hotline, and management is thrilled that grievances have dried up.

file: 1998/1998-05-06_marketing dept_brochures_new prodcut_dominate market_sales_don't make product_business.gif
title: Marketing Sells Product Nobody Makes

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: The marketing department saves the day! Check out these brochures I made.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: This new product will allow us to dominate the market!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But we don't make this product.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: That hasn't hurt our sales so far.

situation: A marketing employee hands out brochures he made and boasts that a new product will let the company dominate the market. Dilbert reads the brochure and points out that the company doesn't actually make this product. The marketer replies that this hasn't hurt sales so far.
punchline: Marketing is so detached from reality that selling a product the company doesn't make is treated as no obstacle to success.
summary: A marketer proudly promotes a brochure-only product that doesn't exist, unbothered because sales have been fine anyway.

file: 1998/1998-07-14_boss's son_pickle juice_pickles_big probelm_household_taught everything.gif
title: Dad's Pickle Juice Wisdom

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My dad taught me everything I know.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He used to say "Don't drink the pickle juice until the pickles are gone."

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Was that a big problem at your house?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Have you ever been hit in the eye with a pickle?

situation: At a meeting table, the Pointy-Haired Boss proudly says his father taught him everything he knows and shares his dad's pickle juice advice. A bald coworker asks if that was a common problem at his house. The Boss responds with an oddly specific question about being hit in the eye with a pickle.
punchline: The Boss's absurd answer implies that his father's trivial-sounding advice was prompted by a bizarre pickle-in-the-eye incident, showing how silly the source of his 'wisdom' is.
summary: A manager shares a nonsensical piece of fatherly advice about pickles and unwittingly hints at a messy childhood mishap.

file: 1998/1998-01-14_coins flipped_pstchic_cincidences_seven rotations_inexplicable hovering_hen noises.gif
title: Psychic Dog Calls Impossible Coin Flip

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just because you guessed a hundred coin flips in a row doesn't mean you're psychic. Coincidences do happen.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I call seven rotations followed by inexplicable hovering and hen noises.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That is luck... luck, luck, luck, luck, luck!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are we done now?

setting: Dilbert's home or office, at a table
situation: Dilbert insists that Dogbert correctly guessing a hundred coin flips in a row is just coincidence. Dogbert then predicts an absurdly specific outcome for the next flip, including seven rotations, hovering and hen noises. The coin does exactly that, and Dilbert can only repeat the word luck while Dogbert asks if they're finished.
punchline: Dogbert's wildly specific and physically impossible prediction comes true, making Dilbert's insistence on coincidence absurd, and his frantic repetition of 'luck' shows he is in denial.
summary: After dismissing a long winning streak as chance, a man watches his dog predict and receive a bizarre, impossible coin toss, leaving his skeptical stance in tatters.

file: 1998/1998-10-10_dogbert_dilbert_snoring_bed_use both nostrils_enjoy yelling.gif
title: Dogbert Yells at Snoring Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can no longer hold this inside.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You call that breathing??! Get the other nostril involved!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I wonder if he'll ever realize that I just enjoy yelling.

situation: Dilbert is asleep in bed while Dogbert stands on the covers, then shouts at him about how he is breathing. Afterward, Dogbert walks away from the bedroom and privately thinks that he simply enjoys yelling.
punchline: Dogbert's supposed concern about Dilbert's breathing is just a pretext, since he secretly yells at people because he enjoys it.
summary: A dog berates his sleeping owner over his nasal technique, then confesses to himself that shouting is the real reward.

file: 1998/1998-06-27_dogbert the ceo_incestment banker_loot place_merge with client_golden parachute_exercise stock options_merger_so long suckers.gif
title: Investment Banker Helps Loot Company

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the C.E.O.

transcript.speaker: Investment Banker
transcript.text: I'm an investment banker. I can help you loot this place and escape.

transcript.speaker: Investment Banker
transcript.text: You'll merge with my other client company. Your golden parachute kicks in. Then you exercise your stock options on the uptick.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You rarely see a merger announcement with the phrase, "So long, suckers."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ouch.

setting: CEO's office, then a conference room where a merger announcement is read
situation: Dogbert is the CEO, and an investment banker visits to offer a plan for helping him loot the company and escape. The plan is to merge with another of the banker's clients, trigger Dogbert's golden parachute, and cash in stock options as the price rises. Later, Alice and Dilbert read the merger announcement, and Alice notes that these announcements rarely say what is really going on.
punchline: The merger is really a scheme for executives to enrich themselves at everyone else's expense, and the only thing missing from the announcement is an honest admission of it.
summary: A banker lays out a merger scheme that lets a chief executive pocket a fortune and bail out, while the employees reading the announcement notice nothing admits the real motive.

file: 1998/1998-08-24_dogbert_con people_insult people_consult_expensive_demeaning.gif
title: Dogbert Discovers Con Plus Insult Equals Consult

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I like to con people. And I like to insult people.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you combine con and insult, you get "consult."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm here to consult you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It sounds expensive and demeaning. ... Okay.

setting: A grassy hill with a rock, then the Boss's office
situation: Dogbert lounges on a rock in a field, musing that he enjoys both conning and insulting people, and realizes that combining the two words gives 'consult.' He then shows up in the Boss's office and announces he's there to consult him. The Boss, despite recognizing it will be expensive and demeaning, agrees anyway.
punchline: The joke treats consulting as a scam of conning and insulting clients, and the Boss's willing acceptance shows managers will pay for it even when they know it's a rip-off.
summary: Dogbert coins a cynical wordplay definition of consulting as cheating plus insulting, and a clueless manager hires him regardless.

file: 1998/1998-01-05_walk at lunch_bomb threat_hoax_yesterday_low morale_lottery ticket_potential irony.gif
title: Bomb Threat and Lottery Irony

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you go for a walk at lunch?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not exactly.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I got a bomb threat. I didn't tell anyone else, just in case it was a hoax.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It was only yesterday that I was saying my morale couldn't be lower.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I bought a lottery ticket to increase the potential irony.

setting: Office, in Dilbert's cubicle and the boss's office
situation: Dilbert asks the boss if he took a walk at lunch, and the boss reveals he received a bomb threat but told no one in case it was a hoax. He then explains that after claiming yesterday his morale couldn't be lower, he bought a lottery ticket to set up a more ironic outcome.
punchline: The boss, apparently expecting disaster, treats a bomb threat as a private matter and buys a lottery ticket purely to heighten the irony of a possible tragic death just after winning.
summary: A boss quietly sits on a bomb threat and then hedges his bad luck by purchasing a lottery ticket for dramatic effect.

file: 1998/1998-09-21_under arrest_stealing  boxes_recycling goals_reuse_recycle_cell_locked up_cubicle.gif
title: Arrested for Reusing Cardboard Boxes

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You're under arrest for stealing empty cardboard boxes!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The company needs those boxes to meet its recycling goals.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: But reuse is better than recycling.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: There's got to be a way out of this cell.

situation: Catbert, acting as a company enforcer, arrests a bald, bespectacled employee who is carrying an empty cardboard box. The employee argues that reusing boxes is environmentally better than recycling them, but Catbert insists the company needs the boxes to hit its recycling targets. In the last panel the employee is locked in a cubicle-wall cell while Catbert walks away.
punchline: The company punishes an employee for the genuinely greener act of reuse because it threatens a recycling metric, showing that hitting the numbers matters more than the actual environmental goal.
summary: A cat-themed corporate enforcer jails a worker whose sensible box reuse spoils the firm's recycling statistics.

file: 1998/1998-01-23_flu_germs_fly through air_sneezed_tissue_sick_ill_contagious_office illness_medical.gif
title: Germs Don't Fly, Except Yours

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't worry about my flu, Alice. Germs don't fly through the air.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: AACHOOO!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remember, germs don't fly through the air.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yours are gonna.

situation: A sick boss sits across from Alice and assures her that his flu is nothing to worry about because germs don't travel through the air. He then sneezes loudly in her direction, blowing her hair back, and repeats his claim. Alice, her hair streaming behind her, retorts that his germs will fly.
punchline: The boss's claim that germs can't travel through the air is disproved at once by his own sneeze, and Alice sarcastically points out that his germs are going to reach her anyway.
summary: A flu-ridden manager insists his illness is harmless to his coworker, then sneezes straight at her with hurricane force.

file: 1998/1998-10-07_time to work_two assignments_essential business_boss solution_impossible_doesn't understand.gif
title: Combine Both Assignments Into One

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have time to do ONE of these two assignments.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One is essential to the business. The other is not. Which ONE do you want me to do?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Both!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I know you WANT both. But if you can only GET one...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Combine them and just do the one.

situation: Dilbert holds up two assignments and tells the Boss he only has time to complete one of them, asking him to choose the essential one. The Boss demands both, and when Dilbert patiently explains that he can only get one, the Boss simply tells him to merge the two assignments into a single task.
punchline: The Boss tries to solve a resource shortage by redefining two jobs as one, ignoring the fact that the total amount of work is unchanged.
summary: Asked to prioritize between two tasks, the Boss refuses to choose and decrees that merging them magically makes the workload fit.

file: 1998/1998-05-13_catbert_hr director_dumped work_moan_scream_staffing levels.gif
title: Catbert Gauges Staffing by Screams

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: When you dumped more work on Wally, did he moan? Or did he scream?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It sounded like this ... Aaoo-muw aahh-ow-ow!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The staffing levels sound about right.

setting: Catbert's H.R. office, with the Boss reclining in a chair
situation: Catbert, the H.R. director, asks the Boss how Wally reacted when given even more work. The Boss imitates Wally's pained cries. Catbert privately concludes from the sound that staffing levels are appropriate.
punchline: Catbert treats the sound of an overworked employee's suffering as proof that staffing is adequate, rather than a sign of understaffing.
summary: An H.R. director judges whether a department has enough staff by how loudly an overloaded worker cries out.

file: 1998/1998-06-10_cubicle roof_skilled worker_low unemployement_roofer_pinged nail_wally_poindexter.gif
title: Roofer Demands Lemonade From Wally

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your cubicle roof is looking good.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Yep.

transcript.speaker: Roofer
transcript.text: I love being a skilled worker in a period of low unemployment. I can get anything I demand.

transcript.speaker: Roofer
transcript.text: Hey, Poindexter, fetch me a lemonade.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Poink

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ouch

setting: Office cubicle area, where a roofer is building a roof on Wally's cubicle
situation: Dilbert and Wally admire the new roof being built on Wally's cubicle while the roofer hammers away on top. The roofer brags that low unemployment lets skilled workers demand anything. He then orders Wally to fetch him a lemonade and drops a nail that pings off Wally's head.
punchline: The roofer, empowered by a tight job market, treats the cubicle's owner like a servant and literally drops nails on him, a reversal of the usual employer-employee power dynamic.
summary: A tradesman building a roof over a cubicle uses his scarce skills as leverage to boss around and accidentally injure the employee below.

file: 1998/1998-05-15_flu darts_stockholders_benefit of stockholders_not employees_401k stock_not real_boss says not real.gif
title: Flu Darts and Imaginary Stock

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one likes being hunted down and shot with flu darts, Wally.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But remember: companies are managed for the benefit of stockholders, not employees.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I own stock. It's in my 401(k) account.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm not supposed to tell you, but none of that is real.

situation: The Boss sits behind his desk and tells Wally that nobody enjoys being hunted down and shot with flu darts, then reminds him that companies exist for stockholders, not employees. Wally objects that he is a stockholder through his 401(k). The Boss confides that his retirement stock isn't real.
punchline: Wally's only claim to being a stockholder, his 401(k), is revealed to be worthless, so he gets none of the benefits the company supposedly exists to provide.
summary: A boss defends putting shareholders first, only to casually admit that the employee's retirement holdings are fictional.

file: 1998/1998-07-02_dogcarts tech support_abuse_slow internet_records_porn_caused by porn.gif
title: Tech Support Blames Your Browsing

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How may I abuse you?

transcript.speaker: Caller
transcript.text: The Internet is slow. What causes that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That can only be caused by you looking at porn.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll need your name for our records.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Click

setting: Dogbert's tech support call center desk
situation: Dogbert answers a tech support line with an openly abusive greeting. A caller asks why the Internet is slow, and Dogbert flatly accuses him of looking at porn. Dogbert then asks for the caller's name for 'our records', and the caller hangs up.
punchline: Dogbert blames the user's browsing habits for a slow connection and then asks for a name to keep on record, so the caller hangs up out of embarrassment and fear of being reported.
summary: A tech support dog meets a complaint about sluggish web speeds with an accusation of illicit browsing and a demand for the caller's identity.

file: 1998/1998-10-12_elbonia_class in cobol_learn on plane_scuba lessons.gif
title: Teaching COBOL in Elbonia, Unprepared

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm sending you to Elbonia to teach a class in COBOL.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know COBOL.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you can learn it on the plane.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I'll take some scuba lessons up there too.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm making my getaway.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is being sent to Elbonia to teach a COBOL class, even though Dilbert admits he does not know COBOL. The Boss suggests he learn it on the flight, and Dilbert sarcastically replies that he might also take scuba lessons there. The Boss, in a thought bubble, slips away quickly while Dilbert glares over the cubicle wall.
punchline: Dilbert mocks the Boss's absurd expectation by proposing equally unrealistic goals, such as scuba diving lessons in a landlocked place, while the Boss only cares about escaping the conversation.
summary: A manager assigns an employee to teach a programming language he has never learned and brushes off the objection with a ridiculous suggestion.

file: 1998/1998-12-01_boss in hospital_no brain function_still talking_double length meetings_accomplish twice as much.gif
title: Brain-Dead Boss Doubles Meeting Length

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: The accident left him with no brain function whatsoever.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: But that hasn't stopped him from talking.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll drive him back to work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I double the length of our staff meetings, we'll accomplish twice as much!

setting: Hospital room, then inside a car
situation: A doctor tells Dilbert that the Boss's accident has left him with no brain function, though he can still talk. Dilbert offers to drive him back to work. In the car, the Boss cheerfully announces his plan to double the length of staff meetings to get twice as much done.
punchline: The Boss's flawed logic is unchanged by being brain-dead, which implies he was already operating with no brain function and that his management ideas, like longer meetings equalling more productivity, are mindless.
summary: After a medical exam finds the Boss has no brain activity yet can still talk, he carries on with business as usual, spouting nonsense management theory.

file: 1998/1998-05-22_agrees with everything_boss_complimentary_meeting_not authentic_sidekick_sycophant_yes man_business.gif
title: Yes Man Flatters Boss's Plan

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's my plan. What does everyone think?

transcript.speaker: Yes Man
transcript.text: Brilliant!

transcript.speaker: Yes Man
transcript.text: That is the best plan ever made!! Wow! Ooh-wah! You da man!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's the type of honest feedback we need.

transcript.speaker: Yes Man
transcript.text: I love it when you exhale in my direction.

situation: The Boss presents his plan to the people seated around the conference table and asks for opinions. A sycophantic coworker gushes with over-the-top praise, calling it the best plan ever made. The Boss then declares this is the honest feedback the company needs, and the toady responds with even more fawning flattery.
punchline: The Boss mistakes obvious, grovelling flattery for honest feedback, and the yes man's final line shows he will say anything to please him.
summary: A boss asks for opinions on his plan and a gushing toady's absurd praise is hailed as the candid input he wants.

file: 1998/1998-10-24_dogbert the consultant_brain wash customoers_long term goal_train customers_mail money_advertsiements_send them product.gif
title: Brainwashing Customers Into Mailing Money

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You must brainwash your customers to prefer your brand for no reason.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The long-term goal is to train your customers to mail you money every time they see your advertisements.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would we send them our product?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hello-o-o, brain stem.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, advises the Boss to brainwash customers into preferring his brand for no reason. He explains the end goal is for customers to mail money every time they see an ad. The Boss asks whether the company would actually send them a product in return.
punchline: The Boss misses the point that brainwashed customers would pay without getting anything, and Dogbert mocks him by saying customers respond on brain-stem reflex alone, implying no product is needed.
summary: A consultant dog pitches advertising as mind control that makes buyers send cash on reflex, and his clueless client wonders if they would still have to deliver goods.

file: 1998/1998-03-08_measurable objective_technical writer_measure good writing_number of words_compare projects to wood_dogmatic babbling manager_cognitive surrender.gif
title: Paying Writers By The Word

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, we need to set measurable objectives for you.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I'm a technical writer. How can you measure good writing?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Everything is measurable if you try hard enough.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Is that your well-reasoned opinion?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Or is it the dogmatic babbling of a manager in total cognitive surrender?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: For example, we could measure the number of words you type.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll have to subtract words you delete. That way we won't motivate the wrong behavior.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: In this edition of Tina's hourly newsletter, I compare our projects to various types of wood.

setting: The Boss's office, then Tina's desk
situation: The Boss tells Tina, a technical writer, that he needs to set measurable objectives for her. She challenges whether good writing can be measured, and he proposes counting the words she types, with deletions subtracted. Tina responds by gaming the metric, churning out a padded hourly newsletter.
punchline: When a manager rewards word count, the writer simply produces lots of meaningless filler, showing that bad metrics motivate exactly the wrong behavior despite the boss's claim to prevent it.
summary: A manager who insists on measuring a writer's output by word count gets a flood of worthless verbiage in return.

file: 1998/1998-01-31_self employed_invent valuable things_exploit them_resource_bad input_dogbert.gif
title: Dogbert Offers Dilbert a Job

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm thinking of quitting and working for myself.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Come work for me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Doing what?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You'll invent valuable things and I'll exploit you ... I mean them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not sure you'd be the best boss, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't give me that input, you "resource."

setting: A table with coffee mugs, apparently an office or meeting room
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he is considering quitting to work for himself. Dogbert offers him a job inventing valuable things, slipping up by saying he will exploit Dilbert. When Dilbert hesitates about Dogbert as a boss, Dogbert dismisses his feedback with corporate jargon.
punchline: Dogbert openly admits he'd exploit Dilbert, then shuts down the objection by calling him a "resource" and his concerns "input", the dehumanizing buzzwords managers use to ignore employees.
summary: A man weighing self-employment is recruited by his scheming dog, who cheerfully reveals his exploitative intentions and brushes off complaints with management-speak.

file: 1998/1998-09-05_12 page response_email_decisons_read reaction_fyi.gif
title: Twelve-Page Reply to an FYI

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, thank you for your twelve-page response to my e-mail last week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But I was only sending it to you as an "FYI." Those decisions are already made.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I read your reaction right, you're wondering why I didn't say FYI on my e-mail.

situation: The Boss thanks Alice for her lengthy twelve-page reply to his email, then explains he only sent it as an FYI because the decisions had already been made. Alice stares wide-eyed and then grimaces with clenched teeth while he guesses she is upset he didn't label the email FYI. Dilbert sits at the table in the foreground, seen from behind.
punchline: The Boss pretends to be considerate while blaming Alice's anger on a missing 'FYI' label, dismissing her feedback because the decisions were never open to input.
summary: After Alice pours effort into a detailed rebuttal, her manager brushes it off, saying the matter was settled and she should have understood his message was merely informational.

file: 1998/1998-12-25_date ends_bonita_engineer_supermodel_eye sockets_kiss_goodnight_engineering.gif
title: Dilbert Woos a Skeleton Supermodel

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I realize we're from different worlds, Bonita.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're a famous supermodel and I'm just a sexy engineer...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But when I gaze into your... um... eye sockets...

transcript.speaker: Bonita
transcript.text: Good night.

setting: Outside a door at the end of a date
situation: Dilbert stands at the end of a date with Bonita, who is a skeleton in a red dress, and gives a romantic speech about their differences. Mid-compliment he stumbles over the fact that her eyes are just empty sockets. Bonita cuts the evening short by saying good night.
punchline: The supposed famous supermodel is a skeleton, and Dilbert's sweet talk falls apart when he has to find something romantic to say about her eye sockets, so she ends the date.
summary: A smitten engineer gives a heartfelt end-of-date speech to his skeletal supermodel companion, only to fumble the compliment and get politely dismissed.

file: 1998/1998-07-20_conversation_cubicle_dwellers_shut up!!_alice_impatience.gif
title: Alice Shouts Down Noisy Cubicle Chatter

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Excuse me. I couldn't avoid hearing your conversation outside my cubicle.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I think I speak for a lot of cubicle dwellers when I say...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: SHUT UP!!

situation: Two male coworkers stand chatting in the aisle right outside Alice's cubicle. Alice politely interrupts, saying she speaks for many cubicle dwellers, then screams at them to shut up, startling the two men.
punchline: Alice sets up a polite, diplomatic complaint on behalf of everyone and then abandons all civility with a deafening shout.
summary: A cubicle worker builds up to a courteous objection about hallway chatter and then simply bellows at the offenders.

file: 1998/1998-01-26_deputy of common sense_apply swift justice_lack of common sense_chocolate gun_irony.gif
title: Deputy of Common Sense's Chocolate Gun

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I appointed myself "Deputy of Common Sense."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I will apply swift justice to those who exhibit a lack of common sense.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, it's swift justice for people who aren't too swift?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And I'm using a chocolate gun for irony.

situation: Dogbert, dressed as a lawman in a hat and gun belt, announces he has appointed himself Deputy of Common Sense while Dilbert types at his desk. Dogbert vows to deliver swift justice to people lacking common sense, and Dilbert points out the wordplay that this punishes people who aren't swift. Dogbert replies that his gun is made of chocolate, for the sake of irony.
punchline: Dogbert's self-appointed law enforcement is absurdly toothless, since his chocolate gun is a deliberate ironic joke about the weapon being harmless.
summary: A self-deputized Dogbert threatens to punish the foolish with a sweet, edible revolver while Dilbert notes the pun in his mission.

file: 1998/1998-07-21_interfered with project_empowering employees_bonus_real boss_body in dumpster_boss acting unusual.gif
title: Boss Suddenly Stops Micromanaging, Offers Bonus

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You haven't interfered with my project in weeks. Something must be wrong.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I believe in empowering my employees and staying out of the way.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Am I going to find my real boss's body in a dumpster?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's extra money in the budget. Would you like a bonus?

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that he has noticed the boss hasn't meddled in his project for weeks. The boss says he believes in empowering employees and staying out of the way, then offers a bonus from extra budget money. Dilbert is so unsettled by this uncharacteristic behavior that he suspects the boss is an impostor who has murdered the real one.
punchline: The boss is so consistently incompetent and meddlesome that sensible, generous behavior makes Dilbert suspect he has been replaced by an impostor who killed the real boss.
summary: A boss who suddenly behaves like a competent, generous manager convinces his employee that the genuine article has been murdered and replaced.

file: 1998/1998-05-10_cubicle walls_detrsoys fabric_acoustical absorbtion_agreemnet_sarcasm.gif
title: Boss Complains About Sticky Note Absorption

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What the...?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, you know we don't allow anything on cubicle walls.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It destroys the acoustic absorption of the fabric.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ouch!! My ears! Don't shout!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You're right! I've ruined the acoustic absorption.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It seemed so harmless. I'll remove it immediately!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why is it worse when they agree with me?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What? Eh?

situation: The Boss scolds Alice for putting a small sticky note on her cubicle wall, claiming it ruins the fabric's acoustic absorption. Alice shouts at him in response, then sarcastically agrees with every point he makes while pretending to be deaf from the noise. The Boss is left bothered by her mock agreement.
punchline: Alice responds to the Boss's absurd rule with loud, exaggerated agreement, and the Boss is more annoyed by her sarcastic compliance than he would be by an argument.
summary: A manager's petty rule about notes on cubicle walls is met with an employee's over-the-top, deafening agreement that leaves him rattled.

file: 1998/1998-11-05_ann_dilbert makes bet_hair on fire_curses_super natural powers_harms coworkers.gif
title: Betting on Swearing-Ignited Matches

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ann, I made a bet with Ted that you could ignite this match by swearing at it.

transcript.speaker: Ann
transcript.text: How dare you bet against me, Ted, you #%@!!*!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dang! How about double or nothing?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I want my dollar.

situation: Dilbert tells Ann he has bet Ted that she can light a match just by swearing at it. Ann angrily curses at Ted for betting against her, and Ted's hair bursts into flames. Ted is reduced to a smoking skeleton while Dilbert, having lost the bet, casually offers double or nothing.
punchline: Ann's cursing turns out to be so powerful that it incinerates Ted instead of the match, yet Dilbert's only concern is the lost wager, while the charred Ted just wants his dollar.
summary: A wager about a coworker's fiery temper goes terribly wrong when her tirade reduces the man who doubted her to a skeleton.

file: 1998/1998-05-26_crown_dogbert_charismatic leaders_fill void_egomaniacal philandering sociopaths.gif
title: Dogbert Crowns Himself Charismatic Leader

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's dinosaur friend
transcript.text: What's the crown for?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There aren't any charismatic leaders in the world lately. I'm going to fill the void.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Don't charismatic leaders usually turn out to be egomaniacal, philandering sociopaths?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And they look good in hats!

setting: A bedroom, with Dogbert standing on a dresser in front of a mirror
situation: Dogbert stands on a dresser wearing a crown while a green dinosaur asks why. Dogbert explains he plans to fill the world's shortage of charismatic leaders. When the dinosaur points out that such leaders tend to be egomaniacal, philandering sociopaths, Dogbert cheerfully dismisses it by citing their good looks in hats.
punchline: Dogbert admits the downsides of charismatic leaders but is only concerned that they look good in hats, satirizing how superficial appeal excuses terrible character in leaders.
summary: A crowned Dogbert announces he will step in as the world's missing charismatic leader and shrugs off warnings about their dark traits in favor of the headwear.

file: 1998/1998-08-20_catbert_evil hr director_regular employees_paid less_contract workers_intangible benefits.gif
title: Intangible Benefits Go to Stockholders

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Yes, regular employees are paid less than contract employees such as yourself.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: But if you join the company, you'll get many intangible benefits.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe your stockholders would like some intangible benefits. They can have mine.

situation: Catbert, acting as the evil H.R. director, tries to recruit Dilbert, a contract employee, into becoming a regular employee. He admits regular employees earn less than contractors but promises intangible benefits. Dilbert sarcastically says the stockholders can have his share of those benefits.
punchline: Dilbert points out that 'intangible benefits' are worthless, so the stockholders who profit from the lower pay are welcome to them.
summary: A scheming H.R. cat tries to lure a well-paid contractor into a lower-paying staff job with vague perks, and the engineer isn't fooled.

file: 1998/1998-12-31_catbert_hr director_sends wally home_wearing shorts_skinhead accuse_evil.gif
title: Catbert Harasses Wally Over Shorts

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Wally, I'm sending you home. Shorts are not acceptable dress.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: These are not shorts!!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Tomorrow I'll accuse him of being a skinhead.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Purr purr

situation: Catbert, acting as H.R. Director, orders Wally to go home because he thinks Wally is wearing shorts. Wally protests that his dark trousers are not shorts. Once Wally is out of the way, Catbert gleefully plans to accuse him of something else the next day.
punchline: Catbert's dress code complaint is just an arbitrary excuse to torment Wally, and he is already plotting his next baseless accusation, purring with malicious delight.
summary: A malevolent H.R. cat sends an employee home over a wardrobe violation that does not exist, then happily schedules a fresh false charge for the following day.

file: 1998/1998-11-01_morale problem_boss solutions_knickname for group_scatalogical_involves monkeys_meeting_decide nickname_suggestions_business.gif
title: Scatological Monkey Nickname Brainstorm

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have a solution to our morale problem.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need a nickname for our group.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can it be something scatological?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Um... no.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How about something that involves monkeys?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't think so.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ooh... but could it be something that's both scatological and involves monkeys?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It's hard to be optimistic while he's so grumpy.

setting: Conference room meeting with a flip chart
situation: The Boss announces that giving the group a nickname will fix their morale problem. Dilbert and Wally keep proposing childish ideas involving scatological humor and monkeys, and the Boss rejects each one. Eventually Dilbert combines both ideas into a single suggestion, and the Boss's grumpiness is remarked upon.
punchline: The Boss's feeble morale fix is undermined by employees who respond with juvenile suggestions, and the grumpy boss himself is shown to be the real source of the morale problem.
summary: A manager tries to boost spirits with a group nickname, but his team's crude and silly suggestions only sour his mood.

file: 1998/1998-08-22_time sheet_detailed_easier to make up_carol_secreatry_crinkles up.gif
title: Carol Fabricates Dilbert's Time Sheet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's my time sheet, in exquisite detail.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Crinkle crinkle wad

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: It's easier to input the numbers if I make them up as I go.

situation: Dilbert hands Carol his carefully detailed time sheet so she can enter it into the computer. She crumples the paper into a ball and tosses it aside. She then explains that it's easier to type the numbers if she just invents them as she goes.
punchline: Dilbert's painstaking time sheet is thrown away unread, showing that the data entry is meaningless and the numbers recorded in the system are essentially fiction.
summary: An employee's meticulous time sheet gets crumpled up by the administrative assistant, who simply invents figures for the computer instead.

file: 1998/1998-10-20_newest hore_team member_headless suit_meetings_never fire_bad decsion_head is in jar.gif
title: Headless Employee, Head in Redmond

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, meet the newest member of your team.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hired him myself. That means I can never fire him; it would look like I made a bad decision.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Microsoft hired his head. It's in a jar in Redmond.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: And we got the part that goes to meetings.

situation: The Boss introduces Alice to a new team member who is just an empty suit with no head, explaining he can never fire the man because it would reflect badly on his hiring decision. Alice responds that Microsoft hired the man's head, which is kept in a jar in Redmond, and the company got only the part that goes to meetings.
punchline: The new hire is literally a headless suit, implying that the talented part (his brain) was snapped up by Microsoft while the company is left with a useless body that merely attends meetings, and the boss refuses to fire him to avoid admitting a mistake.
summary: A manager proudly presents a headless suit as a new hire he can't dismiss, while Alice notes the brains went to a big software company and only the meeting-attending remainder stayed behind.

file: 1998/1998-03-23_famous serial killers_database_name_weapon_tattoo_killer application.gif
title: Killer Application Taken Literally

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My new product is a database of famous serial killers.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You can search the database by name, weapon or tattoo.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Let me guess, Wally: Six months ago our young intern asked you what the term "killer application" meant.

situation: Wally stands by a wall display of mugshots and presents his new product to colleagues in a meeting: a searchable database of famous serial killers. Alice, sitting at the table, deduces the origin of the idea and calls out Wally for it.
punchline: Alice figures out that Wally misunderstood the business term "killer application" when the intern asked about it, and built a literal database of killers.
summary: A colleague's product pitch for a murderer-themed database reveals that he took a software buzzword far too literally.

file: 1998/1998-07-30_useful skills_raising issues_salespeople_new prodcut_have a meeting_oxygen being wasted.gif
title: Raising Issues Instead of Skills

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I have no useful skills or knowledge. I compensate by "raising issues."

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Our salespeople haven't been trained for the new product!!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Someone should have a meeting about that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow, I can actually hear oxygen being wasted.

situation: A coworker stands behind Dilbert's desk and openly admits he has no useful skills, so he makes up for it by raising issues. He then dramatically announces that the salespeople haven't been trained on the new product and suggests someone should hold a meeting about it. Dilbert, typing at his computer, remarks that he can hear oxygen being wasted.
punchline: The coworker contributes nothing but alarmist problem-spotting and calls for meetings instead of solutions, and Dilbert sarcastically notes how pointless his talking is.
summary: A self-aware office windbag proudly fills his lack of ability by sounding alarms and proposing meetings, much to Dilbert's weary disdain.

file: 1998/1998-12-27_new corporate policy_boss reads_alice_falls asleep_boring_wordy dcoument.gif
title: Policy So Boring Alice Sleeps

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, we have a new corporate policy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And I quote...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "... initiate the description of the criteria for requirements..."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "... by developing a framework for the application architecture..."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "...consistent with the planning corridor specified in our strategic initiative."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: (thought) So tired

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you get all that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally, come here for a minute.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Read this and tell me if she's doing any of it right now.

situation: The Boss reads a new corporate policy aloud to Alice, full of dense jargon about frameworks and planning corridors. Alice grows so bored that she falls asleep at her desk. The Boss then calls Wally over and hands him the policy to check whether Alice is complying with it.
punchline: The Boss mistakes Alice's boredom-induced napping for possible compliance with the policy, because the jargon is so meaningless that sleeping could plausibly be what it describes.
summary: A manager recites impenetrable policy language until his employee nods off, then asks a coworker whether her snoring counts as following the rules.

file: 1998/1998-06-13_dangerous asbestos_every room_scientific process_attrition.gif
title: Asbestos Solved by Attrition

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dangerous asbestos has been found in every room in our building.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The problem will be addressed using a ... scientific process.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Something called attrition.

situation: At a meeting table, the Boss reads an announcement from a sheet of paper while Dilbert and a bald coworker listen. He reveals that asbestos is in every room of the building, then says it will be handled by a 'scientific process' that turns out to be attrition, meaning employees will simply leave or die over time.
punchline: The company's plan for dangerous asbestos is to wait for employees to be lost through attrition, dressing up neglect as science and showing callous disregard for worker safety.
summary: A manager announces a building-wide toxic hazard and proudly proposes to fix it by letting staff gradually dwindle away.

file: 1998/1998-04-06_mordac_preventer of information services_guidlines for passwords_six characters_include numbers and letters_upper and lower case_change once a month_touture employees_write nothing down.gif
title: Mordac's Impossible Password Rules

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I am Mordac, the Preventer of Information Services. I bring new guidelines for passwords.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "All passwords must be at least six characters long... include numbers and letters... include a mix of upper and lower case..."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "Use different passwords for each system. Change once a month. Do not write anything down."

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: Squeal like a pig!!!

situation: Mordac, the head of information services, visits Dilbert's cubicle and hands him a sheet of new password guidelines. Dilbert reads the rules aloud: long, mixed-case passwords with numbers, a different one for every system, changed monthly, and never written down. Mordac gleefully taunts Dilbert with a line borrowed from a famous torture scene.
punchline: The password rules are so burdensome and impossible to memorize that enforcing them amounts to torture, which Mordac clearly enjoys inflicting.
summary: An IT security enforcer delivers a list of absurdly strict password requirements and takes sadistic delight in the burden they place on a user.

file: 1998/1998-08-14_moon_nasa hides women_love male engineers_drinking contest_loser_never return_entering contest.gif
title: Moon Party Drinking Contest Backfires

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Somewhere on the moon

transcript.speaker: NASA engineer
transcript.text: So, you discovered where NASA hides the women who love male engineers.

transcript.speaker: NASA engineer
transcript.text: How about a little drinking contest, tough guy? The loser can never return.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: We probably shouldn't have insisted on entering the contest.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I'll miss them.

setting: The surface of the moon, at a party
situation: Dilbert has found a secret lunar party where NASA keeps women who adore male engineers, and the party-hatted engineers challenge him to a drinking contest where the loser can never return to Earth. In the last panel, the women lie drunk and disheveled among empty bottles, having lost the contest themselves.
punchline: The women, who had insisted on entering the contest, lost it and are now stranded on the moon forever, missing the engineers they will never see again.
summary: A secret moonbase party of lovestruck women and nerdy engineers ends with the women stuck on the lunar surface after losing a wager they pushed for.

file: 1998/1998-12-12_boss with spreadsheet_increase page number_exhausted.gif
title: Boss Discovers Spreadsheet Page Number Trick

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nothing is more dangerous than a boss with a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I increase the page number, our sales go up.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm onto something.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: On page 843 the sales would be higher, but I was exhausted.

setting: Office cubicles and a conference room
situation: Dilbert and Wally peek over a cubicle wall and warn that a boss with a spreadsheet is dangerous. The Boss, at his computer, mistakes the page number in the sales report for something that drives sales and decides he is onto something. At a meeting he presents his finding, saying sales would be even higher on page 843 but he got tired of paging ahead.
punchline: The Boss confuses a page number with the data itself, so he thinks he can boost sales just by flipping to a higher page, which proves Dilbert's warning about managers with spreadsheets.
summary: A manager misreads a spreadsheet so badly that he believes turning to later pages produces bigger sales figures, and he presents this discovery to his team.

file: 1998/1998-10-03_evil_catbert_hr director_temporary employee_asks employee_want fulltime status_orientation program.gif
title: Permanent Job Offer Is Orientation

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You've been a great temporary employee. Would you like to be a permanent one?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Yes!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Ha ha ha!!! You simple fool!!!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: What was that?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That was your employee orientation program.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, praises a temp and offers him a permanent position. When the temp eagerly accepts, Catbert cackles and calls him a fool. Catbert then reveals that the cruel laughter was the new employee's entire orientation program.
punchline: The company's idea of orientation is a mocking laugh that tells the new permanent hire how foolish he was to want the job, implying the workplace is miserable.
summary: A grateful temp accepts permanent work from the malicious HR cat, who responds with gleeful mockery and calls it onboarding.

file: 1998/1998-09-16_injury free work_safety award_incentive to avoid injuries.gif
title: Safety Award Incentive Gone Wrong

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The safety award goes to Ted for his five years of injury-free work.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Thank you for this award. Without awards, there would be no incentive to avoid injuries.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: (no dialogue; he glares at Ted)

situation: The Boss presents a safety award to Ted for five years without an injury while coworkers watch. Ted accepts it and cheerfully says that awards are the only reason anyone avoids getting hurt. The Boss, standing beside him, gives him a stern look.
punchline: Ted's thanks implies that employees would otherwise be happy to injure themselves, which insults the idea of the award and the Boss who gave it.
summary: A worker honored for staying unhurt hints that only the prize keeps people from getting injured, and his boss is not amused.

file: 1998/1998-11-23_slow witted coworkers_lunch room_eating lunch_coworkers.gif
title: Slow-Witted Coworkers Drink My Soda

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd love my job if not for my slow-witted co-workers.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Am not.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're drinking my soda again!

situation: Dilbert, Wally and Alice sit together eating lunch. Dilbert complains that he would love his job if it weren't for his slow-witted co-workers. In the last panel Wally, who is holding a soda can, denies something, and Dilbert accuses him of drinking his soda again.
punchline: Dilbert's complaint about slow-witted coworkers is illustrated by Wally, who keeps drinking Dilbert's soda and clumsily denies it while holding the can, showing he is the very kind of coworker Dilbert means.
summary: A lunchtime gripe about dim coworkers is proven right when the nearest one is caught sipping the complainer's drink.

file: 1998/1998-12-18_opposed to plan_emotionally invested_opinion_meeting agenda.gif
title: Emotionally Invested In Uninformed Opinion

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm strongly opposed to your plan.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You haven't read it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Oh, right. But now I'm emotionally invested in my opinion.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: This plan will never work!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's the meeting agenda.

setting: Conference table in a meeting room
situation: A coworker tells Dilbert he is strongly opposed to his plan, but Dilbert points out he hasn't read it. The coworker admits this but says he is already emotionally committed to his opinion. After finally reading the paper, he angrily declares it will never work, only to learn it is just the meeting agenda.
punchline: The coworker is so attached to his uninformed opposition that he rants against a document that turns out to be only the meeting agenda, showing opinions formed without facts are stubbornly defended.
summary: A man refuses to abandon his firm objection to a plan he never read, then furiously condemns what turns out to be a schedule of topics.

file: 1998/1998-12-24_date_supermodel_restaurant_order food_spaghetti_loaf of bread_absorb moisture_sniff mints.gif
title: Supermodel Skeleton Orders Air and Mints

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll have the jumbo spaghetti meal with a loaf of garlic bread.

transcript.speaker: Skeleton Supermodel
transcript.text: I'll absorb moisture from the air and sniff the mints on the way out.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it fun to be a supermodel?

transcript.speaker: Skeleton Supermodel
transcript.text: It was until now.

situation: Dilbert is on a dinner date with a skeletal supermodel. He orders a huge spaghetti meal with garlic bread, while she tells the waitress she will eat nothing but moisture from the air and the smell of the mints. Dilbert, chewing his giant sandwich, asks if being a supermodel is fun, and she replies that it was until now.
punchline: The supermodel's absurdly extreme diet makes her a literal skeleton, and Dilbert's gluttonous eating next to her makes her miserable, so her answer is a deadpan jab at his tactlessness.
summary: A bony model on a date eats only air and breath mints while her companion tucks into a mountain of pasta and bread, and his clumsy question sours the evening.

file: 1998/1998-07-25_management secrets_earthling_fulltime aliens_ufo_plowed into alp_sharing skills_boss and aliens.gif
title: Boss Advises Aliens, UFO Crashes Anyway

transcript.speaker: Alien
transcript.text: Tell us your management secrets, Earthling.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have too many full-time aliens flying this UFO. Downsize half of them, then roll out the ISO 9001 process.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ... But despite all of my help, they still plowed into a snow-covered Alp.

setting: Inside an alien spacecraft, then back on Earth in the office
situation: The Boss has been abducted by green elephant-nosed aliens who ask him to share his management secrets. He advises them to downsize half of the crew and implement the ISO 9001 quality process. Afterward, he tells Dilbert and Alice that the aliens' UFO still crashed into a snowy mountain, and he is now on crutches.
punchline: The Boss's standard downsizing and process-certification advice is worthless, so the aliens crashed anyway, and he shows no awareness that his advice may have caused it.
summary: After being abducted, a clueless manager hands aliens his usual cost-cutting and process advice, then complains that their ship crashed into a mountain despite his guidance.

file: 1998/1998-05-18_comic strip_dogbert_pippy the ziphead_artwork_one joke_reader_cram art.gif
title: Dogbert Cramming Art to Hide Joke

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm creating a comic strip called "Pippy the Ziphead."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm cramming as much artwork in there as possible, so no one will notice there's only one joke.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The joke is on the reader, isn't it?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd better cram some more art in there.

situation: Dogbert sits at a desk drawing panels for his own comic strip, "Pippy the Ziphead," while Dilbert looks on. Dogbert explains he is filling the strip with as much artwork as possible so readers won't notice it contains only one joke. Dilbert points out that the joke is on the reader, and Dogbert responds by deciding to add even more art.
punchline: Dogbert's strategy of distracting people with excess artwork is exposed as a con on the audience, and he reacts by doubling down on the distraction rather than improving the joke.
summary: A dog drawing his own cartoon admits he's piling on illustrations to disguise a thin gag, and when confronted, simply draws more.

file: 1998/1998-03-03_project staus_budget cuts_new prodcut_user interface_target market_too shy_bad sign_no laws_do for living.gif
title: Product So Bad It Should Be Illegal

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Project status

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Due to budget cuts, our new product will have no user interface.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our target market is people who are too shy to return products.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it a bad sign if you spend the day wondering why there are no laws against what you do for a living?

setting: Conference room during a project status presentation, then Dilbert's workplace
situation: Dilbert gives a project status presentation, announcing that budget cuts mean the new product will ship with no user interface. He then explains that the target market is customers too timid to return defective products. In the last panel he asks Dogbert whether it is a bad sign that he wishes his own work were illegal.
punchline: Dilbert's job is so ethically dubious, building a useless product and selling it to timid people, that he wonders why the law doesn't forbid it.
summary: A engineer presents a crippled product aimed at customers who won't complain, then privately wonders why his profession isn't a crime.

file: 1998/1998-05-14_free flu shots_wealth stock holders_hunt down_shoot flu darts_not flu prevention shits.gif
title: Flu Shots Delivered by Hunters

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The company is giving free flu shots, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The shots will be delivered by wealthy stockholders who will hunt you down and shoot you with flu darts.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: At least I won't get the flu, right?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You're probably thinking of the flu prevention shots.

setting: Office cubicle, with a hunting scene imagined in the middle panel
situation: Catbert tells Wally that the company is offering free flu shots, then explains they will be delivered by wealthy stockholders hunting employees with flu darts. Wally hopes at least he will avoid the flu, and Catbert says he must be thinking of the flu prevention shots, implying these darts do the opposite.
punchline: The company's free flu shots are actually flu-infecting darts fired by rich stockholders, not the protective shots Wally expects.
summary: A malicious cat announces a workplace health perk that turns out to be a hunting party where shareholders deliberately give employees the flu.

file: 1998/1998-09-07_rat_answers phone_consulting compnay_good pay_investment banking_phone call.gif
title: Ratbert Turns Down Consulting Job

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Ring

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Hello, I'm a rat.

transcript.speaker: Caller (phone)
transcript.text: This is a consulting company. We'll pay you $200,000 per year to work for us.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm more interested in investment banking.

transcript.speaker: Caller (phone)
transcript.text: *#!@ job market.

setting: Ratbert's desk, answering a phone call
situation: Ratbert, a small yellow rat, hears the phone ring and answers it. A consulting company on the line offers him $200,000 a year even though he announces he is a rat. Ratbert says he would rather work in investment banking, and the frustrated recruiter curses the job market.
punchline: The job market is so desperate for talent that a consulting firm will offer a huge salary to an actual rat, and the rat can still afford to turn it down for a better career.
summary: A recruiter showers a rodent with a lucrative job offer sight unseen, only to be snubbed in favor of a more glamorous field.

file: 1998/1998-12-09_asok dsitraught_can't do work_no response_emails voice mails_pathetic defeated losers_wally.gif
title: Hanging Out With Defeated Losers

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: No one returns my phone calls... No one reads the e-mail I send.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I find myself hanging around with other pathetic, defeated losers.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: No offense.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: None taken.

situation: Asok slumps at a desk, complaining that nobody returns his calls or reads his e-mail. He then admits that he now spends his time with other pathetic, defeated losers, while Wally sits at his computer next to him. Asok apologizes to Wally, who accepts the insult without any concern.
punchline: Wally cheerfully accepts being called a pathetic, defeated loser, which shows how little ambition or pride he has and how thoroughly he fits the description.
summary: A neglected young employee laments being ignored and then unintentionally insults his lazy coworker, who calmly shrugs it off.

file: 1998/1998-09-09_ratbert the consultant_newest partner_least desirable assisngments_consultant cannon_monitor progress.gif
title: Ratbert Fired From Consultant Cannon

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Consulting Partner
transcript.text: As our newest partner, you'll get the least desirable assignments.

transcript.speaker: Consulting Partner
transcript.text: We'll load you in the consultant cannon, shoot you to the client's site and monitor your progress.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: The window is more to the left.

transcript.speaker: Consulting Partner
transcript.text: The client is more to the right.

situation: A senior consulting partner tells Ratbert, the newest partner, that he will get the worst assignments. He then loads Ratbert into a cannon to be shot at the client's site. Ratbert, still inside the barrel, comments that the window is more to the left, and the partner replies that the client is more to the right.
punchline: The consulting firm literally fires its newest consultant out of a cannon, and the partner's aim is so cavalier that Ratbert has to correct the trajectory, since the window is not where the client is.
summary: A consulting firm launches its newest hire out of a cannon to reach clients, with both sides casually debating where to aim.

file: 1998/1998-07-23_real boss_prison tube_spaceship_wear shorts_quality of work_replaced by alien_boss is alien_no one knows.gif
title: The Boss Is Secretly An Alien

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No one suspects that the real boss is in a prison tube on my spaceship.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Is it okay if I wear shorts?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sure. I only care about the quality of your work.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: If our boss were replaced by an alien, would that be a bad thing?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It depends on the alien.

situation: The Boss, who has a tail and little horns and is secretly an alien impostor, gloats in thought that the real boss is imprisoned on his spaceship. When Asok asks about wearing shorts, the alien boss gives an unusually reasonable answer. At lunch Asok wonders whether an alien replacement would be bad, and Dilbert says it depends on the alien.
punchline: The alien impostor is a better, more reasonable boss than the human one, so employees would actually welcome the replacement.
summary: A disguised extraterrestrial manager proves so sensible that his staff would happily keep him over the real boss.

file: 1998/1998-10-30_dogcart the consultant_invisible robot_empty box_train support staff_customers house_sensors.gif
title: Support Staff Gaslight Invisible Robot Customers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Some customers might complain that the invisible robot they bought from us...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ... is nothing but an empty box. I will train our support staff to handle those calls.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Customer's house

transcript.speaker: Support Staff (on phone)
transcript.text: According to our sensors, he's in your house... and he's watching you.

setting: A conference room, then a customer's living room
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, tells the company that customers who bought an invisible robot may complain it is just an empty box. He proposes training support staff to handle those calls, and the final panel shows how: a phone call to a terrified customer, who is told the robot is in his house watching him.
punchline: Instead of admitting the product is a fraud, the support script frightens the customer into believing the nonexistent robot is real and spying on him.
summary: A consultant's answer to complaints about a worthless product is to have support staff scare buyers into believing the invisible robot is lurking in their homes.

file: 1998/1998-02-16_industrial espionage program_secret reports_plan_fire dumb people_perfect cover.gif
title: Industrial Espionage Is Just Firing

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I've been chosen for the industrial espionage program.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: The plan is that I quit this job and go to work for our competitor. Every week I'll send back secret reports.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Bob, this is how we fire dumb people.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: That's why it's the perfect cover.

situation: Carrying a box of his belongings, Bob proudly tells Dilbert and Alice that he has been selected for a secret industrial espionage program. He explains he will quit and join a competitor while sending back secret reports. Alice points out that this is simply how the company gets rid of dumb employees.
punchline: The supposed spy program is a cover story the company uses to fire incompetent people, and Bob is too dim to realize he is being fired, which he takes as proof the cover works.
summary: A cheerful employee carrying his desk contents believes he has landed a covert spy mission, when really he is being politely dismissed.

file: 1998/1998-07-08_sharing hotel rooms_business trips_before sleep_exercise_room_beds_health.gif
title: Dilbert Dreads Roommate's Bedtime Exercises

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate sharing a hotel room on business trips.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I need to do my exercises before I go to sleep. Do you mind?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There are so many ways that this could be bad.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm still a bit winded from yesterday.

setting: Hotel room during a business trip
situation: Dilbert arrives at a shared hotel room with a male coworker and complains about having to share. The coworker announces he needs to do his exercises before sleeping and mentions he is still winded from the day before, leaving Dilbert clutching a book and looking alarmed.
punchline: The coworker's vague, breathless 'exercises' sound alarmingly like something else, so Dilbert imagines the many awkward and disturbing possibilities of sharing a room with him.
summary: A traveling engineer's worst fears about his hotel roommate are confirmed when the man casually mentions his mysterious nightly workout routine.

file: 1998/1998-12-11_financial model_original spreadsheet_developing strategy_pay base_tax rate.gif
title: Boss's Strategy Built on Unknown Assumptions

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I did some financial modeling on my own.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But you don't know any of the assumptions that went into the original spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That didn't stop me from developing a strategy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our pay is based on the tax rate now.

setting: Office, in a meeting or hallway conversation
situation: The Boss hands out a sheet of paper and announces that he did his own financial modeling. Wally points out that he has no idea what assumptions went into the original spreadsheet, but the Boss cheerfully says he developed a strategy anyway. Dilbert then reveals that the resulting strategy ties the employees' pay to the tax rate.
punchline: The Boss built a strategy on a spreadsheet he doesn't understand, and the result is a bizarre compensation scheme that makes the employees' pay depend on the tax rate.
summary: A manager confidently crafts a plan from numbers he can't explain, and the staff discover it has quietly tied their salaries to something outside anyone's control.

file: 1998/1998-09-06_dilbert_deny request_evil incarnate_something specific_dollar estimate_value_chair_quantify job_work tools.gif
title: No Chair Without Dollar Estimate

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why did the I.S. department deny my request for a PC upgrade?

transcript.speaker: I.S. Employee
transcript.text: Because we are evil incarnate!! Buwahahahaha!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I was looking for something more specific.

transcript.speaker: I.S. Employee
transcript.text: You didn't provide a dollar estimate of the benefits.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's ridiculous. I can't put a value on every tool I need to do my job.

transcript.speaker: I.S. Employee
transcript.text: If you can't quantify it, then it must not be necessary.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then why does the company give me a chair? I can't quantify that either?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's one more reason why it stinks to be me.

setting: Dilbert's cubicle and an I.S. department employee's desk in an office
situation: Dilbert asks an I.S. department employee why his PC upgrade request was denied.
