After a gleeful evil answer, the employee explains that Dilbert gave no dollar estimate of the benefits and insists anything unquantifiable must be unnecessary. Dilbert turns this logic against him by asking about his chair, then ends up sitting in his cubicle with no chair, thinking about how bad his lot is.
punchline: Applying the I.S. department's rule that unquantifiable things aren't necessary, the company apparently took away Dilbert's chair, leaving him standing in his cubicle.
summary: A worker's equipment request is rejected for lacking a quantified benefit, and his attempt to mock the rule with a chair example backfires when the chair disappears.

file: 1998/1998-03-27_office supplies_underfunded_three ring binder_spare office supplies.gif
title: Begging Supplies for Underfunded Project

transcript.speaker: Ragged Employee
transcript.text: Can you spare any office supplies? I'm on an underfunded project.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How about a three-ring binder with one ring?

transcript.speaker: Ragged Employee
transcript.text: Score!

transcript.speaker: Ragged Employee
transcript.text: I'll melt into the background and let you get back to your palace and your fancy coffee.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It's a mocha.

situation: A employee in tattered clothes and a blue headband asks a well-dressed coworker for spare office supplies because his project has no budget. The coworker offers a broken three-ring binder with only one ring, and the beggar is thrilled. As he leaves, he sarcastically refers to the coworker's fancy coffee, and the coworker proudly specifies that it's a mocha.
punchline: The employee on the underfunded project is so desperate that a broken binder feels like a windfall, while the comfortable coworker completely misses the point and fixates on correcting the type of coffee.
summary: A budget-starved worker in rags begs a comfortable colleague for leftovers and gratefully accepts a nearly useless binder.

file: 1998/1998-11-11_technical recommendation_keen insights_boss immaturity.gif
title: Boss Relies on Insight, Not Knowledge

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't understand your technical recommendation, Alice.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I will rely on my keen insights about you as an engineer.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That too would require knowledge on your part.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Shush!

situation: Alice presents a technical recommendation, and the Boss admits he doesn't understand it. He says he will instead judge it based on his insights about her as an engineer. Alice points out that this approach would also require knowledge he lacks, and he childishly covers his ears and tells her to shush.
punchline: The Boss can't evaluate the recommendation or the engineer proposing it, and when Alice points out his ignorance he reacts like a child by plugging his ears.
summary: A clueless manager tries to dodge evaluating an engineer's advice by trusting his gut, only to be called out and respond by plugging his ears.

file: 1998/1998-10-15_teaches cobol_elbonia_y2k_year 2000 problem_four day class_cabbge_class dismissed.gif
title: Dilbert Teaches Y2K to Elbonians

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert teaches Cobol in Elbonia

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And that's how you fix your "Year 2000" problem.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This concludes my four-day class. Are there any questions?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: What's a year?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: And is Cobol a kind of cabbage or what?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Class dismissed.

situation: Dilbert finishes a four-day class teaching Cobol programming to a group of Elbonians so they can fix the Year 2000 problem. When he asks for questions, the students reveal they don't know what a year is and think Cobol might be a cabbage. Dilbert gives up and dismisses the class.
punchline: After four days of training, the students lack even the most basic understanding of the concepts, showing that the outsourced Y2K fix is hopeless.
summary: A programmer's lesson to a foreign workforce collapses when the trainees prove they grasp neither calendars nor computer languages.

file: 1998/1998-07-03_humor_joe telling kind_spill something_laugh.gif
title: Dilbert Spills Everything Trying Humor

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I like men who have a sense of humor.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: ...But not the joke-telling kind — the spontaneous kind — like when you spill something and we both laugh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I'm trying too hard.

setting: A dinner table on a date, then Dilbert's living room
situation: Dilbert sits across from a blonde woman on a date. She says she likes men with a spontaneous sense of humor, like when someone spills something and both laugh. In the last panel Dilbert is back home, covered in dark stains, with Dogbert watching from an armchair.
punchline: Dilbert takes her remark about spontaneous spilling so literally that he has deliberately splattered himself with food, and he only realizes afterward that he may be trying too hard.
summary: After a date says she loves accidental spills more than jokes, Dilbert ends up drenched in stains and wonders if he overdid it.

file: 1998/1998-02-15_technical recomendation_useless and weak_decisions_helvetica font_wrong_coach_wally and boss_desk.gif
title: Wally Finds Joy in Font Choice

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I finished the technical recommendation you requested.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: At first I was miffed that you told me what recommendation you wanted.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It made me feel useless and weak.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But rather than dwell on my powerlessness...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I decided to find joy in the one decision I can make.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I chose a Helvetica type font.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And I never looked back.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, so that's what's wrong with it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I coach and I coach, but they still walk out of here all rubber-legged.

situation: Wally delivers a technical recommendation the Boss requested, explaining that he felt powerless because the Boss dictated the conclusion in advance. To cope, he took pleasure in the only decision left to him, choosing the document's font. The Boss, oblivious to the criticism, only notes that the font explains what is wrong with it, then privately wonders why his coaching leaves employees shaken.
punchline: The Boss completely misses that Wally is complaining about being micromanaged and treats the font as the problem, while believing his own coaching is helpful even though employees leave the meeting shaken.
summary: An employee coolly describes how being told his conclusion in advance left him clinging to the one choice he controlled, and his clueless manager hears only a font complaint.

file: 1998/1998-08-10_answering_asking questions_catbert_evil hr director_hiring_interrupted at work_interview_make stronger_work.gif
title: Honest Answer Fails Job Interview

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Are you able to work while being constantly interrupted?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: No. I would be totally ineffective, just like anyone else.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We were done with the section you had to answer honestly.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Oh. In that case, interruptions make me stronger.

setting: Catbert's H.R. office during a job interview
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, interviews a job candidate and asks whether he can work while constantly interrupted. The candidate answers honestly that he cannot. Catbert then explains the honest-answer portion of the interview is over, and the candidate hastily changes his answer to the lie the company wants to hear.
punchline: The interview has a section where honesty is allowed, after which the candidate is expected to lie about enduring terrible working conditions, and he is quick to comply.
summary: A frank applicant learns that hiring interviews reward flattering falsehoods over truthful answers about distracting workplaces.

file: 1998/1998-01-10_less technical terms_ceo_vp_other technologies.gif
title: Dumbing Down For The CEO

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You'll have to write this in less technical terms for me...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Make it even less technical for my boss... even less for our VP... even less for our EVP... much less for our CEO.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...and compared to all the other technologies, there's a big difference in the mouth area.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to rewrite a technical document in simpler terms, then keeps piling on levels of simplification for each higher layer of management up to the CEO. In the last panel Dilbert presents the ultimate dumbed-down version: a poster of a smiley face with a frown, pointing out the difference to other technologies is in the mouth area.
punchline: By the time a technical document is simplified enough for the CEO, it is reduced to a childish smiley-face drawing, implying senior executives can't grasp any real technical content.
summary: A manager demands repeated simplification of a technical report for each rung of the corporate ladder, so Dilbert ends up presenting a frowning smiley face.

file: 1998/1998-04-19_catbert_evil director_look stressed_champion_workplace_stress no more_unpaid overtime_ignite hair_pissed ouff_angry_taken advantage.gif
title: Stress Booklet Demands Unpaid Overtime

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You look stressed out, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I could fix that by becoming a champion for improvements in the workplace.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Or I could give you a little booklet called "Stress No More."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hmm... I wonder which way is best.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: "Stress is your body's way of saying..."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: "...you haven't worked enough unpaid overtime."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I've never seen a woman's forehead ignite her hair before.

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, notices Alice is stressed and offers to either champion workplace improvements or hand her a stress-relief booklet. Alice picks the booklet, which blames stress on not working enough unpaid overtime, and she becomes so furious that her hair catches fire.
punchline: The company's stress remedy is to blame employees for not working free overtime, which is so infuriating that Alice's rage literally sets her hair on fire.
summary: An H.R. pamphlet meant to soothe a worker's anxiety instead insults her so badly that she bursts into flames of anger.

file: 1998/1998-09-18_dogbert_remember name_buddy_big guy_name tag.gif
title: Dogbert Won't Remember Dilbert's Name

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm finding it a burden to remember your name.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: From now on, I'll refer to you as either "Buddy" or "Big Guy."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How about if I get a name tag? Then you could just read it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do I look like I have that kind of time?

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert sits on the couch beside Dilbert, who is reading a book. Dogbert announces that remembering Dilbert's name is too much effort and says he will just call him "Buddy" or "Big Guy." Dilbert offers a name tag as a workaround, but Dogbert dismisses it as too time-consuming.
punchline: Dogbert finds even glancing at a name tag too much effort, showing how little he values Dilbert as a person.
summary: A lazy Dogbert declares Dilbert's name too much trouble to recall, and even rejects the easy fix of reading a name tag.

file: 1998/1998-11-18_unicorn horn_dilbert_date_sign of virility.gif
title: Unicorn Horn Ruins the Date

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Lately, I've been growing a unicorn horn.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In some cultures, this would be a sign of great virility.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's time to admit that I don't know what women want.

setting: A restaurant table on a date
situation: Dilbert sits across a small table from a woman on a date and announces that he has been growing a unicorn horn out of his forehead. He tries to spin it as a sign of virility in some cultures, while his date stares at him blankly. Seeing her reaction, he privately concludes that he has no idea what women want.
punchline: Dilbert's absurd attempt to impress his date with a bizarre physical oddity fails completely, and his thought bubble shows he blames his ignorance of women rather than the horn itself.
summary: A man on a date tries to pass off a strange growth on his forehead as attractive, then wonders why it isn't working.

file: 1998/1998-06-03_cure shyness_nude photos_intenet_react body_scream.gif
title: Internet Rejects Dilbert's Nude Photos

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll cure your shyness by putting nude photos of you on the Internet.

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: AAEEII!! Cough cough UNH

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't know the Internet could reject a body.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I didn't know it could scream.

setting: Dilbert's home, at a computer and later at the breakfast table
situation: Dogbert sits at Dilbert's computer and announces he will cure Dilbert's shyness by posting nude photos of him online. The computer reacts with a scream, coughing and a groan as if in horror. At breakfast, Dilbert and Dogbert trade deadpan remarks about the Internet rejecting a body and screaming.
punchline: The Internet is so appalled by Dilbert's nude photos that it screams and gags, implying he looks so bad that even cyberspace can't stomach him.
summary: Dogbert's plan to cure his owner's bashfulness by uploading naked pictures makes the web itself recoil in disgust.

file: 1998/1998-02-19_loans_funding_scam artist_dogbert on tv_people believe.gif
title: Dogbert's Infomercial Scam Works

transcript.speaker: Dogbert (on TV)
transcript.text: Would you like to make $1,000 per month for a whole year?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert (on TV)
transcript.text: Send $13,000 for complete information about Dogbert no-load funds.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert (on TV)
transcript.text: I'll include my free pamphlet explaining how to lose weight by eating less food.

transcript.speaker: Man (thought)
transcript.text: Show the number.

setting: Dilbert's living room, watching television; a final panel shows a man in an armchair with a notepad
situation: Dilbert watches Dogbert on a TV infomercial that offers $1,000 a month for a year in exchange for $13,000 for information about no-load funds. Dogbert then sweetens the deal with a free pamphlet on losing weight by eating less. A man in an armchair writing on a notepad, apparently ready to order, thinks 'Show the number.'
punchline: The offer is obviously a rip-off (pay $13,000 to get back $12,000, plus a pamphlet stating the obvious), yet the viewer is persuaded and just wants the phone number to order.
summary: A televised pitchman charges a fortune for worthless financial advice and a laughably obvious diet tip, and a gullible viewer is ready to buy.

file: 1998/1998-07-22_earthlings_susupicous_competent and caring_aliens_aline dressed as boss_helpful to carol.gif
title: Aliens Impersonate Boss, Act Helpful

transcript.speaker: Alien
transcript.text: I think the Earthlings are getting suspicious.

transcript.speaker: Alien
transcript.text: Keep acting competent and caring. Our prisoner says that's how leaders act on their world.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, let me do the org chart on my PC. You have too much work already.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Aaagh!

setting: Alien spaceship and then the office
situation: Green aliens have captured the Pointy-Haired Boss and keep him in a tube, while one of them wears a boss costume to impersonate him at work. After noticing the humans are growing suspicious, the alien is told to act competent and caring, as real leaders supposedly do. In the office, the disguised alien offers to do Carol's work for her, and she screams in alarm.
punchline: The boss's uncharacteristically helpful and considerate behavior is so unnatural that his own employee finds it terrifying, implying real managers are neither competent nor caring.
summary: Extraterrestrial impostors posing as a manager try to seem like proper leaders, and the staff are horrified by the unfamiliar kindness.

file: 1998/1998-10-09_strip on nose_oxygen to brain_interesting conversationalist_not optimistic_anti snoring device.gif
title: Nasal Strip Fails To Improve Conversation

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Put this strip on your nose to get more oxygen to your brain.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm hoping it will make you a more interesting conversationalist.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How 'bout that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm no longer optimistic.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert hands Dilbert an adhesive nasal strip, claiming it will send more oxygen to his brain. Dilbert covers his face in embarrassment while applying it, then asks how it looks. Dogbert's hopes for improved conversation are immediately dashed.
punchline: Dogbert hoped extra oxygen would make Dilbert more interesting, but his first remark proves the brain was never the problem, which exposes how dull Dilbert really is.
summary: A scheming dog sticks a breathing aid on his owner's nose in hopes of livening up his talk, then sours on the idea when the first words come out.

file: 1998/1998-01-07_signed ted card_stamp_congratualations_death_family_medical.gif
title: Congratulations Card for a Death

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's see... it looks like you haven't signed Ted's card yet.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: STAMP

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you think "congratulations" is appropriate for a death in his family?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You never know.

situation: Dilbert goes around collecting signatures on a card for Ted and notices Alice hasn't signed yet. She angrily stamps the card without looking up. Dilbert reads what she wrote and asks if 'congratulations' is appropriate for a death in Ted's family.
punchline: Alice's cynical reply 'You never know' implies that Ted might be happy about a relative's death, perhaps for the inheritance, or that she's so bitter she doesn't care how inappropriate her message is.
summary: A coworker circulating a sympathy card is dismayed when the office's most irritable employee stamps it with a cheerful greeting and shrugs off the problem.

file: 1998/1998-07-28_sales man_vendor_offcie_fake personality_buy stuff_blue things_so dumb.gif
title: Salesman Mocks Budget-Dumping Buyers Openly

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And we'll buy a dozen of these. We're trying to spend our budget so it doesn't get cut next year.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: This is great! You guys are so dumb that I don't even have to use my fake personality to make the sale!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And nine of these blue things.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: There's a full moon on the horizon!

setting: Office desk where a vendor is making a sales call
situation: Dilbert sits across a desk from a salesman and orders a dozen items, explaining that his department needs to spend its budget so it won't be cut next year. The salesman gleefully announces that the buyers are so dumb he doesn't need his fake sales personality. As Dilbert keeps ordering, the salesman bends over and moons him.
punchline: The salesman is so contemptuous of customers who waste money to protect their budget that he drops his act entirely and literally moons them while they keep buying.
summary: A vendor who realizes his customers will buy anything gives up on charm and openly shows his disdain.

file: 1998/1998-10-13_teach elbonians_cobol_reschedule_send wally_dilbert doesn't know cobol.gif
title: Rescheduling Instead of Choosing Wally

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why are you sending ME to teach COBOL to the Elbonians? Wally is the one who knows COBOL, not me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wally said he's busy that day.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can't you reschedule the class?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay... Does tomorrow work for you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're solving the wrong problem!

situation: Dilbert objects to being sent to teach COBOL to the Elbonians when Wally is the one who actually knows it. The Boss says Wally is busy that day, so Dilbert suggests rescheduling the class. The Boss misses the point and asks whether Dilbert is free tomorrow instead.
punchline: The Boss treats Dilbert's suggestion as a scheduling problem for Dilbert rather than recognizing that the real issue is that Dilbert doesn't know COBOL.
summary: A boss assigns the wrong person to a training job and responds to the objection by simply changing the date to suit him.

file: 1998/1998-02-25_email chain letter_will die_curse of dogbert_certain death_curse_turns into dogs.gif
title: Chain Letter Curse Turns Coworkers Into Dogs

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh no! I got an e-mail chain letter. It says I'll die if I don't send it to ten more people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But if I forward the message, the "Curse of Dogbert" will be upon me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...so, I figured a curse is better than certain death, right?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Spank you very much.

situation: Dilbert receives an e-mail chain letter threatening death unless he forwards it to ten people, but forwarding it brings the "Curse of Dogbert". He decides the curse is the better option and forwards it. In the last panel Dilbert, Wally and Alice have all been turned into dogs.
punchline: The curse of Dogbert literally turns the victims into dogs, and the transformed Wally can only manage a garbled "Spank you very much" instead of "Thank you very much".
summary: Faced with a threatening chain e-mail, a worker forwards it onward and ends up barking along with his canine-transformed colleagues.

file: 1998/1998-04-27_dogbert the consultant_excellent advice_50k monthly_offer bad advice_45k month.gif
title: Bad Advice Costs Slightly Less

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can give you excellent advice for $50,000 per month...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If budget is a problem, I also offer bad advice for the low price of $45,000 per month.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not a good sign.

setting: The Boss's office, then a hallway with a cubicle wall
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, pitches his services to the seated Boss, quoting a high monthly fee for excellent advice and a barely cheaper rate for bad advice. In the last panel, the Boss runs past carrying scissors while Dilbert and Alice peer over a cubicle wall and comment on it.
punchline: The bad advice is only slightly cheaper than the good, which shows consulting fees are absurd, and the Boss running with scissors suggests he is already acting on the bad advice.
summary: A consultant dog sells both good and bad guidance at nearly the same exorbitant price, and soon the boss is sprinting around the office with scissors.

file: 1998/1998-02-12_fashion headquarters_supermodel_beauty mark_look unhealthy_silly putty_sexy unhealthy.gif
title: Dogbert's Tumor Becomes Supermodel Asset

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Fashion Headquarters

transcript.speaker: Fashion Executive
transcript.text: You could be our next supermodel. I love the tumor.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's a beauty mark.

transcript.speaker: Fashion Executive
transcript.text: We prefer our supermodels to look unhealthy, in a sexy way.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay, it's a tumor.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can add a few more. It's just "Silly Putty."

transcript.speaker: Fashion Executive
transcript.text: No, it would be easy to overdo that sort of thing.

situation: Dogbert stands on a pedestal while a fashion executive evaluates him as a potential supermodel. She admires the lump on his head, and Dogbert first calls it a beauty mark, then admits it's a tumor when she says they like their models to look unhealthy. He offers to fake more tumors with Silly Putty, but she says that would be overdoing it.
punchline: The fashion industry's taste for looking sickly is so extreme that a genuine tumor counts as an asset, and the only worry is having too much of a good thing.
summary: A fashion scout is delighted by Dogbert's head growth because her industry prizes an unwell look, and she only objects when he offers to fake extras.

file: 1998/1998-04-03_warning lables_slices anti depressants_cause fatique_memory loss_lack of sex_disorientation.gif
title: Antidepressant Warning Label Memory Loss

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Look at the warning label on Alice's antidepressants.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It can cause fatigue, disorientation, memory loss, and lack of sex.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wonder how long we've been taking them.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: There's no way to know.

setting: Conference room table at the office
situation: Dilbert, Wally and Alice sit at a meeting table while Wally reads the warning label on Alice's antidepressant bottle. The listed side effects include fatigue, disorientation and memory loss. Dilbert wonders how long they have all been taking the pills, and Wally points out that memory loss means nobody can tell.
punchline: The drug's memory-loss side effect means they cannot remember how long they have been medicated, implying the whole office has been on antidepressants for ages without realising it.
summary: Coworkers reading a pill bottle's side effects realize they may have been drugged for so long that they can't recall when it started.

file: 1998/1998-12-08_email_alice ignores asok_voice mail_doesn't respond.gif
title: Alice Evades Every Communication Channel

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Alice, you never responded to my e-mail.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Maybe I could ask my question now, in person?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Send me a voice mail.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Will you respond to voice mail?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Sometimes the phone company loses them.

situation: Asok peeks into Alice's cubicle to complain that she never answered his e-mail. When he offers to ask his question in person, Alice tells him to send a voice mail instead. He asks if she will actually answer voice mail, and she says the phone company sometimes loses them.
punchline: Alice has an excuse ready for every communication method, making it clear she simply doesn't want to answer Asok's question at all.
summary: A coworker tries email, a face-to-face chat and voice mail in turn, and the person he's chasing shuts down each route with a new excuse.

file: 1998/1998-03-05_chaos theory_management_name for it_meeting_confused_business.gif
title: Chaos Theory of Management Announced

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, I'll be using the chaos theory of management.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And this will be different how?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now there's a name for it.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces to his team at a meeting that he will now be using the chaos theory of management. The employees look confused, with question marks over their heads. Wally asks how this will differ from what he has been doing, and the Boss cheerfully replies that now there is a name for it.
punchline: The Boss's management has always been chaotic, so adopting the 'chaos theory' label changes nothing except giving his incompetence a fancy name, and he fails to notice the insult.
summary: A manager proudly rebrands his random, disorganized leadership style as a formal theory, oblivious to the fact that his staff sees no difference.

file: 1998/1998-02-21_catbert_evil hr diretor_personal lives_strict dress code_homes_one less decision_make every day.gif
title: Dress Code Enforced at Home

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your personal lives reflect on this company.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: From now on, a strict dress code will be enforced in your homes.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: On the plus side, it's one less decision I have to make every day.

setting: Conference room, then an employee's home living room
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, tells two employees at a meeting that their personal lives reflect on the company and announces a strict dress code that will apply inside their own homes. In the final panel, a man at home wears an absurd blue ruffled outfit, a mohawk-like wig and yellow boots while his dog rests on the couch, trying to find a silver lining.
punchline: The employee is forced to wear a ridiculous mandated outfit at home and sarcastically reassures himself that at least he no longer has to choose what to wear each day.
summary: Human resources extends the company dress code into employees' houses, leaving one worker in a ridiculous mandated costume making the best of it.

file: 1998/1998-08-12_cubicle_land on moon_temperature_oxygen levels_space program_hoax_nasa hiding_love engineers.gif
title: Cubicle Lands On Moon Party

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We're the first cubicle to land on the moon.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The temperature and oxygen levels are fine. Apparently the space program is a hoax.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: NASA must be hiding something here.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Hi. We're the women who love engineers.

setting: The surface of the moon, after a cubicle has landed
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert land on the moon in a flying cubicle. Dilbert steps out and notes that the temperature and oxygen are fine, concluding the space program must be a hoax. Dogbert suggests NASA is hiding something, and then two women holding cocktails appear and introduce themselves as the women who love engineers.
punchline: NASA is indeed hiding something on the moon: a secret colony of women who love engineers, a group the strip treats as practically mythical.
summary: After touching down on the moon in a flying cubicle, a pair of travelers find a breathable atmosphere and a surprise welcoming party of adoring women.

file: 1998/1998-12-05_report shows raise_raises cancelled_pretend to work_dilbert.gif
title: Imaginary Raise, Pretend Work

transcript.speaker: HR Employee
transcript.text: This report shows how much your raise would be if raises hadn't been canceled.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow! My imaginary life is doing great!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now back to pretending to work.

situation: A co-worker hands Dilbert a report showing what his raise would have been if raises had not been canceled. Dilbert reads it and cheerfully notes that his imaginary life is going well. He then sits at his computer and thinks about getting back to pretending to work.
punchline: Since the company has canceled raises, Dilbert responds by pretending to work, implying that employees who receive fake pay will give fake effort in return.
summary: A worker handed a hypothetical pay-raise report for a raise that was never given decides to match the company's make-believe with make-believe effort.

file: 1998/1998-11-07_presentation_humorless blobs_room full_no humor_big fat men.gif
title: Humorless Blobs Reject Dilbert's Cartoon

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The presentation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This cartoon says it all! Hee hee!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh. I just realized you're all humorless blobs.

transcript.speaker: Audience member
transcript.text: Join us, Dilbert. Be a blob.

transcript.speaker: Audience member
transcript.text: Yes... humor is uncalled for.

situation: Dilbert gives a presentation and points to a cartoon on an overhead projector, laughing at how well it sums things up. He looks at his stony-faced audience of bald, expressionless men and realizes none of them find it funny. They invite him to become a humorless blob like them and tell him humor is not wanted.
punchline: The audience is so devoid of humor that they respond to a joke by trying to recruit Dilbert into their joyless conformity.
summary: A presenter's attempt at levity falls flat in front of a room of grim, identical colleagues who urge him to give up on humor.

file: 1998/1998-07-27_dilbert_mother_buy wquipment_budget cut_navy seal_mom proud_blocks reality_doesn't hear son_family.gif
title: Mom Proud of Wasteful Budget Spending

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My boss told me to buy a bunch of equipment we don't need.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That way our budget won't get cut next year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: I'm so proud of you, son.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do you say that with a straight face?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: I try to imagine you as a Navy SEAL.

situation: Dilbert visits his mother in her kitchen and explains that his boss told him to buy unnecessary equipment so the department's budget won't be cut next year. His mother responds that she is proud of him. When Dilbert asks how she can say that with a straight face, she reveals she copes by imagining he is a Navy SEAL.
punchline: His mother can only be proud of his wasteful, pointless corporate work by pretending he has a completely different and more heroic job.
summary: A son confesses to his mom about a silly spending scheme at work, and she copes with her pride by fantasizing he does something far more impressive.

file: 1998/1998-06-24_dogbert the ceo_stock price_personal gain_budget cuts_products_relevant.gif
title: CEO Dogbert Games the Stock Price

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the C.E.O.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've decided to manipulate our stock price for personal gain.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll spin off a few divisions, buy back some of our stock and announce massive budget cuts.

transcript.speaker: Executive
transcript.text: Um... do you even know what products we make?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How would that be relevant?

situation: Dogbert, now the CEO, tells his executive team he plans to manipulate the company's stock price for his own gain, outlining spin-offs, stock buybacks and announced budget cuts. An executive timidly asks whether Dogbert even knows what products the company makes.
punchline: Dogbert dismisses the question because a CEO focused on financial engineering and personal gain considers the company's actual products irrelevant.
summary: A newly installed canine chief executive reveals his plan to juice the share price and shrugs off any need to understand what the firm actually sells.

file: 1998/1998-12-17_radio to work_alice_breaks radio_sound of breaking.gif
title: Alice Silences the Coworker's Radio

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Hey, Alice, I brought my radio to work. You can hear it from your cubicle too.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is there anything in particular that you want to hear?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Yes, there is.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Bam bam bam

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey!

situation: A cheerful coworker tells Alice he has brought a radio to work that she can hear from her cubicle, and offers to play anything she wants. Alice takes the radio and smashes it, sending debris flying over the cubicle wall into Dilbert's cubicle, where he protests.
punchline: Alice's request is the sound of the radio being destroyed, and the flying wreckage hits innocent bystander Dilbert.
summary: Offered her choice of music from a coworker's new radio, Alice opts for the noise of it being smashed to pieces.

file: 1998/1998-12-02_microsoft headquarters_misspelled word_spell checking software_market power_new word industry.gif
title: Microsoft Makes Typos Industry Standard

transcript.speaker: Caption
transcript.text: Microsoft Headquarters

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: We misspelled a word in our spell-checking software.

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: You know what to do.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Um... use our market power to make the new word an industry standard?

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: And...?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Kill myself as an example to others?

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: In our booth at "Comdex."

situation: A Microsoft employee confesses that the company's spell-checking software contains a misspelled word. An unseen superior prompts him through the 'correct' response: abuse the company's market dominance to turn the error into an industry standard, then publicly kill himself at the Comdex trade show booth as a warning to others.
punchline: Microsoft's response to a mistake is to use monopoly power to redefine the error as the standard rather than fix it, and then to make a grisly public example of the employee responsible.
summary: A software giant's staffer learns that the company fixes its blunders by bending the whole industry to match them and by sacrificing the culprit in public.

file: 1998/1998-04-18_new guy_looks smarter_look dumber_ooga.gif
title: New Guy's Rapid Dumbing Down

transcript.speaker: New Guy
transcript.text: Alice, I'm the new guy. I look smarter than the people who already work here.

transcript.speaker: New Guy
transcript.text: As you get to know me, I'll look dumber and dumber.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That was fast.

transcript.speaker: New Guy
transcript.text: Ooga.

situation: A new employee introduces himself to Alice, claiming he currently looks smarter than the existing staff. He warns that she will see him look dumber as she gets to know him, and then shakes her hand. Alice remarks on how quickly it happened, as he responds with a caveman-like grunt.
punchline: The new guy's prediction that he'll seem dumber over time comes true almost instantly when he grunts 'Ooga,' proving he is already dumb.
summary: A newcomer predicts his reputation will decline as colleagues get to know him, then proves it within seconds with a primitive grunt.

file: 1998/1998-08-26_excellent performance_no bonus_lost fortune_elbonian collpase_fault for working here.gif
title: No Bonus Thanks to Elbonia

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your performance was excellent, but there's no bonus this year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why not?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company lost a fortune in the Elbonian currency collapse.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But in a way, it's your own fault for working here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks. That takes the sting out.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that despite excellent performance he won't receive a bonus because the company lost a fortune in the Elbonian currency collapse. The Boss then adds that it's Dilbert's own fault for working at the company. Dilbert responds with sarcastic thanks.
punchline: Blaming the employee for the company's losses simply because he works there is absurd, and Dilbert's sarcastic 'that takes the sting out' shows it makes the insult worse, not better.
summary: A manager denies a high-performing employee his bonus due to a foreign currency loss and then insultingly suggests the employee brought it on himself.

file: 1998/1998-02-13_dogbert the supermodel_lingerie shoot_short round guy_black socks_ice.gif
title: Dogbert's Supermodel Black Sock Sexiness

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Supermodel

transcript.speaker: Photographer
transcript.text: Your first assignment is a lingerie shoot. You'll be wearing black socks.

transcript.speaker: Photographer
transcript.text: There's nothing sexier than a short, round guy in black socks.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wow! This works!

transcript.speaker: Photographer
transcript.text: Quick! Get me a big block of ice to sit on!

situation: Dogbert begins a career as a supermodel, and a blond photographer in a robe tells him his first job is a lingerie shoot wearing black socks. The photographer claims a short, round guy in black socks is the sexiest thing possible. Dogbert admires himself in a hand mirror while the photographer, visibly flustered and sweating, asks for ice.
punchline: The photographer is so overheated by Dogbert's black-sock look that he demands a block of ice to sit on, proving Dogbert's modeling approach works.
summary: A smitten photographer is so aroused by a sock-clad Dogbert that he needs ice to cool down.

file: 1998/1998-07-18_myron not moron_run spell check_suggestions_spell check.gif
title: Spell Check Turns Myron Into Moron

transcript.speaker: Myron
transcript.text: My name is Myron, not Moron!

transcript.speaker: Myron
transcript.text: Next time that you run spell check, don't automatically take its suggestions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's "spell check"?

situation: An angry employee named Myron stands before the Boss's desk holding a printed document. He complains that his name was changed from Myron to Moron, and instructs the Boss not to blindly accept spell check suggestions. The Boss sits blankly and thinks to himself that he doesn't know what spell check is.
punchline: The Boss is so clueless about technology that he doesn't know what spell check is, yet his document called an employee a moron, which suggests the label may suit the Boss himself.
summary: A furious employee scolds his boss for letting software autocorrect his name into an insult, but the boss doesn't even know the tool exists.

file: 1998/1998-10-08_not policy_fire morons_expensive_make your job unpleasent_so you quit_porject_bitten by coyoytes_vested.gif
title: Making Your Job Unpleasant Until Quitting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's not my policy to fire morons, Donald. Firing is expensive.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's my policy to make your job so unpleasant that you quit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, your project involves being bitten by coyotes?

transcript.speaker: Donald
transcript.text: Only two more years and I'm vested.

setting: Office, with a coyote-infested project area in the final panel
situation: The Boss tells Donald, an employee he considers a moron, that he won't fire him because firing costs money. Instead he assigns Donald miserable work to force him to resign. Dilbert later asks about the project, which turns out to involve Donald being bitten by coyotes.
punchline: Donald is willing to endure literal coyote attacks for two more years just to qualify for his pension benefits, showing how unpleasant a job can get before someone quits.
summary: A manager avoids the cost of firing by handing an employee a painful assignment, but the employee stoically endures the animal attacks to secure his retirement benefits.

file: 1998/1998-03-09_very technical_gallery_google eyed marketeers.gif
title: Gallery of Googly-Eyed Marketeers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is very technical. I'll explain...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Snap.

transcript.speaker: Sign
transcript.text: Gallery of googly-eyed marketeers

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Drool! Good one.

setting: Office meeting room and a nearby wall
situation: Dilbert starts to give a technical explanation to a marketing person across the table, who goes wide-eyed and glazed over. Dilbert snaps a photo of the vacant, googly-eyed stare. He then pins it on a wall display of similar photos while Wally approves.
punchline: Marketing people reliably go glassy-eyed whenever engineers explain anything technical, so Dilbert collects the evidence as a trophy gallery.
summary: An engineer photographs the blank, bug-eyed stare of a marketer hearing technical talk and adds it to his wall of similar shots.

file: 1998/1998-10-06_shovel_full of assignments_get done_most importatnt_identify acronyms_never been used.gif
title: Most Important Assignment: Unused Acronyms

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's another shovel full of assignments.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How am I supposed to get all of that done?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Only do the most important ones.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "Identify all the acronyms that have never been used."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's an important one.

situation: The Boss arrives carrying a literal shovel piled high with papers and dumps yet another stack of assignments on Dilbert. When Dilbert protests that he can't finish it all, the Boss tells him to do only the most important ones. Dilbert reads one task aloud, which is to identify acronyms that have never been used, and the Boss insists that one is important.
punchline: The Boss's sense of priority is absurd, since he considers a nonsensical, pointless task to be among the most important ones.
summary: A manager shovels a mountain of work onto an employee, then declares that a ridiculous busywork task deserves top priority.

file: 1998/1998-02-01_meeting_introductions_alice_breakdown_bad company_bad boss_freak out at meeting_business.gif
title: Alice Mortified by Reporting Chain

transcript.speaker: Meeting Leader
transcript.text: Let's start by introducing ourselves.

transcript.speaker: Susan Block
transcript.text: I'm Susan Block from I.T.G. I work for Emily Wooten.

transcript.speaker: Max Blumf
transcript.text: I'm Max Blumf. I work for Susan.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm Alice. I work for... uh... I...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Aaagh!!! I'm filled with shame by association!!!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why me? Why why why

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Please take me to your group! I'm not tainted!!!

transcript.speaker: Meeting Leader
transcript.text: Can we start over? I forgot who the first three people are.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Sob

situation: At the start of a meeting, attendees introduce themselves by naming the person they work for. As the chain of reporting builds, Alice reaches her turn and realizes she reports to the Boss, then has a loud breakdown and begs the others to take her into their group. The meeting leader, distracted by the commotion, asks to start over.
punchline: Alice is so ashamed of working for her incompetent boss that she falls apart in front of strangers, and the meeting leader is only concerned that he forgot everyone's names.
summary: A routine round of introductions turns into a meltdown when Alice is forced to admit who her manager is.

file: 1998/1998-01-02_nobel prize commitee_theories_understand_science_simpilist soultrion_heories_vote ourselves.gif
title: Nobel Committee Picks Randomly From Pile

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Nobel Prize Committee

transcript.speaker: Committee Member 1
transcript.text: Okay, we've narrowed it down to the theories we don't understand.

transcript.speaker: Committee Member 1
transcript.text: In science, the simplest solution is usually the best. Which of these theories is the simplest solution?

transcript.speaker: Committee Member 2
transcript.text: Well... that would be whatever is on top of the pile.

transcript.speaker: Committee Member 3
transcript.text: Are we sure we can't vote for ourselves?

setting: Nobel Prize Committee meeting room with a stack of binders
situation: Three wild-haired scientists on the Nobel Prize Committee have narrowed the candidates down to theories they cannot understand. When one asks which theory is the simplest, another points out that it is simply whichever is on top of the pile. The third then wonders whether they can vote for themselves.
punchline: The committee admits it picks prize winners by grabbing whatever is on top of a pile of theories it doesn't understand, and one member would rather just award the prize to himself.
summary: Prestigious award judges who can't comprehend the research choose the winner by whatever lies on top of the stack, and one wishes to nominate himself.

file: 1998/1998-04-12_criticize coworkers_look smart_nuts_dogbert therapist_weekly sessions_run out of money_vure_therapy_paid by hour_fasle memory_aliens_psychology.gif
title: Dogbert's Profitable Therapy Sessions

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I criticize my co-workers to make myself look smart.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Apparently it isn't working.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: What do you mean by that?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Nothing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ooh, that reminds me to add nuts to my grocery list.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend that we have weekly sessions until you run out of money.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Can you cure me?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No, I'm paid by the hour. I'll give you problems you've never even heard of.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We have a few minutes today. Would you like a false memory?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Maybe something with aliens?

setting: Dogbert's therapy office with a reclining chair
situation: Dogbert acts as a psychotherapist while a man lies on the couch confessing that he criticizes co-workers to seem smart. Dogbert insults him, ignores him to jot down a grocery list, and then admits he has no intention of curing him because he bills by the hour. In the end he offers to implant a false memory, and the patient eagerly requests one involving aliens.
punchline: The therapist openly admits he profits from keeping patients sick and even sells fabricated memories, and the patient happily goes along with it.
summary: A pooch playing psychiatrist mocks, ignores and milks a patient for cash before selling him an invented alien encounter.

file: 1998/1998-08-30_document prcedures_requirement_engineers_submit time cards_magic cylinder_trash can_gone by morning_five years_no one complained.gif
title: Time Cards Vanish Into Magic Cylinder

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need to document your procedures. It's an ISO 9000 requirement.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... the engineers submit their time cards and then you do what?

transcript.speaker: Timekeeper
transcript.text: I put them in a pile until I'm sure they're all here.

transcript.speaker: Timekeeper
transcript.text: Then I move them to the magic cylinder.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The trash can?

transcript.speaker: Timekeeper
transcript.text: No, it's a magic cylinder. I put my work in there and by morning it's gone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've been giving you my time cards for five years.

transcript.speaker: Timekeeper
transcript.text: No one has complained yet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: After today, I am not rounding to the nearest fifteen minutes.

situation: Dilbert interviews a time-card clerk to document her procedures for an ISO 9000 requirement. She explains that she stacks the engineers' time cards and then puts them in a 'magic cylinder' that makes them disappear by morning, which Dilbert recognizes as a trash can. Realizing his time cards have been discarded for five years, he decides to stop rounding his hours.
punchline: Since nobody has ever processed or noticed the time cards, Dilbert realizes he can pad his reported hours without consequence.
summary: An employee discovers that the paperwork he's faithfully submitted for years has simply been thrown away, and decides to exploit the lack of oversight.

file: 1998/1998-04-14_obnoxious_useless coworker_needed cooperation_expiration date_cologne.gif
title: Coworkers Trash Departed Colleague Politely Pretending

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm glad he quit. He was such an obnoxious, useless co-worker.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: We had to be nice to him because we needed his cooperation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The jerk!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: He should check the expiration date on his cologne!

transcript.speaker: Colleague (thought)
transcript.text: Next time, I will NOT give two weeks' notice.

situation: After a colleague has quit, Alice, Dilbert and Wally sit around a conference table and gleefully insult him, admitting they only pretended to be nice because they needed his cooperation. In the final panel, another coworker silently listens and thinks that he will not give two weeks' notice when he quits.
punchline: Hearing how viciously his colleagues badmouth a departed coworker, the remaining employee realizes he would be next and decides to leave without notice.
summary: A trio of officemates tear into a recently departed coworker, and the one listener decides he'll skip the courtesy of advance notice when his own turn comes.

file: 1998/1998-10-19_catbert_hr director_not allowed_eat desk_semi plausible reason_hate.gif
title: Catbert's Honest Reason for Policy

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: New policy: Employees are not allowed to eat at their desks.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Because why? I need a semi-plausible reason.

transcript.speaker: Computer
transcript.text: Because I hate you.

setting: Catbert's H.R. office, seated at his computer
situation: Catbert, the H.R. Director, types out a new policy banning employees from eating at their desks. He pauses to wonder what reason to give, since he needs something that sounds semi-plausible. He then types the real reason: he simply hates the employees.
punchline: The H.R. director's actual rationale for workplace policy is plain malice, which he drops in place of a plausible-sounding justification.
summary: A malicious personnel chief drafts a desk-dining ban and, lacking a believable excuse, simply admits that spite is the motive.

file: 1998/1998-08-07_digitized_indexed_worlds greatest art_last supper_composition cluttered_delete_replace_clip art_bagels.gif
title: Boss Edits The Last Supper

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We've digitized and indexed the world's greatest art. This is "The Last Supper."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nice, but...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The composition is cluttered. Delete a few of those guys. Do you have any clip art of bagels?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do they look happy?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Compared to me, yes.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, at his computer
situation: Dilbert shows the Boss a digitized, indexed version of Leonardo da Vinci's The Last Supper on his computer. The Boss critiques it as cluttered, asks him to delete some of the apostles and add bagel clip art, then asks whether the figures look happy. Dilbert dryly replies that they look happier than he does.
punchline: The Boss treats a masterpiece like a sloppy slide deck to be tweaked with clip art, and Dilbert's deadpan answer shows how miserable the pointless editing makes him.
summary: A manager casually demands that a famous painting be trimmed and decorated with bagel images, leaving the employee more unhappy than the doomed dinner guests.

file: 1998/1998-06-16_drug treatment program_admit problem_proactive_pointy hored_hallucinations_with drawl_ink blotch test.gif
title: Inkblot Test Terrifies Alice in Rehab

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Drug treatment program

transcript.speaker: Counselor
transcript.text: The first step is to admit you have a drug problem.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I don't.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My pointy-haired boss forced me to be here because he thinks it makes him look proactive.

transcript.speaker: Counselor
transcript.text: Hallucinations are common during withdrawal. Let's do an inkblot test.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Aaagh!!

situation: A counselor tells Alice that the first step in recovery is admitting a drug problem, but she says she has none and explains that her boss sent her there to look proactive. The counselor then shows her an inkblot card, which turns out to look like her boss with his pointy hair, and she screams.
punchline: Alice sees her boss in the inkblot, which the counselor takes as a drug hallucination, though it really shows how awful dealing with her boss is.
summary: A woman sent to rehab by her image-conscious manager is dismissed as hallucinating when a test card reminds her of him.

file: 1998/1998-09-01_project_needs attention_meeting_helper for porject_engineers_business.gif
title: Meeting Skipped, Project Dumped on Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This project needs your complete attention.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally's right. Forget the other projects and focus on that one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did I miss anything at the meeting?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We got you a little helper for your project.

setting: Conference room, then a lunch table in the break area
situation: In a meeting, Wally and Alice insist that a certain project deserves someone's complete attention, telling that person to drop all other projects. In the last panel Dilbert, who was absent because he was eating lunch, asks if he missed anything. Wally cheerfully reveals that the meeting assigned him the project along with a 'helper'.
punchline: Dilbert skipped the meeting and was punished by having a new project and a so-called helper dumped on him in his absence, with the helper likely being useless extra work.
summary: A meeting full of coworkers decides how a missing colleague should spend his time, and he finds out only after he turns up for lunch.

file: 1998/1998-08-13_dilbert_moon landing_weekend_send a shuttle_male engineers_status.gif
title: Moon Colony of Engineer-Loving Women

transcript.speaker: Blonde Woman
transcript.text: NASA put all the women who love engineers on the moon. They say it's an important experiment.

transcript.speaker: Woman with Black Hair
transcript.text: Every weekend they send a shuttle full of male NASA engineers to check on our status.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Uh-oh. We have company.

setting: The surface of the moon, with craters and a rocky outpost
situation: Dilbert sits on the moon surrounded by adoring women, including two dark-haired women who cling to him and a blonde woman who explains the setup. They reveal that NASA put all the women who love engineers on the moon as an experiment, with weekly shuttles of male engineers visiting. In the last panel, a group of engineers in party hats, with drinks, realizes more visitors have arrived.
punchline: The dream of being surrounded by women who love engineers is revealed to be a convenient NASA 'experiment' that the engineers are secretly enjoying as weekend parties, and the unexpected newcomer threatens their private fun.
summary: Dilbert finds himself on a lunar colony of admiring women, only to learn it is a government program and that other engineers are already partying nearby.

file: 1998/1998-12-04_face time_promotion paper work_send photos_vp.gif
title: Promotion Through Mailed Photos

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you want to get promoted, you need lots of "face time" with your V.P.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend sending photos of yourself every week.

transcript.speaker: VP
transcript.text: More photos... he must be a relative.

transcript.speaker: Assistant
transcript.text: I'll start the promotion paperwork.

setting: Outdoors on a rocky hill, then a VP's office
situation: Dogbert advises Dilbert that getting promoted requires lots of 'face time' with the VP, and suggests mailing photos of himself every week. In the VP's office, the VP looks through the stack of photos Dilbert sent and concludes he must be a relative, so his assistant begins the promotion paperwork.
punchline: Dogbert takes 'face time' literally, and the VP's nepotism-driven assumption that a photo-sender must be family means the absurd advice actually works.
summary: A dog's literal take on career advice leads a manager to promote a stranger whose pictures he assumes mean kinship.

file: 1998/1998-08-28_department mascot_industrious beaver_woodchuck_perky.gif
title: Beaver Mascot Is Actually Woodchuck

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our department mascot will be the industrious beaver.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's a picture of a woodchuck.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He looks perky. That's close enough.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He could be a beaver who lives in a hole.

setting: Conference room during a department meeting
situation: The Boss announces that the department mascot will be an industrious beaver, pointing to a picture on an easel. Dilbert points out that the picture actually shows a woodchuck. The Boss dismisses the error, saying the animal looks perky enough and could just be a beaver who lives in a hole.
punchline: The Boss refuses to admit his mistake and invents an absurd rationalization so that a woodchuck can stand in for a beaver.
summary: A manager picks the wrong animal for the team emblem and brushes off the correction with a flimsy excuse.

file: 1998/1998-11-30_alice_recipient_of stone of quality_motivational rock_says thanks_costs engraved_knocks out boss_police arrive_find rock.gif
title: Stone of Quality Gets Weaponized

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, you're the first recipient of the motivational "Stone of Quality."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It cost a thousand dollars to have it engraved. It's my way of saying "Thanks."

transcript.speaker: Police Officer
transcript.text: There's no weapon, but I found this cool motivational rock.

situation: The Boss presents Alice with a motivational "Stone of Quality" and brags that engraving it cost a thousand dollars, calling it his way of saying thanks. In the final panel, police officers investigate the Boss lying unconscious on the floor and find only the rock, while Alice peeks out from behind the cubicle wall.
punchline: Alice responded to the cheap, pointless 'reward' by knocking out the Boss with the rock, turning the motivational stone into the weapon the police can't identify.
summary: A manager hands out an overpriced engraved rock as thanks, and the recipient promptly uses it to put him on the floor.

file: 1998/1998-01-28_deputy of common sense_motivate emplyees_insulting gifts_symbolism_chess pieces_same team_pawns_saving rooks.gif
title: Chess Pieces as Insulting Gifts

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Deputy of Common Sense

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You are accused of trying to motivate your employees with insulting gifts.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're missing the symbolism. I gave them chess pieces to show that we're all on the same team.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Specifically, you gave them pawns.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm saving the rooks for bonus day.

setting: The Boss's office, with Dogbert acting as Deputy of Common Sense
situation: Dogbert, in a police-style cap as the Deputy of Common Sense, accuses the Boss of trying to motivate employees with insulting gifts. The Boss defends himself by claiming the chess pieces symbolize teamwork. Dogbert points out that the employees only got pawns, and the Boss reveals he is saving the better pieces for bonus day.
punchline: The Boss's gift of chess pawns confirms that he views employees as expendable pieces, and his plan to hand out rooks at bonus time shows he thinks cheap tokens of symbolism can substitute for real rewards.
summary: A self-satisfied manager defends his cheap morale-boosting trinkets as meaningful symbolism, only to expose how little he values his staff.

file: 1998/1998-02-04_career talk_boss_office_work you_health deteriorates_obsolete_downsize_plan work fast_ill.gif
title: Boss's Career Plan: Burnout, Then Downsizing

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like to talk about my career path.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My plan is to work you until your health deteriorates and your skills are obsolete. Then I'll downsize you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm ill.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Really? I've never had a plan work this fast before.

situation: Dilbert asks the Boss to discuss his career path. The Boss cheerfully explains that his plan is to overwork Dilbert until his health fails and his skills become outdated, then lay him off. Dilbert announces that he is already ill, and the Boss is pleased that the plan is succeeding so quickly.
punchline: The Boss treats Dilbert's sudden illness as proof that his exploitative plan is working ahead of schedule, showing that he sees employees as disposable resources.
summary: A worker asks about his future at the company and learns that management intends to run him into the ground before discarding him.

file: 1998/1998-03-31_necktie_getting shorter_casual clothes_six months_necktie gone_bald.gif
title: Shrinking Necktie, Unnoticed Baldness

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it my imagination, or is your necktie getting shorter every day?

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Heh heh...

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I'm gradually moving toward casual clothes. In six months this necktie will be gone and no one will notice.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Everyone noticed when you went bald.

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I'm bald?

situation: Dilbert notices that a coworker's necktie seems to be getting shorter each day. The coworker explains he is slowly phasing out his tie so that nobody will notice when he is finally dressing casually. Dilbert points out that everyone noticed when he went bald, and the coworker is shocked to learn he is bald.
punchline: The coworker's theory that gradual change goes unnoticed is undercut by the revelation that he is bald and apparently never realized it.
summary: A man trims his tie bit by bit to sneak into casual dress, only to learn he has been oblivious to his own baldness.

file: 1998/1998-05-21_hideous sycophant_no hope_career advancement_lifestyle choice.gif
title: Insulting the Office Suck-Up

transcript.speaker: Allen
transcript.text: So, Allen, what's it like to be a hideous sycophant?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's okay.

transcript.speaker: Allen
transcript.text: What's it like to have no hope of career advancement?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not bad.

transcript.speaker: Allen
transcript.text: Were you born that way or is it a lifestyle choice?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll ask Mom, but I think it was bad parenting.

setting: Office corridor and then a cafeteria table
situation: Allen, a coworker with a flower in his mouth, is asked a series of insulting questions about being a sycophant with no career prospects. The speaker in the first panel is mislabeled as Allen in the printed dialogue; the questions are posed to Allen by the other character, and Allen answers blandly. In the last panel, he is asked whether he was born that way or chose it, and he replies that it was probably bad parenting.
punchline: The suck-up shrugs off every insult with calm indifference, and even deadpans that his sycophancy was likely caused by bad parenting, deflecting blame to his mother.
summary: A man with a flower in his mouth endures a barrage of insults about his groveling nature and offers only mild, deadpan answers.

file: 1998/1998-05-12_college_dilmom_filberts mother_investment_results of college_sons cubicle_education.gif
title: Mom Visits Dilbert's Underwhelming Cubicle

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: It's so exciting to visit my son's cubicle!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: I worked hard to put you through college. Now I'll see the results of my investment!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Um... you did attend classes, right?

setting: A car, then Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dilbert drives his excited mother to his workplace, with the family dog in the back seat. She says she worked hard to pay for his college and looks forward to seeing the results. When she sees his small, drab cubicle, she doubts whether he ever attended classes.
punchline: His mother sees his tiny, bland cubicle as the payoff for her college investment and is so unimpressed that she wonders if he skipped class.
summary: A proud mother tours her grown son's cramped office cubicle and suspects the tuition money was wasted.

file: 1998/1998-05-11_cubicle_box_explination_work environment_dilberts mother_dilmom.gif
title: Explaining Cubicles to Dilbert's Mom

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Someday I'd like to see your office.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a cubicle, Mom.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: What's a cubicle?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Imagine the most beautiful place on Earth...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Mom
transcript.text: Okay, I've got it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now imagine you can never go there because you work in a box.

situation: Dilbert's mother, stirring a pot on the stove, says she'd like to visit his office. Dilbert tells her it's a cubicle and, when she doesn't know what that is, walks her through an analogy: picture the most beautiful place on Earth, then imagine you can never go there because you work in a box.
punchline: Dilbert explains that a cubicle is the opposite of paradise: it keeps you boxed in at work and away from anywhere pleasant.
summary: A son uses a daydream of paradise to explain to his mother how confining and joyless his cubicle is.

file: 1998/1998-03-01_good news_budgets_calculations_salary bidget_vacation days_got greedy.gif
title: Boss's Magic Budget Math Backfires

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Good news on your budgets. I did some recalculating last night.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I found a way to give more money to every project without increasing the total budget for projects!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: Does your new way involve poor math skills?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ignore the skeptic.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Hey, I have a suggestion!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Maybe you could recalculate our salary budget next.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And when was the last time you recalculated our vacation days?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I calculate that we have an hour left for this meeting. But I'm interested in your calculation.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think we got greedy when we asked if he had change for a five.

setting: Conference room during a budget meeting
situation: The Boss announces he has recalculated project budgets so every project gets more money without raising the total. Dilbert questions his math, and Carol and Dilbert then suggest he also recalculate their salaries and vacation days. In the final panel the three of them are happily counting stacks of cash, implying the Boss's magic math paid out for them.
punchline: The Boss's impossible recalculation was taken literally by the employees, who asked him to make change for a five and ended up with piles of money, showing they exploited his bad math and got greedy.
summary: After the Boss claims he can boost every budget for free, his staff test his arithmetic and walk away clutching handfuls of cash.

file: 1998/1998-03-17_men 25% more pay_math skills_praise for math skills_33% more.gif
title: Pay Gap Math Correction

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This article says men are paid 25% more than women. How do you explain that?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Actually, it says women make 75¢ for every dollar that men make. That's 33% more for men.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I suppose there's almost no chance you'll praise me for my math skills right now.

situation: Alice, holding an article, asks the Boss and Dilbert to explain why men are paid 25% more than women. The Boss, reading a magazine, corrects her statistic, noting that 75 cents on the dollar actually works out to 33% more for men. He then smugly fishes for praise for his math skills while Alice glares at him.
punchline: The Boss responds to a question about gender pay inequality by pedantically correcting the percentage, missing the point entirely and expecting a compliment for his arithmetic.
summary: A manager answers a colleague's complaint about unequal pay by nitpicking her figures and then angles for applause for being good at maths.

file: 1998/1998-12-14_dogbert_cuter with ears up_could kill_dilbert_impossible to be cuter.gif
title: Dogbert's Cuteness Threat Backfires

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I discovered I'm much cuter when I put my ears up.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It seems impossible that I could be any cuter than I was.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you aren't.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I could kill you and no jury would believe I did it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, THAT was cute.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert stands on the arm of the couch with his ears perked up and boasts about how adorable he looks. Dilbert, reading a newspaper, suggests he may not be cuter at all. Dogbert replies that he could murder Dilbert and no jury would believe it, which Dilbert admits is cute.
punchline: Dogbert's menacing threat only works because he is so cute, and Dilbert grudgingly concedes that the threat itself proves his point.
summary: A fluffy-eared Dogbert claims to be irresistibly adorable, then proves it by delivering a chilling threat that nobody could take seriously.

file: 1998/1998-12-20_direction signs_conference_arrow_pointing right_need pointing left_spooky_flipped sign.gif
title: Boss Wants Venue Moved For Arrows

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have a problem.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I ordered these direction signs for our conference tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But they all point to the right. I need left arrows.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is it too late to change the site of the conference to match the arrows?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, that would put us in the middle of the lake.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I suppose we could use helicopters to build a deep-water platform hotel...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: By tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, but get two bids...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Spooky.

situation: The Boss complains that the conference direction signs he ordered all point right when he needs left. He asks Dilbert whether the conference venue can be moved to match the arrows, and Dilbert sarcastically suggests building a deep-water platform hotel in the lake by helicopter. The Boss takes the suggestion seriously, then notices that flipping the sign solves his problem.
punchline: The Boss seriously considers an absurdly expensive construction project, only to discover that turning the arrow around fixes it, and he finds this 'spooky' rather than obvious.
summary: A manager would rather relocate an entire event than notice that a sign can simply be rotated.

file: 1998/1998-05-25_theory testing_dogbert_people told what to do_quit job_build pyramid_dolt_honesty doesn't mix.gif
title: Dogbert Tests Obedience With Pyramid Demand

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I will now test my theory that people like to be told what to do.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Quit your job and build me a pyramid, you homely dolt!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I liked it until the dolt part.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've noticed that honesty doesn't mix well with anything.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dogbert sits on the couch beside Dilbert, who is reading a Tech EE magazine, and announces an experiment to see if people like being told what to do. He then orders Dilbert to quit his job and build him a pyramid, insulting him in the process. Dilbert says he was fine with the command until Dogbert called him a dolt.
punchline: Dilbert is perfectly willing to obey a ridiculous order, and only objects to the insult, which suggests Dogbert's theory holds up and that his bluntness is the only thing that spoils the effect.
summary: A scheming dog's experiment in bossing his owner around works fine until the name-calling gets in the way.

file: 1998/1998-01-20_dogbert_metal detector_psychic powers_skeptic_skeptic drawers_unicorns.gif
title: Skeptic Sweeps Sock Drawer for Unicorns

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert and the Skeptic

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If your controlled tests have never found psychic powers, how do you know the tests work for that sort of thing?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
