transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to do some personal business during my lunch hour.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Normally I would work through lunch.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But this will take a full hour.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It would only take two minutes if I used the Internet.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But the Internet is for business use only!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our company has a limited number of zeroes and ones.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When they're gone, they're gone!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Furthermore...

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You mocked him for a full hour.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now it's time to eat.

setting: Office cubicles and the Boss's office
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he will run personal errands at lunch and explains that using the Internet would cut the task to two minutes. The Boss forbids personal Internet use and claims the company has a limited supply of zeroes and ones, then rambles on with a lecture. By the end, the lecture has eaten up the entire lunch hour.
punchline: The Boss's absurd lecture about rationing digital zeroes and ones wastes Dilbert's whole lunch hour, so the pointless rule costs far more time than the Internet would have.
summary: A worker's request to save time online is met with a nonsensical speech that burns up his whole break.

file: 1998/1998-11-09_catbert_hr director_tiny raises_nothing to motivate_alice complains.gif
title: Catbert Denies Raises to Preserve Motivation

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I work hard, but all I get are tiny raises.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: If we gave you everything you wanted, then you would have nothing to motivate you.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I don't want to be motivated.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That's why I enjoy doing it!

situation: Alice complains to Catbert, the H.R. Director, that her hard work only earns her tiny raises. Catbert replies that giving her everything she wanted would leave her with nothing to motivate her. When she says she doesn't want to be motivated, Catbert happily says that's why he enjoys his job.
punchline: Catbert's motivational excuse for stingy raises is really a cover for his enjoyment of frustrating employees, since motivation is exactly what Alice doesn't want.
summary: An employee protests her meagre pay increases, and the human resources cat turns his sadism into a management philosophy.

file: 1998/1998-06-20_m_new ceo_ethical person_sinking ship_plunder treasure_take challenge.gif
title: Ethical CEO Candidates Won't Plunder

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: An executive search firm is trying to find a new C.E.O. for us.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: It'll be tough.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: No ethical person would board a sinking ship just to plunder its treasure.

transcript.speaker: Recruiter
transcript.text: Are you ready to take the challenge?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oh, I'll take more than that!

setting: Office hallway and an executive recruiter's office
situation: Dilbert tells a coworker that an executive search firm is looking for a new CEO for the struggling company, and the coworker says it will be hard to find a candidate. In the last panel, a recruiter asks Dogbert, the candidate, if he is ready for the challenge.
punchline: Dogbert, as an unethical candidate, is happy to board the sinking company just to plunder it, so he will take far more than the challenge.
summary: A failing company struggles to recruit a new chief executive until an opportunistic dog volunteers to loot it.

file: 1998/1998-03-13_hideous treatment_employees_elbnina factory_forced to wear clamps_no union_business.gif
title: Clamped Heads, Swift Workplace Complaint Fix

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Here's my report on the hideous treatment of employees in our Elbonian factory.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The employees are forced to wear huge clamps on their heads.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Then I said, "The employees can't complain because they have no union."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Swift.

situation: Alice presents the Boss with a report on terrible conditions at the Elbonian factory, including workers being forced to wear huge clamps on their heads. In the last panel she sits in the cafeteria with Wally and Dilbert, all wearing the clamps, as she explains that she told the Boss the workers can't complain because they have no union. Wally approves of how swiftly the Boss acted.
punchline: Alice's report on abusive treatment backfired, because the Boss responded by clamping the heads of the people who reported it, so they cannot complain either.
summary: A report on cruel factory conditions gets the whistleblowers fitted with the same head restraints they described.

file: 1998/1998-02-26_dogbert curse_sends chain letter_die if didnt_worlds smartest garbageman_send chain letters.gif
title: Garbage Man Curses Chain Letter Sender

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And the "Dogbert Curse" strikes anyone who sends a chain letter. But the letter said I'd die if I didn't.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're the world's smartest garbage man; how would you handle this?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Did you know there's also a "Garbage Man's Curse" for people who send chain letters?

setting: Outdoors by a trash can, near Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert frets to a garbage man about a chain letter that threatens death if he doesn't pass it on, while the garbage man collects trash. Dilbert asks the 'world's smartest garbage man' for advice. The garbage man replies that there is also a 'Garbage Man's Curse' for chain letter senders, and in the last panel Dogbert appears dressed as a mummy.
punchline: The garbage man's solution to a chain letter curse is to invent a rival curse that punishes anyone who sends it, turning the superstition against itself.
summary: A worried man seeks a trash collector's wisdom about a threatening chain letter and is offered a counter-curse instead of reassurance.

file: 1998/1998-05-01_alice_promotion_dont know_hired a strsnger_out side of company_the boss_obstructs progress.gif
title: Promotion Denied, Outsider Hired Instead

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I checked with the other managers; they don't know you well enough to promote you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So we've decided to hire someone from outside the company.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: At least the other managers have heard my name now.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I didn't use your real name.

situation: The Boss tells Alice that she can't be promoted because the other managers don't know her well enough, so an outsider will be hired for the job instead. As she leaves, Alice bitterly remarks that at least the managers now know her name, and the Boss reveals he didn't even use her real name when he asked about her.
punchline: Alice's small consolation that she got some visibility is crushed when the Boss admits he never actually used her name, so she remains unknown and the promotion process was a sham.
summary: A manager passes over his own employee for promotion because nobody knows her, then admits he never even mentioned her by name.

file: 1998/1998-06-06_company strategy_wandering cubcilem_first to market.gif
title: Deducing Strategy From Cubicle Wandering

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our Pointy-Haired Boss won't tell me our company's strategy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I spend my days wandering from cubicle to cubicle, trying to deduce the strategy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So far I've ruled out "first to market."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And "premiere" anything.

situation: Dilbert peers over cubicle walls and tells a coworker that The Boss refuses to reveal the company's strategy. Since nobody will tell him, he spends his days wandering between cubicles trying to deduce it. He reports that he has ruled out being first to market, and Wally adds that they can also rule out being premiere at anything.
punchline: Wally and Dilbert deduce the company's strategy by elimination, and every strategy they cross off is a claim to excellence, implying the company is mediocre and slow at everything.
summary: With no strategy handed down from above, an engineer reverse-engineers it by process of elimination and finds only things the company is not good at.

file: 1998/1998-02-18_info meerical_invest savings_sell educational info_avoid scams_phase two.gif
title: Infomercial Scam Phase Two

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm going to make an infommercial.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm targeting the people who want to invest their savings but don't know how.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hope you plan to sell educational information about how to avoid scams.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Good idea for phase two!

situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert he is making an infomercial aimed at people who want to invest their savings but don't know how. Dilbert hopes he will sell educational material on avoiding scams, and Dogbert cheerfully says that will be phase two.
punchline: Dogbert's infomercial is itself a scam, and he plans to sell victims a guide to avoiding scams only after he has already fleefed them.
summary: A scheming dog plans to fleece naive investors with a late-night sales pitch, then sell them the cure afterward.

file: 1998/1998-05-31_pharmacy_two cashiers_stres meds_two lines_que up.gif
title: Pharmacy Queue Strategy Meltdown

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: PHARMACY

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is this one line or two?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll hedge my bets by standing in the middle.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This guy is confused too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Get behind me... Get behind me... Get behind me... Get behind me...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh-no! He's forming a new line behind the fast cashier!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He's distracted! I take the angle! I win!

transcript.speaker: Cashier
transcript.text: Stress medications are the other line.

situation: Dilbert arrives at a pharmacy and can't tell whether there is one line or two, so he stands in the middle to hedge his bets. He mentally wills another customer to line up behind him, then competes with him to reach the faster cashier, finally shoving past him. When he reaches the counter, the cashier tells him he is in the wrong line and that stress medications are handled at the other one.
punchline: Dilbert's frantic, ruthless fight over a checkout line leaves him so stressed that he has ended up at the wrong counter, needing the very stress medication he was racing toward.
summary: A man's cutthroat scheming to win the fastest pharmacy line backfires when he learns he was queuing for the wrong service all along.

file: 1998/1998-11-19_signed form_alter dna_legal documents_look stupid_not funny.gif
title: Dilbert's Unicorn Horn Legal Fine Print

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Don't complain to me. You signed the form giving us permission to alter your DNA.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: No one reads legal documents before signing them. It makes you look stupid.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have a point.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That is SO not funny.

setting: Office, with Catbert on a desk
situation: Dilbert has sprouted a unicorn horn and confronts Catbert, the evil HR director, about it. Catbert points out that Dilbert signed a form permitting DNA alteration without reading it, and says nobody reads legal documents because it makes them look stupid. Dilbert concedes the point and then complains the horn pun is not funny.
punchline: Dilbert is forced to admit that never reading what he signs made him a victim of his own carelessness, and his weary acceptance is delivered while wearing a ridiculous unicorn horn.
summary: A horn-headed employee learns the hard way that the paperwork he blindly signed let HR rewrite his genes.

file: 1998/1998-07-24_boss replaced_highly intelligent alien_held captive_hideous aliem prison_just an observation.gif
title: Boss Replaced by Intelligent Alien

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently my boss has been replaced by a highly intelligent alien.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That means my real boss is being held captive in some sort of hideous alien prison.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What do you plan to do about it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was just an observation.

setting: Dilbert's living room, on the couch
situation: Dilbert sits on his couch and tells Dogbert he suspects his boss has been swapped out for a highly intelligent alien. He reasons that the real boss must therefore be imprisoned somewhere by aliens. When Dogbert asks what he intends to do about it, Dilbert admits he has no plan and was merely making an observation.
punchline: Dilbert prefers the idea of an alien replacement to a boss who is simply this incompetent, and he has no intention of doing anything about it, so the alien theory stays a passive observation rather than a call to action.
summary: Dilbert muses to his dog that his manager seems to have been swapped for a brilliant extraterrestrial, then shrugs off any suggestion of taking action.

file: 1998/1998-12-19_hate your plan_real plan_opposite_nice worm_offers worms.gif
title: Reverse Psychology Plan Presentation, Then Worms

transcript.speaker: Meeting attendees
transcript.text: We hate your plan!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good, because the REAL plan is the opposite of what I just showed you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who wants a nice worm?

situation: Dilbert presents a plan to a roomful of coworkers, who shout that they hate it. He cheerfully says the real plan is the opposite of what he showed them and points to a card labeled 'Real Plan'. Then he holds up a dangling worm and offers it to the angry group.
punchline: After a clumsy bait-and-switch of a plan, Dilbert gives up on logic entirely and offers the hostile crowd a worm as a bizarre peace offering.
summary: A presenter's rejected proposal turns out to be a decoy, and he pacifies the angry audience by offering them a worm.

file: 1998/1998-06-28_future of company_project leader_passion fro success_extra pay_vague preference_allergy medication.gif
title: Passion for Success or Allergy Medication

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our next product will determine the future of our company!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need a project leader who has a passion for success!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Would that leader get extra pay?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's not about money, Wally. It's about a passion for success!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: All I have is a vague preference. How about you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, I'm feeling something... maybe it's...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, it's just my allergy medication.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What was it like?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It tingled.

situation: The Boss announces that the next product will decide the company's future and asks for a project leader with a passion for success. Wally asks about extra pay and then admits he only has a vague preference. Dilbert thinks he feels the passion rising, but it turns out to be allergy medication.
punchline: The only thing resembling passion in the room is a medication side effect, showing that the manager's demand for passion is hollow and nobody feels it without being paid.
summary: A manager demands a passionate project leader without offering pay, and the one stirring of enthusiasm turns out to be a pharmaceutical effect.

file: 1998/1998-01-15_skeptics association_psychic rat_passport_drivers licence_fake id_dna test_never been cloned.gif
title: Proving Identity to the Skeptics

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is this the "Skeptics Association"?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need your help to prove my rat isn't psychic.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My name is Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, I can prove it; I have a passport and a driver's license.

transcript.speaker: Skeptics Association
transcript.text: Well, yeah, it's easy to get a fake ID, but...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Hours later ...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...Okay, what if I take a DNA test?

transcript.speaker: Skeptics Association
transcript.text: No, I can't prove I've never been cloned!!

setting: Dilbert's phone call to the Skeptics Association
situation: Dilbert phones the Skeptics Association to get help proving his rat isn't psychic. The skeptic on the line first demands that Dilbert prove his own identity, dismissing his passport and driver's license as possibly fake. Hours later Dilbert is still on the phone, offering a DNA test, and the skeptic says even that can't rule out cloning.
punchline: Skeptics are so extreme in their doubt that they can't accept any proof of identity, so Dilbert never even gets to the question about the rat.
summary: A phone call seeking a debunker for a supposedly psychic pet turns into an endless argument over whether the caller can prove he is who he says he is.

file: 1998/1998-08-18_user manual_review_left empty_blad engineer_draft_characters.gif
title: Alice Rewrites Manual With Drama

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wally, did you review my draft of the user manual yet?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The characters in the examples gave me no reason to care about them. It left me empty.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Sadly, user "B" could never love user "A" because he was a bald engineer.

situation: Alice's draft of the user manual is being reviewed by Wally, who hands it back and complains that the characters in the examples were uninteresting and left him emotionally empty. Alice responds by revising it, rewriting the example users as the tragic figures of a romance, with user B unable to love user A because he is a bald engineer.
punchline: Alice takes the absurd feedback literally and sarcastically turns dry user manual examples into a melodramatic love story, mocking Wally with the fact that he himself is a bald engineer.
summary: A colleague is given a pointlessly emotional critique of a technical document and answers by writing a soap opera into it.

file: 1998/1998-02-11_silly putty_fake beauty mark_too much beauty_fashion headquarters_heroin chic_dogs with tumors.gif
title: Dogbert's Beauty Mark Inspires Fashion

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you have any "silly putty" I can use as a fake beauty mark?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you should use less.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There's no such thing as too much beauty.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Meanwhile, at fashion headquarters...

transcript.speaker: Fashion Executive
transcript.text: We got away with "heroin chic." What's next?

transcript.speaker: Fashion Designer
transcript.text: How about dogs with tumors?

setting: Dilbert's home, then a fashion company's headquarters
situation: Dogbert asks Dilbert for silly putty to use as a fake beauty mark, and Dilbert suggests he use less when he sees the lumpy result. Dogbert insists you can never have too much beauty. At a fashion company, executives brainstorm their next trend and are inspired by dogs with tumors.
punchline: The fashion industry will turn anything grotesque, even Dogbert's ridiculous lump of putty, into the next fashionable trend, following its earlier 'heroin chic' fad.
summary: A dog's oversized fake beauty mark gets mocked at home but unknowingly gives fashion executives their next shocking trend idea.

file: 1998/1998-01-09_mobster_rival family_hit team_sympathy card_surprise tomorrow_write funny song_burried.gif
title: Funny Song for Mobster's Funeral Party

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ted's brother was a mobster. Last week he was killed by a rival family's hit team.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We got Ted a sympathy card, then it snowballed into a surprise party for tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My job is to write a funny song.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: For he's a buried good fellow... For he's a buried good fellow... Which nobody can deny.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good.

setting: Dilbert's desk at home or the office
situation: Dilbert explains to Dogbert that Ted's brother, a mobster, was killed by a rival family's hit team. A sympathy card has somehow snowballed into a surprise party for Ted, and Dilbert has been assigned to write a funny song. Dogbert sings a parody of 'For He's a Jolly Good Fellow' about a 'buried good fellow', and Dilbert approves.
punchline: Dilbert is tasked with writing a funny song for a party meant to comfort someone grieving, and he approves of a darkly inappropriate parody celebrating the dead mobster as 'buried'.
summary: A sympathy card for a coworker mushrooms into a surprise party, and the song assigned to Dilbert becomes a morbid parody about the victim's burial.

file: 1998/1998-01-19_mental powers_predicting_proven psychic_scientific methid_testing.gif
title: Debunker Proves He's Psychic

transcript.speaker: Skeptic
transcript.text: I've used the scientific method to debunk 100% of the people who claim they have mental powers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you saying that every test you perform turns out the way you predict it will?

transcript.speaker: Skeptic
transcript.text: What's your point?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You've proven that you're psychic!!

setting: A living room or office with two armchairs, as if in a therapy or consultation session
situation: A man in glasses and a mustache, seated in an armchair with a teacup, boasts that he has used the scientific method to debunk every person claiming mental powers. Dogbert, lounging on the other chair, points out that all of his tests turn out exactly as he predicted. He concludes the man has actually proven that he himself is psychic.
punchline: If every test result matches his prediction, the skeptic's perfect forecasting record is itself evidence of psychic ability, undermining his own debunking.
summary: A self-assured skeptic brags about his flawless record of exposing psychics, only for Dogbert to turn his own success rate against him.

file: 1998/1998-04-22_tech conference_attractive woman_brush hand_key_concierge_hotel_check in_men dominated.gif
title: Hotel Clerk Shuts Down Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Hotel Clerk
transcript.text: Before I check you in, let me explain something...

transcript.speaker: Hotel Clerk
transcript.text: You're here for a technology conference. I am the only attractive woman who will talk to you for days. I am not free for coffee later.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I brush your hand when you give me the key?

transcript.speaker: Hotel Clerk
transcript.text: I'll toss it to you.

situation: Dilbert arrives at a hotel to check in for a technology conference. The clerk preemptively warns him that she is the only attractive woman who will talk to him for days and that she is not available for coffee. Dilbert, starved for contact, meekly asks if he can at least brush her hand when she hands over the key, and she says she will toss it instead.
punchline: Technology conference attendees are so socially isolated that Dilbert settles for a fleeting hand brush, and even that is denied, underscoring the stereotype of lonely, overwhelmingly male tech crowds.
summary: A hotel clerk preemptively rejects a tech conference guest's advances, and he is reduced to begging for an accidental touch of her hand.

file: 1998/1998-02-27_victim of curse_20-20_john stossel_shows cure_commercial_valuable information_old nemesis_tv shows.gif
title: Cursed Man Awaits Stossel's Cure

transcript.speaker: TV
transcript.text: Are you the victim of a curse?

transcript.speaker: Man in hat
transcript.text: Yes, I am.

transcript.speaker: TV
transcript.text: Next on "20/20," John Stossel shows you the cure.

transcript.speaker: Man in hat
transcript.text: Ha! After the commercial I will get valuable information for people like me!

transcript.speaker: Wizard
transcript.text: Well, well. It seems my old nemesis, John Stossel, has been busy.

characters: Man in a cap (a viewer cursed by a wizard)
setting: A living room, with a man watching TV in an armchair
situation: A man in a cap sits in an armchair watching TV, and when an announcer asks if viewers are victims of a curse, he answers yes. A teaser says John Stossel on "20/20" will show the cure, so he excitedly says he will get useful information for people like him. A wizard, who is evidently the one who cursed him, appears at the doorway and remarks that his old nemesis Stossel has been busy.
punchline: The man really is cursed by a wizard, and the TV newsmagazine's cure teaser turns out to concern the wizard's literal nemesis, so the show's consumer-advice style of reporting is played as a genuine curse-breaking tip.
summary: A cursed man gets his hopes up when a TV news show promises a cure, only to have the wizard behind his curse show up and reveal a grudge against the reporter.

file: 1998/1998-02-03_new policy_discriminate against single people_legal_marital staus_no reason_home_polygamists.gif
title: Boss Targets Single People for Overtime

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My new policy is to discriminate against single people. It's totally legal!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Write your marital status on this list, so I know who has no reason to go home at night.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dang! What are the odds you'd all be polygamists?

situation: The Boss announces a policy of discriminating against single people, claiming it is legal, and asks his employees to write their marital status on a list so he knows who has no reason to go home at night. When he reads the list, every employee has claimed to be married, leaving him baffled.
punchline: The employees all lied about being married to dodge extra work, so the Boss, failing to realize he's been fooled, concludes that they must all be polygamists.
summary: A manager tries to identify unattached workers to exploit, but everyone falsely claims a spouse, which he mistakes for a startling run of polygamy.

file: 1998/1998-09-10_rather the consultant_200k per year.gif
title: Ratbert Consultant Knows Only His Salary

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ratbert the consultant

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I'm making $200,000 per year!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (Ratbert hums happily; music notes shown, no spoken words)

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Apparently that's all I know.

setting: Conference room during a business meeting
situation: Ratbert, acting as a highly paid consultant, sits at a conference table between two clients and announces his salary. The clients listen with unimpressed, stern expressions while Ratbert cheerfully hums. When pressed for substance, he admits his salary is the only thing he knows.
punchline: The overpaid consultant has no actual expertise or useful advice to offer; the only thing he can contribute is the fact that he is being paid a lot.
summary: A well-paid consultant sitting with clients reveals that his only real knowledge is how much money he earns.

file: 1998/1998-06-26_dogebert the ceo_united charities_honored_company health plan_leadership_free clinics.gif
title: Dogbert Cancels Health Plan, Boosts Charity

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the C.E.O.

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: The "United Charities" would like you to be chairman this year.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd be honored.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oh, and while you're up, cancel the company health plan.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: One week later

transcript.speaker: Charity Spokesman
transcript.text: Under his leadership, our free clinics have handled twice as many people.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thanks.

setting: Dogbert's CEO office, then a United Charities award event
situation: Dogbert, as CEO, is asked by his secretary to chair United Charities and accepts, then casually orders her to cancel the company health plan. A week later a charity spokesman praises Dogbert for doubling the number of people served by the free clinics, and presents him with a trophy.
punchline: Dogbert created the surge in free clinic patients himself by cancelling employees' health insurance, so he gets credit for charity success that his own cruelty caused.
summary: A scheming canine executive takes over a charity and promptly manufactures its success by stripping his own staff of medical coverage.

file: 1998/1998-01-24_slight flu_copy to wally_project_least reason to live.gif
title: Give Your Flu to Wally

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I finished my work despite having a slight flu. Here's your copy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... You should give that copy to Wally.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wally isn't on this project.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I know. I just figure he has the least reason to live.

situation: A sickly, pimply coworker hands Dilbert a copy of his finished work, mentioning he has a slight flu. Dilbert suggests the copy should go to Wally instead, since Wally isn't on the project. The coworker admits he knows that and is deliberately targeting Wally because he thinks Wally has the least reason to live.
punchline: The sick coworker is deliberately trying to pass his flu to Wally, chosen as the person whose life is least worth protecting.
summary: A flu-ridden employee tries to hand his germ-covered paperwork to the coworker he considers most expendable.

file: 1998/1998-05-02_catbert_evil director_qualified external applicants_headless man_mime_cromagnon man_invisible cubicle_relocation costs.gif
title: Catbert's Absurd Pool of Job Applicants

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm having trouble finding qualified external applicants.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: All I have are a headless man, a mime, and a frozen Cro-Magnon guy we found in a glacier.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does the mime bring his own invisible cubicle? I love those!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Only if we pay his relocation costs.

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, reports to the Boss that he can't find qualified outside job candidates, listing a headless man, a mime and a frozen caveman as his only options. The Boss ignores the absurdity and enthusiastically asks whether the mime brings an invisible cubicle. Catbert replies that it depends on whether the company pays relocation costs.
punchline: Even with ridiculous candidates, the Boss only cares about cheap perks like an invisible cubicle, and Catbert treats the imaginary cubicle as a real expense tied to relocation costs.
summary: An H.R. cat complains that his applicant pool consists of bizarre oddities, and his boss responds by getting excited about a mime's imaginary office furniture.

file: 1998/1998-04-20_important conference_creat interaction_local and global issues_being sarcastic_sounds exciting.gif
title: Sarcastic Ears Review Conference Brochure

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm going to a very important conference.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What's it for?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The brochure says the goal is to "create interaction around local and global issues of the coming century."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're being sarcastic with your ears again.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It sounds so exciting!

setting: Dilbert's home, with Dogbert sitting on a dresser while Dilbert irons
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he is going to a very important conference and, when asked its purpose, reads out the brochure's vague goal. Dogbert responds with a flat, enthusiastic-sounding remark while his ears droop or flatten, which Dilbert recognizes as sarcasm.
punchline: Dogbert's words claim excitement, but his ears give away his sarcasm, mocking the buzzword-filled, meaningless purpose of the conference.
summary: A man reads a jargon-heavy conference brochure to his dog, who feigns enthusiasm while his body language reveals he is unimpressed.

file: 1998/1998-08-03_schedule_vigorous wedgie_boss.gif
title: Boss's Schedule Says Vigorous Wedgie

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let's see what's on my schedule today.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: "Give vigorous wedgie to myself."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You're right - he will do whatever is on his schedule.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ow!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Vigorously?

setting: The Boss's office, with Dilbert and Wally in a hallway or doorway
situation: The Boss sits at his desk and reads his schedule, which instructs him to give himself a vigorous wedgie. Offscreen we hear him yelp in pain as Wally and Dilbert discuss how he always follows his schedule exactly.
punchline: The Boss is so mindlessly obedient to his own schedule that he will inflict a painful wedgie on himself just because it was written down.
summary: A manager blindly obeys his calendar entry and hurts himself, to the observation of two employees who knew he would.

file: 1998/1998-09-04_assign priority_chance in a million_process voucher_you're a one_long process_lies.gif
title: Priority One Means One in a Million

transcript.speaker: Bald Employee
transcript.text: How long will it take to process my voucher?

transcript.speaker: Accounting Clerk
transcript.text: I assign a priority to everyone. I'm happy to say you're a "one."

transcript.speaker: Accounting Clerk
transcript.text: One chance in a million.

situation: A bald employee in glasses and a green tie asks a clerk at her computer how long it will take to process his expense voucher. She cheerfully says she gives everyone a priority and he is a "one". In the final panel her thought bubble reveals what the "one" really means.
punchline: The clerk's reassuring-sounding top priority is actually a private joke: he has only a one-in-a-million chance of ever getting reimbursed.
summary: A worker is told his reimbursement request is top priority, while the clerk privately believes it will almost certainly never get done.

file: 1998/1998-03-02_help on assignment_no brainer_interface design_make beige_decisions_can't go wrong.gif
title: Beige Advice From a No-Brainer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need help on the assignment that you said is a "no brainer."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's easy. Just skip the "interface design" phase and make everything beige. You can't go wrong with beige.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I always know where to go for no-brainer decisions.

situation: Dilbert asks the Boss for help with a project the Boss had called a no-brainer. The Boss casually advises him to skip the interface design phase entirely and make everything beige. Dilbert silently reflects that the Boss is the right source for brainless decisions.
punchline: Dilbert's thought implies the Boss is the ideal authority on no-brainer decisions because his advice is utterly mindless.
summary: A boss offers lazy, thoughtless design advice, and his employee quietly notes that he is the perfect source for decisions requiring no brain.

file: 1998/1998-02-28_pressure makes diamonds_garbage more compact_slogans_meeting_strong job market_engineers_irritation makes perals_pressure makes whine_business.gif
title: Pressure Makes Diamonds, Garbage, Whine

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our new slogan is, "Pressure makes diamonds."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How about, "Pressure makes garbage more compact"? I wonder if that one is taken.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hate this strong job market for engineers.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: "Irritation makes pearls." Or maybe "Pressure makes whine."

situation: The Boss announces a new motivational slogan, "Pressure makes diamonds," at a meeting. Wally responds with sarcastic alternative slogans that mock the idea of pressuring employees. The Boss, privately thinking, resents that engineers are hard to push around because of the strong job market.
punchline: Wally's sarcastic slogans show that pressure on employees just produces garbage and whining, while the Boss's thought reveals he'd mistreat engineers more if the job market let him.
summary: A manager's inspirational slogan gets mocked by a snarky engineer, while the manager quietly wishes he had more power over his staff.

file: 1998/1998-02-17_catbert_evil hr diretor_company's goal_double efficiency_downsize_marketing_good at math_business.gif
title: Double Efficiency Means Half Get Fired

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The company's goal is to double the efficiency of all employees.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Question: If we double our efficiency, won't you downsize half of us?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Don't talk to anyone in marketing; they aren't so good at math.

setting: Company meeting with Catbert addressing the staff
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, announces that the company wants to double the efficiency of every employee. Dilbert raises his hand and points out that doubling efficiency would let the company lay off half the workforce. Catbert responds by warning the group not to share this logic with the marketing department.
punchline: Catbert implicitly confirms that the layoffs are the real plan, and his only concern is that marketing staff are too bad at math to see through the scheme.
summary: An efficiency drive is exposed as a layoff plan, and the evil H.R. chief just hopes the innumerate marketing people won't catch on.

file: 1998/1998-03-10_elbonia_inspect factory_trip justification_aproval_unreasonably withheld.gif
title: Approving the Trip You Ordered

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I'm sending you to Elbonia to inspect our factory.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Fill out a trip justification form for my approval.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So, I need your approval to do what you told me to do?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It will not be unreasonably withheld.

situation: The Boss tells Alice he is sending her to Elbonia to inspect the company factory, then tells her to fill out a trip justification form for his approval. Alice points out the absurdity that she needs his approval for something he ordered her to do. The Boss reassures her he won't unreasonably withhold it.
punchline: The Boss orders a trip and then demands a form seeking his own approval, and his reassurance that approval won't be unreasonably withheld is meaningless since he already made the decision.
summary: A manager assigns an overseas trip to an employee and then insists she formally request his permission for it.

file: 1998/1998-04-15_eds farewell gift_treated like dirt_guilty_five dollars.gif
title: Fining Ed for Farewell Gift

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm collecting for Ed's farewell gift.

transcript.speaker: Ed
transcript.text: Ed, you treated me like dirt. I find you guilty and I fine you five dollars.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I just put that in there.

transcript.speaker: Ed
transcript.text: Come back if you get more.

situation: A coworker comes around holding an envelope to collect money for the farewell gift of a departing employee named Ed. Ed, who has been treated badly by colleagues, pronounces them guilty and fines them five dollars to put in the envelope. The coworker explains she already put that in, and Ed replies she should come back if she gets more.
punchline: Ed's coworkers are so unpleasant that the farewell gift money is just the pitiful fine he imposes on himself, and the amount is so low it cannot cover anything more.
summary: A departing employee who was mistreated by his colleagues pays his own tiny fine toward his own going-away present, and nobody even tries to give more.

file: 1998/1998-06-23_personal gopher_special unifrom_show status.gif
title: Dogbert's Literal Gopher Employee

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the C.E.O.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I need a personal "gopher." Are you interested?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Good. You'll wear a special uniform and have a special office to show your status.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sheesh. I haven't made a bank shot yet.

situation: Dogbert, acting as CEO, offers Dilbert a job as his personal "gopher." Dilbert accepts, and Dogbert promises a special uniform and office as status symbols. In the last panel Dilbert sits in a hole in the carpet wearing a gopher costume while Dogbert tosses crumpled paper at his head, trying to bank a shot into him.
punchline: Dogbert interprets "gopher" literally, so the 'special office' is a hole in the floor and the new employee becomes a target for his paper-ball game.
summary: A dog boss hires an assistant to be his gopher and turns the job title into a very literal costume, burrow and target practice.

file: 1998/1998-10-22_alice_drivers license_ed les mann_edward mann_headless man_name_new hire_office.gif
title: Headless New Guy's Pun Name

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: According to his driver's license, the new guy's name is Edward Mann.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is his middle name Lester?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How did you know that?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What we have here is an Ed Les Mann.

situation: Alice reads the driver's license of the new hire, who is a headless empty shirt and tie standing beside them. A bald, bespectacled coworker holding a coffee mug guesses the man's middle name is Lester, then reveals he was building a pun.
punchline: The name Edward Lester Mann sounds like 'headless man', which fits the new guy who literally has no head.
summary: A coworker steers a conversation about a new hire's name toward a groan-worthy pun on his missing head.

file: 1998/1998-11-28_chief financial offcier_one sentence descriptions_projects_critical budget deciosns_semi colons.gif
title: Five-Page Single Sentence Project Description

transcript.speaker: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.text: I need one-sentence descriptions of each of your projects.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're planning to make critical budget decisions based on THAT?

transcript.speaker: Chief Financial Officer
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wow. Five pages without using a period.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank God for semi-colons.

setting: Conference room meeting, then Dilbert's cubicle
situation: The Chief Financial Officer demands one-sentence descriptions of each project so he can make budget decisions. Dilbert objects that this is too little information for critical decisions, but the CFO confirms his plan. Dilbert then complies by writing a five-page 'single sentence' held together with semi-colons.
punchline: Dilbert technically obeys the absurd one-sentence rule by stringing five pages together with semi-colons, defeating the purpose of brevity.
summary: Told to compress his projects into single sentences, an engineer maliciously complies by producing a sprawling five-page run-on.

file: 1998/1998-06-14_donate computer_most insane_not work on project_manipulate.gif
title: Insanity Controls Reality at Work

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dogbert's First Law of Business

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Reality is always controlled by the people who are most insane.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Example

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Thanks for agreeing to work on my project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I never agreed to work on your project.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You can't change your mind now! It's too late to get someone else!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um... I'm not changing my mind. I clearly said I would not work on your project.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You lying weasel! I'll ruin you!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay! Okay! I'll work on your project!

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wally, thanks for agreeing to donate your computer to my project.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What?

situation: Dogbert introduces his law that the most insane people control reality, then a demonstration follows. A coworker insists Dilbert agreed to work on her project, and when he denies it she escalates to accusations and threats until he caves. She then immediately uses the same tactic on Wally, claiming he agreed to donate his computer.
punchline: Behaving irrationally and aggressively wins out over reason, so the coworker gets what she wants and promptly repeats the trick on her next victim.
summary: A pushy coworker bullies Dilbert into helping her by pretending he already said yes, then tries the same trick on Wally.
keywords: too late to get someone else

file: 1998/1998-03-25_personal habitat_cubicle_less cluttered_personal storage unit.gif
title: Personal Habitat Replaces Cluttered Cubicle

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your cubicle has been replaced by a "personal habitat."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's exactly like your cubicle but much less cluttered.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hey, all my stuff is in the trash can!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's a funny thing to call your personal storage unit.

situation: Dogbert, acting as a facilities consultant, tells Wally that his cubicle has been replaced by a "personal habitat" that is just like the old one but tidier. Wally discovers all his belongings have been dumped into a trash can. Dogbert cheerfully relabels the trash can as his personal storage unit.
punchline: Rebranding the cubicle as a "habitat" and the trash can as a "storage unit" is euphemistic corporate spin used to disguise the fact that Wally's possessions were simply thrown away.
summary: A consultant dog spins the loss of an employee's belongings into a fancy new workspace concept, complete with a garbage can marketed as storage.

file: 1998/1998-09-19_no meetings_change software_software settings_boss_good work.gif
title: Tinkering With Settings Until Something Breaks

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't have any meetings today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll change all my software settings until something doesn't work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Keep up the good work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Keep up the good managing.

situation: Dilbert sits alone in his cubicle, pleased that he has no meetings, and decides to fill the free time by randomly changing his software settings until something stops working. The Boss walks past and cheerfully tells him to keep up the good work, and Dilbert sarcastically returns the compliment about managing.
punchline: Dilbert's idea of productive free time is deliberately breaking his own software, and when the oblivious Boss praises him, Dilbert sarcastically mirrors the compliment, implying the Boss's management is equally pointless.
summary: With a rare meeting-free day, an idle Dilbert amuses himself by fiddling with his computer until it breaks, and an oblivious boss praises him anyway.

file: 1998/1998-07-01_dogberts tech support_software_cat scan machine_break room_insert head_trickster dogbert_prnak_cowoorker_labor market_engineering.gif
title: Dogbert Sends Caller to Cat Scan

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Our software is perfect. The problem must be with you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Go to the cat scan machine in the break room and insert your head. I'll monitor you from here.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you see the problem?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I blame the tight labor market.

setting: Dogbert's tech support desk and the office break room
situation: Working a tech support line, Dogbert insists the software is flawless and that the caller must be the problem. He tells the caller to put his head into a cat scan machine in the break room while he watches from his desk. A coworker stands nearby with a coffee mug as the caller's head is stuck in the machine.
punchline: When asked if he sees the problem, the coworker watching the head scan blames the tight labor market, implying the real problem is that the company can't find better employees.
summary: A tech support dog pushes a user into a head scan to prove the fault lies with the user, and a bystander wryly blames the hiring climate.

file: 1998/1998-02-22_happy birthday alice_gift_charity money_team spitit_ash tray_dont smoke_ashtray as gift.gif
title: Birthday Gifts and Team Spirit

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Happy birthday, Alice!

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: I was planning to get a gift...

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: But then I thought...

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Why not give the money to charity in Alice's name?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Really? Which charity?

transcript.speaker: Bald Coworker
transcript.text: Umm... "The United Society of Poor People with Major Health Problems."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: ...and Dilbert got me an ashtray, even though I don't smoke.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You don't?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: They say this sort of thing builds team spirit.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It must be gradual.

situation: A bald coworker wishes Alice a happy birthday and explains he donated money to a vaguely named charity in her name instead of buying a gift. Dilbert gives her a wrapped present, which turns out to be an ashtray, though Alice doesn't smoke and Dilbert didn't know.
punchline: Alice sarcastically notes that these thoughtless, mismatched gifts supposedly build team spirit, and Dilbert dryly observes that the effect must be very gradual, since the gifts show how little the team actually knows or cares about each other.
summary: A lazy charity donation and a thoughtless ashtray for a non-smoker show how hollow forced workplace birthday gestures are at building camaraderie.

file: 1998/1998-03-18_judged by accomplishments_not gender_14th patent_lunch banquet_honor alice.gif
title: Judged by Accomplishments, Not Outfit

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Alice, one day I hope we can be judged by our accomplishments and not our gender.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I got my fourteenth patent today. I'm on my way to a lunch banquet in my honor.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: And you wore THAT?

situation: Tina tells Alice she hopes women can someday be judged by their accomplishments rather than gender. Alice mentions she just earned her fourteenth patent and is heading to a banquet held in her honor. Tina responds by criticizing Alice's outfit.
punchline: Tina, who just argued for judging women by accomplishments, immediately judges Alice's appearance instead, undercutting her own statement with hypocrisy.
summary: A coworker pleads for achievement over appearance, then promptly sneers at the outfit of a colleague who is about to be honored for her inventions.

file: 1998/1998-02-20_dogbert the consultant_knowledge assets_unmistakable message_boss_consultant_business.gif
title: Knowledge Assets Send Unmistakable Message

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: From now on, refer to your employees as "knowledge assets."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That will send an unmistakable message.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He calls us "knowledge assets" now. He must think we're complete morons.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's an unmistakable message.

setting: A consulting session in the boss's office, then Dilbert talking to Dogbert on the couch
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, advises the boss to start calling his employees "knowledge assets" because of the message it sends. Later Dilbert complains that the boss now uses this label for the staff and concludes the boss must think they are morons. Dogbert, still lounging on the couch, confirms that this is exactly the unmistakable message.
punchline: The fancy corporate buzzword is actually a condescending label, and Dogbert deadpans that the 'unmistakable message' it sends is that management thinks employees are idiots.
summary: A consultant dog coaches a manager to adopt a trendy name for his staff, and the staff correctly decode it as an insult.

file: 1998/1998-11-03_%#!!_anger_burning walls eyebrow_curse_demonstrate power_eyebrows burn off_scream.gif
title: Cursing Until Wally's Eyebrow Burns

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: If you anger me, I will curse at you until your eyebrows burn off.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I will demonstrate my power by burning Wally's left eyebrow.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ow! Ow! That's not an eyebrow!

situation: At a meeting, Tina warns her coworkers that if they anger her she will curse at them until their eyebrows burn off. To prove her power she singles out Wally and starts cursing at him. Wally yelps in pain and protests that what she is burning is not actually his eyebrow.
punchline: Tina's threat of eyebrow-burning profanity is real enough to hurt Wally, but she has picked the wrong body part, as the thing smoking on his face isn't an eyebrow.
summary: A coworker threatens to scorch people's eyebrows with her swearing, then proves it on Wally, though not quite where she aimed.

file: 1998/1998-07-09_exercise shorts_got own room_jumping jacks_naked jumping jacks_pack clothes_sharing hotel room_single occupancy_scared dilbert.gif
title: Wally's Naked Jumping Jacks Solution

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Sharing a hotel room

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I forgot to pack my exercise shorts.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I guess I can do my jumping jacks without clothes. It's just us guys.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Single occupancy isn't so hard to get.

setting: A shared hotel room on a business trip
situation: Wally and Dilbert are sharing a hotel room, and Wally says he forgot to pack exercise shorts. He casually suggests doing his jumping jacks naked since they are both guys, and Dilbert reacts with alarm. In the last panel Wally lies contentedly in bed, thinking that Dilbert must have gotten his own room.
punchline: Wally's threat of naked jumping jacks was enough to scare Dilbert into paying for a separate room, leaving Wally with the single occupancy he wanted all along.
summary: A coworker's awkward offer to exercise in the nude drives his roommate out of their shared hotel room, leaving him alone in comfort.

file: 1998/1998-06-12_what vendor_too late_indecisive dullards.gif
title: Reopening Vendor Choice Summons Devil

transcript.speaker: Meeting Attendee
transcript.text: I'd like to reopen the question of what vendor we'll use, even though it's too late to change anything.

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: I darn you to heck! You will spend an eternity with other indecisive dullards!

transcript.speaker: Meeting Attendee
transcript.text: Where are you taking me??!!

transcript.speaker: Devil
transcript.text: Here is fine.

situation: During a meeting, a coworker proposes reopening the vendor selection decision even though he admits it's too late to change anything. A devil in a red costume carrying a large spoon appears and condemns him to eternity with other indecisive people. When the terrified man asks where he's being taken, the devil says right here is fine, implying the meeting is already hell.
punchline: The devil says 'here is fine' because an endless meeting full of indecisive people is already the equivalent of hell.
summary: A man who wants to revisit a settled vendor decision is damned by a devil, who reveals that the meeting room is punishment enough.

file: 1998/1998-11-13_non employee certification_messenger_secretary_receptionist_carol_dilbert_process raise.gif
title: Non-Employee Certification Form Absurdity

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You need to sign the non-employee certification form before I process your raise.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But this would be a lie. I'm not a non-employee.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'm only the messenger.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where did it come from?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: The file cabinet.

situation: Carol, the boss's assistant, hands Dilbert a form and says he must certify he is a non-employee before his raise can be processed. Dilbert objects that signing would be a lie, and tries to find out who created the form. Carol can only say she is the messenger and that it came from the file cabinet.
punchline: The nonsensical bureaucratic requirement has no accountable author, since it simply emerged from a file cabinet, so no one can be blamed or asked to fix it.
summary: An employee is told to sign a falsehood to receive his raise, but the paperwork's origin turns out to be an anonymous filing cabinet.

file: 1998/1998-09-24_meeting objectives_accuracy of info_facts_guilty person.gif
title: Guilty Person Demands Fact Checking

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Who said I wasn't meeting my objectives?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't remember.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Therefore, I have no reason to doubt the accuracy of the information.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Check the facts!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That sounds like something a guilty person would say.

situation: Carol, the Boss's assistant, demands to know who claimed she wasn't meeting her objectives. The Boss can't remember the source but decides the information must be accurate anyway. When Carol asks him to check the facts, he treats her request as evidence of her guilt.
punchline: The Boss uses circular logic: forgetting the source of an accusation makes it trustworthy, and any attempt to defend yourself is proof of guilt.
summary: A boss dismisses an employee's request to verify an accusation against her by claiming that asking for proof is itself suspicious.

file: 1998/1998-03-14_call back_one hour_time zone.gif
title: Boss Baffled by Time Zones

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll call you back in one hour, Irene.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're in a different time zone, so you'll get the call in... um... three hours.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Really? You're three hours ahead? Then that means... whoa! You're freaking me out here!

setting: Office hallway and the Boss's office
situation: Dilbert walks past a cubicle wall while the Boss, off-panel, tells a caller named Irene he'll call back in an hour. He then tries to work out the time zone difference and says she'll get the call in three hours. When he learns she is three hours ahead, he sits at his desk phone and becomes rattled by the implications.
punchline: The Boss is so bad at basic time zone arithmetic that he gets freaked out by the idea of someone being ahead of him in time, as if it implied time travel.
summary: A manager fumbles a simple call-back promise to a colleague in another time zone and gets spooked by the concept of being three hours behind.

file: 1998/1998-06-18_strategy lockup meeting_meeting won't end_new strategy_wedge my broom.gif
title: Janitor Locks Executives In Meeting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our top executives are in a special strategy lockup meeting.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The meeting won't end until they agree on a new strategy, so it might be a while.

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: Maybe if I wedge my broom here I won't forget where I put it.

setting: Conference room and adjoining office corridor
situation: Dilbert and Alice explain that the top executives are locked in a strategy meeting that cannot end until they agree on a new strategy. In the last panel a janitor wedges his broom against the door of that room, apparently just to remember where he left it, which effectively locks the executives in.
punchline: The janitor's casual attempt to keep track of his broom accidentally traps the executives, which will make an already interminable strategy meeting literally inescapable.
summary: An office worker casually props a broom against a door, unaware he is sealing a roomful of executives inside their endless planning session.

file: 1998/1998-05-09_less perfectionist_apathy_low standards_positive traits_intrapreneurial spirit.gif
title: Wally Teaches Alice Imperfection

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, you'd get more accomplished if you were less of a perfectionist.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've asked Wally to work with you - to teach you how to be less perfect.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: When did apathy and low standards become positive traits?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I call it the intrapreneurial spirit.

setting: The Boss's office and Alice's cubicle
situation: The Boss tells Alice that her perfectionism is hurting her productivity and announces that he has assigned Wally to coach her in being less perfect. Alice, annoyed, asks when apathy and low standards turned into virtues, and Wally cheerfully rebrands his slacking as the 'intrapreneurial spirit'.
punchline: Wally, the laziest employee, dresses up his apathy and low standards with a buzzword, and management treats him as a role model for how to do less careful work.
summary: A manager sends the office slacker to mentor a conscientious coworker, and the slacker spins his laziness as entrepreneurial initiative.

file: 1998/1998-05-05_catbert_evil hr director_balance_life and work_worked 80 hrs week_selfish hag.gif
title: Catbert Demands Alice Work More

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Alice, the experts say you need to balance work and home life.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You worked 80 hours last week. That's less than half of the hours in a week.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Give us some balance, you selfish hag.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: This conversation took a nasty turn.

situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, tells Alice that experts recommend balancing work and home life. He then points out that her 80-hour work week is less than half the hours in a week, and demands that she give the company more. Alice looks on in dismay at the twisted logic.
punchline: Catbert twists the idea of work-life balance into a demand for even more work, since 80 hours is technically less than half of the 168 hours in a week.
summary: An evil personnel chief hijacks the notion of work-life balance to guilt an exhausted employee into giving the company even more of her time.
keywords: half the hours in a week

file: 1998/1998-07-26_hallway_boss_dilbert_tissue_write down_rips_ink blot_mishandled_ignored.gif
title: Boss Takes Notes on Tissue

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need some management fire power.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The VP of Marketing says we can't use the vendor we selected . . .

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Let me write this down.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you want some paper?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, I'll use this tissue... Oops.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Anyway, the other vendor can't deliver.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oops.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have some note paper.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, this is fine.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oops.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All you have is a blotch on a scrap.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's more of a reminder than a detailed note.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hmm... It's not so useful when I put it with the others.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for management backing because the vendor they chose has been vetoed by the VP of Marketing and the alternative can't deliver. The boss insists on taking notes on a tissue instead of the paper Dilbert offers, and it shreds under his pen. By the end his desk is littered with torn scraps that tell him nothing.
punchline: The boss's stubborn refusal to use real paper leaves him with a pile of useless scraps, so he'll never act on Dilbert's request.
summary: A manager insists on scribbling notes on a flimsy tissue, tearing it to shreds while his employee's urgent problem goes unrecorded.

file: 1998/1998-11-21_unicornitis_cell normalizer_dna sample_genius garbageman.gif
title: Garbage Man Cures Dilbert's Unicornitis

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Looks like someone has a bad case of unicornitis.

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: I've got a pre-horn sample of your DNA in the truck. I could fix you up with my cell normalizer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do you have my DNA in your truck?

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: It's for exactly this sort of situation.

setting: Outdoors beside a garbage truck and trash can
situation: Dilbert, who has sprouted a unicorn-like horn from his forehead, is approached by a garbage man at his truck. The garbage man diagnoses the condition, reveals he has a sample of Dilbert's pre-horn DNA, and produces a bulky cell normalizer gun to cure him. When Dilbert asks why the garbage man has his DNA at all, he gives a vague, unhelpful answer.
punchline: The garbage man's absurdly convenient DNA stockpile is justified with a circular non-answer, highlighting how bizarrely prepared and unexplained his technology is.
summary: A sanitation worker casually offers to reverse a coworker's strange horn growth with a high-tech gadget and a secretly kept DNA sample.

file: 1998/1998-07-12_boring meeting_fidgeting_distarcted_pens.gif
title: Fidgeting Through Endless Boring Meeting

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't believe I get paid for this.

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Blah blah.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This thing lasts two more hours.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe I should fidget with my pen.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm too late. Now I'd look uncreative.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Fidget.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wonder how long I can hold my breath.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Fidget.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Fidget.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Whump!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ooh, two pens. What would that be like?

setting: Conference room during a long meeting
situation: Dilbert sits through a droning meeting, thinking about how he gets paid for this and how many hours remain. He considers fidgeting with a pen but decides he is too late, while Wally has already been fidgeting. Dilbert passes out from holding his breath, falling over with his feet in the air, and Wally keeps fidgeting, musing about using two pens.
punchline: Wally is so absorbed in his own pen fidgeting that he doesn't notice Dilbert has passed out from holding his breath, showing how numbing and self-absorbing pointless meetings are.
summary: A meeting so tedious that one man keeps himself entertained with pens while his coworker knocks himself out trying to hold his breath.

file: 1998/1998-09-26_dogbert_ratbert_couch_living room_conversation_gaps in conversation_fill in gaps_random.gif
title: Ratbert's Awkward Couch Small Talk

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Do you mind if I fill the gaps in our conversation with random observations?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: So, you got a little pillow there, eh?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Eh?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: When I say, "Eh?", that's your cue to answer.

situation: Ratbert asks Dogbert, who is lounging on the couch with a remote and a pillow, for permission to fill silences with random observations. Dogbert curtly says no, but Ratbert goes ahead with small talk about the pillow and then pushes for a reply. He ends by explaining that his "Eh?" is Dogbert's cue to respond.
punchline: Ratbert ignores Dogbert's refusal and awkwardly lectures him on the rules of his own clumsy small talk, demanding a response that Dogbert clearly doesn't want to give.
summary: A chatty little rat plows ahead with pointless banter at his unwilling, couch-bound companion and then scolds him for not replying on cue.

file: 1998/1998-09-22_catbert_hr diretor_improve perfromance_feel bad_faults_boss lists faults_hoping for improvement.gif
title: Shaming Employees Into Better Performance

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You can improve an employee's performance by making him feel bad about himself.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So, although that wouldn't work on me, it works fine on other people?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Exactly.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll read your faults one at a time. Tell me when your performance improves.

setting: Office, H.R. director's office and Dilbert's cubicle
situation: Catbert, the H.R. Director, advises the Boss that making employees feel bad about themselves improves their performance. The Boss checks that this wouldn't work on him but would work on others, then promptly goes to Dilbert with a list of faults, reading them aloud and waiting for improvement.
punchline: The Boss embraces a cruel management tactic instantly, assuming it only affects other people, and treats berating Dilbert as a legitimate way to raise productivity.
summary: After learning from HR that shame boosts output, a smug manager goes straight to an employee and starts reciting his shortcomings.

file: 1998/1998-11-12_dogbert_acting like king_monarch system_crown.gif
title: Emergency Monarch System Test

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I am your king! Bow before me, peasant!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: This was a test of the Emergency Monarch System.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If this were a real monarchy, you would already be wretched.

situation: Dogbert, wearing a paper crown, announces to Dilbert that he is the king and demands he bow. Dilbert calmly keeps reading his newspaper in his bathrobe. Dogbert then declares it was only a test of the Emergency Monarch System, parodying an emergency broadcast announcement.
punchline: Parodying the Emergency Broadcast System tone, Dogbert deadpans that if this were a real monarchy, Dilbert would already be wretched, implying that subjects under a real ruler are miserable.
summary: Dogbert crowns himself and demands obedience, then passes it off as a drill with a grim remark about life under real rulers.

file: 1998/1998-10-21_new guy_name_wallet_hunts for wallet_appears like hug.gif
title: Alice Frisks the New Guy

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If we're going to work together, I should know your name.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Let's see if you have a wallet with some identification.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Geez, Alice, could you let the new guy settle in first?

situation: Alice confronts the new coworker in his cubicle and demands to know his name. When he doesn't answer, she grabs him and starts searching his clothes for a wallet with ID. Wally watches from the side and asks her to give the new guy time to settle in, as it looks like she is hugging him.
punchline: Alice is so aggressive and impatient that she physically pats down the new hire for identification rather than simply waiting for him to introduce himself.
summary: A pushy coworker rummages through a newcomer's pockets to learn who he is, and a bystander begs her to back off.

file: 1998/1998-08-21_intangible benefits_earn money_tangible benefits_emplyees_stcokholders_stockholder meeting.gif
title: Intangible Benefits for Stockholders Too

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The employees aren't falling for the old "intangible benefits" story anymore.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh-oh. We don't earn enough money to give tangible benefits to employees AND stockholders.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Stockholder meeting

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ... Now let's discuss your intangible benefits...

setting: Executive office, then a stockholder meeting room
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells the Boss that employees no longer accept vague 'intangible benefits' in place of real ones. The Boss realizes the company can't afford tangible benefits for both employees and stockholders, so at the stockholder meeting he pitches intangible benefits to the stockholders instead. A stockholder brandishes a gun and another swings a cane in anger.
punchline: Management happily fobs employees off with intangible benefits, but when the same treatment is applied to the stockholders, they react with violent fury.
summary: When workers stop accepting empty perks, the boss tries the same dodge on the company's investors, who respond with armed outrage.

file: 1998/1998-05-29_fertility drugs in coffeee_bloated_hoagie_evidence of pregnancy_weight gain.gif
title: Fertility Drugs and a Hoagie

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I've been eating like crazy since Dogbert put the fertility drugs in my coffee.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I'm guessing I have ten or fifteen babies in there. It's hard to keep them fed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And your only evidence of pregnancy is weight gain?

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Here comes another hoagie, kids!

setting: Office break room or table where Dilbert and Tina are having coffee
situation: Tina tells Dilbert she has been eating constantly since Dogbert slipped fertility drugs into her coffee, and she assumes she is carrying ten or fifteen babies. Dilbert skeptically asks if her only evidence is weight gain. Tina responds by cheerfully biting into a hoagie and announcing it to her imaginary babies.
punchline: Tina's 'pregnancy' is just overeating, and she keeps rationalizing her weight gain and appetite as feeding a litter of babies rather than admitting she's simply eating too much.
summary: A woman convinces herself that her growing appetite and waistline prove she's carrying a dozen babies, and she happily keeps eating for them.

file: 1998/1998-05-19_clown_small head_random things_pippy_artistic integrity_creating comic_bitter_dogbert created.gif
title: Dogbert's Artistic Integrity Comic Critique

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your comic strip seems to be nothing but a clown with a small head who says random things.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's Pippy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm maintaining my artistic integrity by creating a comic that no one will enjoy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The important thing is that you enjoy it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The first two were okay, but now I'm just bitter.

setting: Dilbert's desk at home or the office, with Dogbert seated across drawing comics
situation: Dilbert reviews Dogbert's homemade comic strip and complains that it is only a small-headed clown saying random things. Dogbert, drawing at the desk, says he is preserving his artistic integrity by making something nobody will like. Dilbert offers the consoling idea that his own enjoyment is what matters.
punchline: Dogbert admits that even his own enjoyment has run out, so the supposed reward of artistic integrity has left him merely bitter.
summary: A dog drawing a deliberately unlikeable comic discovers that pleasing only himself has stopped working too.

file: 1998/1998-01-12_blind people_excellent hearing_brain compensates_telekinetic power_watch televison_power to watch tv.gif
title: Ratbert's Dumb Telekinetic Television Power

transcript.speaker: Man in cap
transcript.text: Blind people often have excellent hearing. The brain compensates for any lost function by bolstering others.

transcript.speaker: Man in cap
transcript.text: In all likelihood, Ratbert, you're so dumb that you have telekinetic power.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Wow!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: I have the power to watch television!

setting: A living room, with the two sitting on a couch
situation: A man in a blue cap explains that the brain compensates for lost function, as blind people often have excellent hearing. He then tells Ratbert that he is so dumb he probably has telekinetic power. Ratbert is thrilled and walks off thinking that his special power is the ability to watch television.
punchline: Ratbert is so dumb that he mistakes the mundane ability to watch TV for a telekinetic superpower, which proves the man's insult right.
