summary: A man insists that stupidity must be balanced by a hidden talent, and the gullible little rat proudly claims the most ordinary skill imaginable as his gift.

file: 1998/1998-04-28_low priced consultant_reasonably priced_roll around hamburger patties.gif
title: Cheap Consultant Recommends Hamburger Rolling

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I saved a lot of money by hiring a low-priced consultant.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: These aren't the best recommendations in the world, but the price was very reasonable.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I don't like this one about rolling around on unwashed hamburger patties.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Keep an open mind.

situation: The Boss brags at a meeting that he saved money by hiring a cheap consultant, then hands out the consultant's recommendations while admitting they are poor. A staff member reading the report objects to a recommendation about rolling around on unwashed hamburger patties, and the Boss tells him to keep an open mind.
punchline: The Boss values the low price of the consultant over the quality of advice, so he defends an absurd and unsanitary recommendation by asking employees to keep an open mind.
summary: A manager proudly hires a bargain consultant whose bizarre advice involves wallowing in raw burger meat, and he expects his team to just accept it.

file: 1998/1998-10-27_ambiguity_another situation_irrational concerns_headphones_pretend to listen.gif
title: Boss Pretends To Hear Concerns

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's the plan. Now I will pretend to listen to your irrational concerns.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Go!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is another situation where ambiguity would be better.

situation: The Boss presents a vague flowchart plan at a meeting, then announces he will only pretend to listen to his team's concerns. He puts on headphones, listens to music, and leans back in his chair while Dilbert and a coworker sit at the table. Dilbert remarks that this is another case where ambiguity would be preferable.
punchline: The Boss is so openly dismissive of employee feedback that Dilbert wishes he would at least keep up the pretense, since being told you are being ignored is worse than ambiguity.
summary: A manager cheerfully admits he won't really hear objections and tunes out with headphones, leaving his staff wishing for a little less honesty.

file: 1998/1998-08-29_powerless peon_agent of change_dynamic work group_business card_paper trail.gif
title: Agent of Change, No Paper Trail

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't think of yourself as a powerless peon in a box.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're an agent of change in a dynamic, natural work group!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I put that on my business cards?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd rather not leave a paper trail.

situation: The Boss tries to motivate Dilbert by telling him he is not a powerless peon in a box but an agent of change in a dynamic, natural work group. Dilbert asks whether he can put that grand title on his business cards. The Boss refuses, saying he doesn't want to leave a paper trail.
punchline: The Boss's inspiring title is empty flattery, and he won't put it in writing because he doesn't want to be held to it.
summary: A manager showers his employee with lofty praise but backs away the moment it might be made official.

file: 1998/1998-03-06_telecommute dogbert_personalities_zero a number_debate_try to develop personality.gif
title: Telecommuting Requires a Personality, Dogbert Disagrees

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It takes a certain type of personality to telecommute, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Just because other people have personalities doesn't mean you should try to develop one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a personality!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Let's not get into that "is zero a number" debate again.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with both on a purple couch while he works from home in a bathrobe
situation: Dilbert, relaxing at home in a robe with a mug of coffee, remarks to Dogbert that telecommuting suits only a certain type of personality. Dogbert replies that Dilbert shouldn't bother trying to develop a personality just because others have one. Dilbert insists he has one, and Dogbert dismisses the claim.
punchline: Dogbert compares Dilbert's personality to zero, implying it is nothing at all, and refuses to rehash the old debate over whether zero counts as a number.
summary: A man working from home mentions the personality needed for remote work and gets a dismissive put-down from his dog, who insinuates he has none at all.

file: 1998/1998-04-02_improve moral_prescribing anti depressants_unwarranted optimism_dead end job_pills_hr prescribed drugs_employees happiness.gif
title: HR Prescribes Antidepressants for Morale

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Human Resources is prescribing powerful antidepressants to improve morale.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: The label says it may cause "unwarranted optimism about your dead-end job."

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I gotta get me some of that.

situation: Tina, holding a pill bottle at a meeting, announces that Human Resources is giving employees powerful antidepressants to boost morale. She reads the warning label aloud, which admits the drug causes false optimism about a dead-end job. A coworker eagerly asks for some while Tina tips the pills straight into her mouth.
punchline: Management would rather medicate employees into false cheer than fix the bad jobs causing the low morale, and the side effect is openly described as delusion.
summary: Instead of improving working conditions, the company hands out mood-altering pills whose label admits they just make people foolishly hopeful about hopeless careers.

file: 1998/1998-08-06_digital archive_worlds greatest art_fix the errors_artists_errors_too much blue.gif
title: Fixing the Masters' Blue Period

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We won the bid to create a digital archive of the world's greatest art.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This will give us a chance to fix any errors made by the artists.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Errors?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: For example, there was a guy who used too much blue for a whole period.

situation: The Boss tells Wally and Dilbert that the company has won a contract to digitally archive the world's greatest art. He then explains that the project is an opportunity to correct the artists' mistakes. When Wally questions this, the Boss cites an artist who overused blue for an entire period.
punchline: The Boss thinks he can improve masterpieces by editing out the 'mistakes', and his example is Picasso's Blue Period, which was a deliberate artistic choice rather than an error.
summary: A manager treats the digitization of famous artworks as a chance to correct the painters' supposed blunders, revealing he misunderstands what art is.

file: 1998/1998-03-29_2 percent raise_not challenging_exceeded golas_no complaining_walls performance_complained all year_weasel_stab him in back.gif
title: Raise Penalty for Not Complaining

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can only give you a two percent raise this year, Alice.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because your job was not very challenging.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How could you possibly think it wasn't challenging?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You exceeded all your goals without complaining.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Compare that to Wally's performance. He complained all year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And he missed every goal! Now that's a challenging job!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wally is a filthy weasel!!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe his hygiene isn't the best, but he was right when he said you would stab him in the back.

situation: The Boss tells Alice she is getting only a two percent raise because her job wasn't challenging, since she met all her goals without complaining. He contrasts her with Wally, who complained all year and missed every goal, and so is judged to have had a challenging job. Alice explodes in anger at Wally, which the Boss takes as proof of Wally's prediction.
punchline: The Boss rewards complaining and failure over quiet competence, then treats Alice's justified outburst as confirmation of Wally's claim that she would stab him in the back.
summary: A manager docks a high-performing employee's raise because she never complained, while crediting a whining underperformer for having a tougher job.

file: 1998/1998-05-17_pompous airbag_deflate_arrogance_tricvia_intelligence_elbonia_wet laundry_chewy casserole.gif
title: Deflating the Pompous Office Airbag

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you the pompous airbag of the office?

transcript.speaker: Pompous Coworker
transcript.text: Indeed.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've been asked to deflate you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My sources tell me that you combine arrogance with trivia and try to pass it off as intelligence.

transcript.speaker: Pompous Coworker
transcript.text: That's because I'm surrounded by fools who don't even know the capital of Elbonia!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I have a signed statement from your wife...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...that you put wet laundry in the oven last night.

transcript.speaker: Pompous Coworker
transcript.text: That explains the chewy casserole she served me this morning.

situation: Dogbert visits a self-important coworker in his cubicle and announces he has been asked to deflate the man's ego. The coworker boasts about his superior knowledge and mocks everyone else's ignorance. Dogbert then produces a signed statement from the man's wife claiming he put wet laundry in the oven.
punchline: The pompous know-it-all is exposed as foolish by his own mistake, and he only realizes it when he connects the wet laundry to the chewy casserole he was served.
summary: A talking dog sent to puncture an office blowhard's ego does it with a spouse's testimony about a ridiculous household blunder.

file: 1998/1998-07-10_web pages_urls_replace urls_uniform resource locators.gif
title: Replacing URLs With Uniform Resource Locators

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't see why our web pages need URLs. Get rid of them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did that make any sense at all?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, it's brilliant.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Give me a month and I'll replace our URLs with Uniform Resource Locators.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Perfect.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to get rid of the URLs on the company's web pages, not understanding what they are. After checking that his own order made sense, he accepts Dilbert's flattery. Dilbert then offers to spend a month replacing URLs with Uniform Resource Locators, which is the same thing, and the Boss is delighted.
punchline: Dilbert sells the clueless Boss a month of pointless work by renaming URLs to what the acronym stands for, and the Boss is happy because he cannot tell the difference.
summary: A technically ignorant manager orders the removal of web addresses and is placated when his engineer promises to swap them for their own spelled-out name.

file: 1998/1998-03-21_catbert_evil hr director_boss prevents new job_great job_outrageous_bad situation worse_human resource promise.gif
title: Catbert Forbids Great Jobs Here

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My boss is preventing me from transfering to a great job.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That's outrageous! There shouldn't be any great jobs in this company.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Once again, you've made a bad situation worse.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That's the Human Resources promise.

situation: Dilbert visits Catbert, the evil H.R. director, to complain that his boss is blocking his transfer to a great job. Catbert agrees it is outrageous, but only because he believes no great jobs should exist at the company. He then tells Dilbert he has made a bad situation worse.
punchline: Instead of helping with the complaint, H.R. makes things worse and treats this as its official promise, mocking human resources departments for being harmful rather than helpful to employees.
summary: An employee asks the feline personnel chief for help escaping a boss's roadblock and learns that the department's real mission is making his predicament worse.

file: 1998/1998-02-08_employee resigned_exit interview_stand in_disgusting senseless slaughter_english language_stellar leadership_inspirational motto_prerogative_hygiene_misunderstood geniuses.gif
title: Dogbert Stands In For Exit Interview

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've been hired by an employee who just resigned.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll be his stand-in for the exit interview.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd like to begin by discussing your senseless slaughter of the English language.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ... and on April 8th, you were heard saying, "We have to nip that problem in the butt."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now let's talk about your stellar leadership.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your inspirational motto is ...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "If I want you to do something that's a waste of time, it's my prerogative!"

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Moving on to hygiene...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm probably one of those misunderstood geniuses.

situation: Dogbert arrives, hired by a resigned employee to act as his stand-in for the exit interview. He sits across from The Boss and reads out a list of the Boss's flaws: his butchered idioms, his wasteful management motto, and his hygiene. The Boss sits through the criticism without realizing he is being insulted.
punchline: The Boss is so oblivious that, after being told about his bad grammar, terrible leadership and poor hygiene, he concludes he must be a misunderstood genius.
summary: A hired canine delivers a resigned worker's scathing feedback to a boss who hears only praise for himself.

file: 1998/1998-05-20_sychophant_puckered lips_boss sidekick_introductions.gif
title: Boss Shows Off Nodding Sycophant

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, this is Allen, my new sycophant.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: His head nods whenever I talk. But that's not the best part...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Very impressive.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is that great or what?

situation: The Pointy-Haired Boss introduces Dilbert to Allen, his new employee, whom he openly calls his sycophant. Allen's head nods whenever the Boss speaks, and the Boss boasts about this as if it were a prized feature. Dilbert politely calls it impressive while the Boss gloats.
punchline: The Boss proudly treats a yes-man who nods at everything he says as a great asset, showing he values flattery over competence.
summary: A manager brags about his newest underling, whose chief talent is bobbing his head in agreement with everything the manager says.

file: 1998/1998-03-30_above salary midpoint_stock options_interpersonal skills.gif
title: Boss Confuses Alice's Stock Options

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't give you a raise because you're above the salary midpoint. But at least your stock options are doing great!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I don't have any stock options.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh. I'm probably thinking of me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Next, it says I should coach you on your interpersonal skills.

setting: The Boss's office, during a performance review
situation: The Boss tells Alice during a review that she can't get a raise because she is above the salary midpoint, then tries to console her by praising her stock options. Alice points out she has none, and the Boss admits he was thinking of himself. He then moves on to coaching her on interpersonal skills while Alice grits her teeth in anger.
punchline: The Boss blunders with a self-serving mix-up about stock options, then has the nerve to critique Alice's interpersonal skills when his own are clearly terrible.
summary: A manager denies his employee a raise, accidentally reveals that only he has stock options, and then lectures her about people skills.

file: 1998/1998-02-09_going forward basis_time travel_concept of time_boss understnds_got lucky.gif
title: Boss Rules Out Time Travel

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I suggest that you deal with the issue on a going forward basis.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks for ruling out time travel. You're usually not that helpful.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Are you saying he understands the concept of "time" now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or he just got lucky on this one.

setting: The Boss's office, then the office lunch table
situation: The Boss advises Dilbert to handle a problem on a 'going forward basis'. Dilbert sarcastically thanks him for ruling out time travel, since the Boss is normally unhelpful. At lunch Dilbert tells Alice and Wally about it, and they wonder whether the Boss actually grasps the concept of time or was just lucky.
punchline: Dilbert mocks the Boss's vague management jargon by treating it as a rare piece of useful advice, and suggests the Boss may not truly understand time at all and simply got lucky.
summary: A manager's buzzword-laden advice to fix things from now on earns his employee's sarcastic gratitude and a lunchtime debate over whether he grasped what he said.

file: 1998/1998-06-11_technical skills_marketing_valaubale_ire_balled up paper_cheerleader squad_business.gif
title: Too Valuable To Fire Backfires

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Unlike you people in marketing, I have highly sought technical skills.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm too valuable to fire. So from now on, I'll deliver my project status on a balled-up piece of paper.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is the cheerleader squad ready?

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Grrr.

situation: At a meeting, Wally boasts to a marketing colleague and the Boss that his technical skills make him too valuable to fire, and announces he'll deliver project status on a balled-up piece of paper. The Boss responds by asking whether the cheerleader squad is ready, and Wally ends up cowering on the floor as Carol growls.
punchline: Wally's smug claim of job security is met with a threat of punishment, as the Boss calls for a cheerleader squad to presumably beat him up, showing that being irreplaceable doesn't protect him from consequences.
summary: After bragging that his rare skills make him untouchable and mocking the marketing staff, Wally gets ambushed when the Boss summons some muscle.

file: 1998/1998-10-28_dogcart the consultant_target market_gullible moron_commercials_sincere actor.gif
title: Targeting the Gullible Moron Segment

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Our target market is the gullible moron segment.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Our commercials will feature an actor who seems sincere.

transcript.speaker: Actor on TV
transcript.text: I care about the rain forest... and you.

transcript.speaker: Actor on TV
transcript.text: I like kittens ... and you.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Wow... we made it into his top two.

setting: A conference room during a consulting session, then a couple's living room
situation: Dogbert, acting as a marketing consultant, tells The Boss that the company's target market is gullible morons and that commercials will use a sincere-seeming actor. A TV demo shows the actor claiming to care about the rain forest and the viewer. In the final panel, a couple on a couch watch another commercial and the woman happily reacts as if the actor genuinely likes her.
punchline: The ad works exactly as Dogbert predicted: the viewers are so gullible that they feel flattered by a scripted actor's insincere affection, proving they are the target market.
summary: A consultant's cynical advertising plan is instantly validated when a couple on a sofa swoons over a television pitchman's fake affection.

file: 1998/1998-01-27_deputy of common sense_four hour meeting_behind schedule_agenda_morale is low.gif
title: Deputy Arrests Four-Hour Meeting Scheduler

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Deputy of Common Sense

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Freeze!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You scheduled a four-hour meeting to find out why people are behind schedule!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, look at the agenda! The fourth hour is a discussion about why morale is low!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Shoot him.

situation: Dogbert, dressed as the Deputy of Common Sense with a badge, hat and holster, confronts the Boss at a meeting table, accusing him of scheduling a four-hour meeting to investigate why people are behind schedule. The Boss defends himself by pointing to the agenda, which includes an hour on why morale is low. Alice, seated nearby, calmly suggests shooting him.
punchline: The Boss's defense actually makes things worse, since adding a discussion of low morale to a marathon meeting only confirms the foolishness, and Alice's deadpan call to shoot him shows how fed up everyone is.
summary: A common-sense lawman busts a manager for burning half a workday on a meeting about lateness, and the manager's excuse only damns him further.

file: 1998/1998-10-29_dogbert the consultant_ad campign_tony sincereity_introdcue prodcut_invisible robot_empty box.gif
title: Selling the Invisible Robot

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the Consultant

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Our ad campaign featuring phony sincerity is working.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In phase two, we'll introduce our newest product, the invisible robot.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: We don't know how to make an invisible robot.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you know how to make an empty box?

situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, sits at a meeting table with Dilbert and a big-haired company executive. After the executive praises the phony-sincerity ad campaign, Dogbert announces the next product will be an invisible robot. When she objects that they can't build one, he points out that an empty box is easy to make.
punchline: Dogbert proposes selling an empty box as an 'invisible robot', implying that customers who fall for phony sincerity will buy a nonexistent product.
summary: A consultant cheerfully plans to follow a deceptive ad campaign by marketing an empty package as a product that cannot be seen.

file: 1998/1998-03-15_brand equity_increasing skills_kleenex engineers_sneeze_kleenex_engineers.gif
title: Wally, the Kleenex of Engineers

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: While you toil in utter futility, I'm building my personal "brand equity."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm increasing my skills and my contacts every day.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My dream is to become the "Kleenex" of engineers!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: 'Scuse me. I have real work to do.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Ooh... sneeze coming.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Aaaah...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Choo!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I think of Wally as the "Kleenex" of engineers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Me too.

situation: Wally brags to Dilbert that he is building his personal brand equity and wants to become the "Kleenex" of engineers. Alice, in a hurry, pushes past him, grabs his head to sneeze into his shirt, and then says she thinks of Wally as the "Kleenex" of engineers. Dilbert agrees.
punchline: Wally wants to be the household-name brand of engineering, but Alice and Dilbert see him as a disposable tissue she can sneeze into.
summary: A self-promoting coworker hopes to become a famous brand name, only to be literally used as a tissue by a colleague.

file: 1998/1998-06-07_cofffee_tired_downward spiral_immobile_bring coffee.gif
title: Coffee-Deprived Dilbert Mobbed by Coworkers

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need coffee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But I'm too tired to go get it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm in a downward spiral!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My arms go limp. The antidote is only yards away but I am immobile.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe someone will notice and bring coffee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My co-workers found me. I'm saved!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As the frenzied mob yanked off my trousers, someone spilled coffee on me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wow, lucky.

situation: Dilbert is so tired and desperate for coffee that he slumps in his chair, too exhausted to walk to the coffee. When coworkers finally find him, they seem to rescue him, but off-panel they pull off his trousers. Afterward Dilbert stands covered in spilled coffee, and Dogbert remarks on his luck.
punchline: Dilbert gets his coffee only as a side effect of being humiliated by a mob that strips off his pants, and Dogbert sarcastically calls that lucky.
summary: A caffeine-starved engineer collapses in his chair hoping for rescue, and the help that arrives turns out far worse than the exhaustion.

file: 1998/1998-08-17_motivational message_employees_first day_rest of the week_business.gif
title: Boss's Useless Motivational Voicemail Message

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is today's motivational message for all employees.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Today is the first day of the rest of the week.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Or is it?

setting: The Boss's office, at his desk in a large blue chair
situation: The Boss sits in his chair holding a phone and records a motivational message for all employees. He delivers a feeble twist on the familiar 'first day of the rest of your life' slogan, then privately second-guesses even that trivial statement in a thought bubble.
punchline: The boss's motivational message is a meaningless platitude, and he is so clueless that he doubts even his own empty statement.
summary: A manager phones in an inspirational slogan to his staff that says nothing, then wonders whether it was even correct.
keywords: first day of the rest of the week

file: 1998/1998-04-10_no layoffs_after merger_catbert_evil director_frozen asteroid_protective space suits_not a team player.gif
title: No Layoffs, Just Frozen Asteroid

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: There will be no layoffs after the merger.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: However, many of you will be transferred to jobs on a frozen asteroid.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Will we have protective space suits?

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I label you "not a team player."

setting: Conference room during a post-merger HR announcement
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells a meeting of employees that there will be no layoffs after the merger. He then reveals that many will be transferred to jobs on a frozen asteroid. When an employee asks a practical question about protective space suits, Catbert brands him as 'not a team player.'
punchline: Management technically avoids layoffs by sending people to an absurdly deadly posting, and anyone who raises a reasonable concern is punished with a damaging label.
summary: An HR chief promises job security after a merger, then sends staff to a lethal outpost and smears the one who questions it.

file: 1998/1998-02-10_imgination_sexier_everyday_super model_kryptonite.gif
title: Dogbert Decides to Be Supermodel

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is it my imagination or am I getting sexier every day?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The mirror doesn't lie. I am getting sexier.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've decided to be a supermodel.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, but stay away from kryptonite.

setting: Dilbert's home living room and kitchen table
situation: Dogbert lounges on the couch musing in thought bubbles that he is getting sexier every day, then checks a hand mirror to confirm it. At breakfast he announces to Dilbert that he will become a supermodel, and Dilbert, pouring cereal, gives a deadpan reply.
punchline: Dilbert conflates 'supermodel' with 'superman' and warns Dogbert about kryptonite, a dry pun that mocks Dogbert's vanity and self-delusion.
summary: After admiring himself in a mirror, a vain dog declares a modeling career and his roommate responds with a superhero joke.

file: 1998/1998-05-04_strange dream_alice_research_someone else dream_graose_seedless_science.gif
title: Nothing Duller Than Someone's Dream

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I had a strange dream last night.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Research has shown that nothing is less interesting than hearing about someone else's dream.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: ...But this was no ordinary grape. It was a seedless!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: My brain is gnawing its way out!

situation: Alice stands at a meeting table and announces she had a strange dream. A colleague (Asok) cites research that nothing is less interesting than hearing someone else's dream, but Alice presses on anyway, describing a dream about a seedless grape. Asok clutches his head in agony as his boredom becomes unbearable.
punchline: Alice ignores the warning that dream stories are boring and proves it by narrating an absurdly mundane dream about a seedless grape, driving a listener to desperation.
summary: A coworker is warned that recounting dreams is dull, yet she plows ahead with a pointless fruit-based tale that leaves her audience in agony.

file: 1998/1998-03-16_woman paid 75 cents_every dollar men_highest paid engineer_average woman_problem.gif
title: Highest Paid Engineer Disproves Pay Gap

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I just read that the average woman is paid 75 cents for every dollar that men make. It's an outrage!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm the highest paid engineer in the company.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's impossible. The article says "average women" earn less.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Suddenly, the problem comes into focus.

situation: A female coworker with a bowl-shaped haircut tells Alice, who is typing at her computer, about an article claiming women earn 75 cents for every dollar men make. Alice replies that she is the highest paid engineer in the company. The coworker insists that is impossible because the article says average women earn less, and Alice remarks that this explains the problem.
punchline: The coworker mistakes a statistical average for a rule applying to every individual woman, so she cannot accept that Alice earns the most, which Alice sarcastically says reveals the real problem.
summary: A colleague's outrage over a pay statistic collapses when she refuses to believe that an individual woman could out-earn everyone, since averages supposedly forbid it.

file: 1998/1998-09-08_consulting form_bushel_money_twenty hours of work_good reasons_clients_travel.gif
title: Bushel of Money, Twenty-Hour Days

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: Come work for our consulting firm and you will get this bushel of money.

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: All we want in return is twenty hours of work each day...

transcript.speaker: Consultant
transcript.text: ...with clients who hate you for a variety of good reasons.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: At least there's no travel, right?

setting: Office, in front of a wooden dresser
situation: A consultant in a suit holds a bushel basket full of cash and pitches a job at his consulting firm to Ratbert. He reveals the catch in stages: twenty hours of work a day, plus clients who hate you for good reasons. Ratbert, tempted by the money, hopefully asks whether at least there is no travel.
punchline: Ratbert accepts the absurd workload and hated-by-clients terms and only asks about travel, implying the job will be even worse than he hopes, since consulting normally involves constant travel.
summary: A recruiter dangles a basket of cash in front of Ratbert while gradually confessing how miserable the consulting job really is.

file: 1998/1998-06-09_demand for engineers_supply_increasing insolence_decreasing prodcutivity_hire engineer_equilibrium restored.gif
title: Engineer Restores Supply-Demand Equilibrium Through Insolence

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This week I discovered that the demand for engineers exceeds the supply.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I responded by increasing my insolence and decreasing my productivity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I will never hire another engineer as long as I'm alive.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Equilibrium has been restored.

situation: At a meeting, Wally announces that he has realized engineers are in high demand and short supply. He explains that he reacted by being more insolent and less productive. The Boss, fed up, vows never to hire another engineer, and Wally cheerfully declares that balance has been restored.
punchline: Wally exploits his market leverage by behaving badly until his boss stops wanting engineers, which he sarcastically frames as the economic market rebalancing itself.
summary: Realizing that engineers are scarce, a lazy employee deliberately becomes a worse worker until his boss swears off hiring any more of them.

file: 1998/1998-04-05_variance im depreciation_four hour meeting_stale dount_nothing to report_wasted donut_threw donut_meeting_everyone alseep_business.gif
title: Stale Donut Weapon Against Droning Presenter

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: ...Now let's look at our year-to-date variance in depreciation.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Only five minutes left of our four hour meeting.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: If he keeps droning, there won't be any time for my presentation.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I spent a whole week preparing my presentation.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Everyone else is already asleep.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: My only hope is to stun the presenter with a stale donut.

transcript.speaker: Presenter
transcript.text: As you can see, there's nothing to report.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I wasted a donut.

setting: Conference room during a long meeting
situation: A presenter drones on about depreciation variance while the whole room sleeps through a four-hour meeting. Alice, who spent a week preparing her own presentation, grows desperate and throws a stale donut at the presenter to stop him. The throw misses or has no effect, and the presenter just continues.
punchline: Alice's desperate, absurd attempt to interrupt the presenter with a donut fails, and she is left regretting the wasted donut rather than getting her turn.
summary: A frustrated employee hurls a stale pastry at a boring speaker to claim her time, only to regret the loss of the snack.

file: 1998/1998-04-24_speaks with author_comic strip_burned out_funny everyday_books_media_speaking_book signing_entertainment.gif
title: Burned-Out Cartoonist Stalls Book Signing

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: At the conference

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I liked your talk about your comic strip. Do you ever feel burned out?

transcript.speaker: Cartoonist
transcript.text: You have to be funny every day. Then there are the books, the media, the speaking. So much stress...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oops.

setting: A book signing table at a conference
situation: Dilbert is standing in a line at a conference to get a book signed by a cartoonist who gave a talk about his comic strip. Dilbert asks if the cartoonist ever feels burned out, and the cartoonist unloads a long list of stress and complaints while the line of people waiting behind Dilbert grows visibly irritated.
punchline: Dilbert's casual question prompts a long complaint that holds up the signing line, so the people behind him end up angry at him for it.
summary: A fan's polite question gets a venting author talking so long that the queue behind him turns hostile.

file: 1998/1998-01-06_performance review_ding you_keep informed_peek at computer_unread messages.gif
title: Twelve Thousand Unread Messages

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Performance review

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, I had to ding you for not keeping me informed about your project.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: May I take a peek at your computer?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You have twelve thousand unread messages.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, it's a little late for that now.

setting: The Boss's office during a performance review
situation: The Boss tells Alice during her performance review that he is marking her down for not keeping him informed about her project. Alice asks to look at his computer and discovers he has twelve thousand unread messages. The Boss shrugs it off, saying it's too late to matter now.
punchline: The Boss penalizes Alice for not keeping him informed when he has clearly ignored thousands of messages, and he refuses to reconsider once his own negligence is exposed.
summary: A manager blames an employee for poor communication, only for her to reveal his inbox is overflowing with messages he never opened.

file: 1998/1998-12-26_maintain urgency_speed is key_faster than competition_sign stuff_logical questions_motivational messages.gif
title: Urgency Speech Versus Unsigned Paperwork

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We must maintain a sense of urgency. Speed is the key. We must be faster than the competition.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does that mean you'll sign the stuff that's been on your desk for a month?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Logical questions don't mix with motivational messages.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss gives a rousing speech demanding urgency and speed to beat the competition. Dilbert points out that the boss has let paperwork sit unsigned on his desk for a month. The Boss dismisses the question as incompatible with his motivational message.
punchline: The boss demands speed from everyone else while being the bottleneck himself, and deflects the fair criticism by claiming logic has no place in a pep talk.
summary: A manager preaches the need for speed but brushes off a pointed reminder that he himself has been sitting on approvals for weeks.

file: 1998/1998-01-29_deputy of common sense_safety inspector_after insepction_determine pay_decrease in accidents_trips wally.gif
title: Safety Inspector Trips Coworkers for Pay

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Deputy of Common Sense

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you the government safety inspector?

transcript.speaker: Safety Inspector
transcript.text: Yup. I love my job.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Watch your step!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hey!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How does your boss determine your pay?

transcript.speaker: Safety Inspector
transcript.text: It's based on the decrease in accidents after my inspection.

setting: Office, on and around a filing cabinet
situation: Dogbert, wearing a police-style hat as the Deputy of Common Sense, questions a government safety inspector who says he loves his job. The inspector's foot sends Wally tumbling just after Dogbert warns him to watch his step. Dogbert then asks how the inspector is paid, revealing his pay depends on how much accidents decrease after his inspections.
punchline: The safety inspector's pay depends on accidents decreasing after his visit, so he has a perverse incentive to make everyone nervous or to cause accidents beforehand, which would make later reductions look like improvements.
summary: A pay scheme that rewards an inspector for fewer accidents after his visit invites him to make things worse beforehand.

file: 1998/1998-11-22_zero disabling injuries_injury_fill forms_resignation forms_cinjury report.gif
title: Injury Reports Disguised As Resignations

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our goal this year is zero disabling injuries.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Last year our goal was twenty-six disabling injuries.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In retrospect, that was a mistake.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We had to injure nine employees to meet the goal.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you have an injury, fill out these forms immediately.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: These are resignation forms.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you cover the word "resignation" with your thumb, it's an injury report.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: This place makes me sick.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We'll miss you.

setting: Conference room during a company safety meeting
situation: The Boss announces a goal of zero disabling injuries, admitting that last year's goal of twenty-six injuries led to nine employees being deliberately injured. He then hands out forms for injured workers that are actually resignation forms. When Wally says the place makes him sick, Dilbert says they will miss him.
punchline: The company hits its zero-injuries target not by making the workplace safer but by forcing anyone who reports an injury to resign, so the statistics look perfect while employees suffer.
summary: A manager chases a perfect safety record by quietly turning injury paperwork into a way to push hurt workers out the door.

file: 1998/1998-06-08_catbert_evil hr director_bad news_reading papaers_low unemployment rate_cubicle roof.gif
title: Catbert Fears Employees Reading Newspapers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Bad news: The employees are reading a newspaper.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: If they see the low unemployment rate, they'll know the balance of power has swung their way.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I plan to use the cat as a gargoyle on my cubicle roof.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you run a current through him you can zap bugs.

setting: The Boss's office, then a break area with employees reading newspapers
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, warns the pointy-haired boss that employees are reading a newspaper and might learn about the low unemployment rate. If they do, they will realize they have more bargaining power. In the last panel, Wally, Dilbert and Alice read the paper and, rather than exploiting their leverage, Wally plans to mount Catbert on his cubicle roof as a gargoyle.
punchline: The employees learn they hold the power, and their first use of it is to fantasize about turning the H.R. director into a bug-zapping gargoyle.
summary: Management frets that a good job market will empower staff, and the staff promptly respond by plotting to decorate a cubicle with their H.R. chief.

file: 1998/1998-05-03_new employee_obsolete computer_spirit crush_cubicle_safety hazrds_look busy_meaningful assignment_wait_binder_desk.gif
title: Crushing the New Hire's Spirit

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, this is our newest employee, Matt.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would you mind... crushing his spirit?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This little box will be your home for sixty hours a week.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It comes with an obsolete computer and a binder about safety hazards.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your challenge is to look busy until someone gives you a meaningful assignment.

transcript.speaker: Matt
transcript.text: How long will that take?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm still waiting for mine.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Safety tip 1: Don't sit near any obsolete computers.

situation: The Boss introduces new employee Matt to Dilbert and casually asks Dilbert to crush the newcomer's spirit. Dilbert cheerfully obliges by showing Matt his tiny cubicle, obsolete computer and safety binder, and explaining that his job is to look busy. When Matt asks how long until he gets real work, Dilbert says he is still waiting himself, and Matt reads the binder's safety tip.
punchline: Dilbert has been waiting years for a meaningful assignment himself, showing that the new hire's hopeful expectations are hopeless, and even the safety binder advises avoiding the very computer he's been given.
summary: A veteran employee gives a fresh recruit a bleak orientation that reveals how little real work and equipment the company provides.

file: 1998/1998-09-12_built a ring_computer_display_one character_technology.gif
title: Dilbert's One-Character Computer Ring

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I built a ring with a tiny computer in it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It only displays one character at a time.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then what good is it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No time for chit-chat. I'm surfin' the net!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't make me come over there.

situation: Dilbert shows Dogbert a ring he built with a tiny computer inside. When Dogbert asks what use it is given that it displays only one character at a time, Dilbert brushes him off, claiming to be too busy surfing the net on it. Dogbert threatens him for the absurd claim.
punchline: Dilbert claims to be surfing the net on a ring that shows one character at a time, which is an absurdly impractical way to browse, and Dogbert mockingly threatens him over it.
summary: An engineer proudly wears a homemade micro-computer ring that can show only a single letter, then pretends it's a fully functional web browser.

file: 1998/1998-02-06_company_knows about wally_phone call logs_web hits_emails_urine test_college grades_salary_family_business_money.gif
title: Catbert Threatens Wally With Impersonators

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Catbert: Evil H.R. Director

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The company knows everything about you, Wally.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We have logs of all your phone calls, web hits and e-mail. We have your urine test, college grades, salary and family contacts...

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It's against our policy to kill employees and replace them with low-paid impersonators, but I wanted you to know it's feasible.

setting: Catbert's H.R. office, across a desk from Wally
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, sits at his desk and tells Wally the company holds extensive records on him, including phone logs, web history, email, urine test, grades, salary and family contacts. He then adds that company policy forbids killing employees and replacing them with cheap impersonators, though he wants Wally to know it could be done.
punchline: Catbert presents a menacing threat as a policy reminder, implying the company has enough personal data and enough contempt for employees to make a murder-and-replacement scheme entirely doable.
summary: A sinister HR cat lists all the personal data the firm has collected on a worker, then ominously hints that swapping him for a cheaper lookalike is technically possible.

file: 1998/1998-11-15_organization chart_phone lists shreded_picking clean_headhunters_steal away_double pay_drains initiative.gif
title: Boss Shreds Phone Lists Against Headhunters

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: From now on, the organization chart will not be distributed.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And the internal phone lists will be shredded.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Crumple

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This will prevent headhunters from easily picking us clean.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why would headhunters call us?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They want to steal you away and double your pay at another company.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: What makes you think we won't leave on our own anyway?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because working here drains all of your initiative.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let's prove him wrong!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah! I'm not shredding my phone list!

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces that the org chart won't be distributed and phone lists will be shredded to keep headhunters from poaching employees. Wally asks why headhunters would call them, and the Boss explains they'd offer double pay elsewhere. When challenged on why staff wouldn't just leave on their own, the Boss says the job has drained their initiative, and the employees respond by defiantly vowing to keep their phone lists.
punchline: The Boss's retention strategy relies on employees being too demoralized to act, and the best act of rebellion the employees can muster is merely not shredding a phone list.
summary: A manager tries to stop talent poaching by destroying contact lists, admitting his workers are too listless to leave, and they weakly protest by keeping their directories.

file: 1998/1998-11-27_new cfo_babbling idiot_offcie_dilbert questions.gif
title: New CFO or Babbling Idiot

transcript.speaker: Man in suit
transcript.text: Then we need to PV the DCF and get the ROI to the EOC ASAP.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you our new CFO or a babbling idiot who just happened to wander by?

transcript.speaker: Man in suit
transcript.text: Which one pays more?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The mystery deepens.

situation: A man in a suit stands by Dilbert's desk and rattles off a string of finance acronyms. Dilbert asks whether he is the company's new CFO or just a babbling idiot who wandered in. The man responds by asking which role pays more, leaving Dilbert still unable to tell.
punchline: The visitor's answer is a question about pay, which is exactly what either a real executive or a clueless wanderer might say, so Dilbert still can't tell them apart.
summary: A stranger spouting financial jargon can't be told apart from a new executive, and his reply only makes the confusion worse.

file: 1998/1998-08-15_vital information_deadline_boss request_traded work ethic_banana_break room.gif
title: Work Ethic Traded for a Banana

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need this vital information by one o'clock.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I do a shoddy job, I can finish this and still make it to lunch!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Today I traded my work ethic for a banana.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I ate that banana years ago.

setting: Office cubicle and break room at lunchtime
situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a paper and demands vital information by one o'clock. Dilbert thinks that doing sloppy work will let him finish in time for lunch. At the lunch table he peels a banana and says he traded his work ethic for it, and Alice replies that she did the same long ago.
punchline: Dilbert's shortcut to lunch costs him his work ethic, and Alice's reply shows that she sold out her own standards years ago, so lowering your standards to get through the workday is treated as normal.
summary: A rushed deadline leads Dilbert to knowingly do sloppy work so he can lunch on time, and a coworker reveals she gave up her own standards long before.

file: 1998/1998-10-25_improve communications_two pennies_give two cents worth_cute_avoid seeing boss_pretend dead_nickel.gif
title: Two Cents Worth Communication Scheme

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In order to improve communications...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Please don't.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Every morning I'll give you two pennies.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Every afternoon, you return them and "give me your two cents' worth."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Get it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's cute.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: So, I get to keep the money if I avoid seeing you?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How much will you pay me to ignore your voice mail too?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'll pretend you're dead for a nickel.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I hate them all.

situation: The Boss announces a communication-improvement scheme in which he hands Alice two pennies each morning and she returns them in the afternoon with her 'two cents' worth.' He proudly explains the pun, but Alice turns the scheme around by treating the pennies as payment for avoiding him, then offers to ignore his voice mail and pretend he's dead for a nickel.
punchline: Alice twists the boss's cutesy pun into a bribery arrangement, showing she'd gladly be paid to avoid communicating with him and even pretend he's dead.
summary: A pun-loving manager tries to boost communication with pocket change, and his hostile employee instead prices out how much it would cost to be left alone.

file: 1998/1998-03-20_letter of refrence_job in division_prone to anger and denail.gif
title: The Boss's Backhanded Reference Letter

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll need a letter of reference to apply for a job in another division.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No problem.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ... For a man of his hygiene, he doesn't steal as much as you'd think. I suspect he's on drugs.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: And then he says you're prone to anger and denial. Is that true?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No!!

setting: Office of The Boss, then an interviewer's office in another division
situation: Dilbert asks his boss for a letter of reference so he can transfer to another division, and the boss cheerfully agrees. While writing, the boss pens insulting remarks about Dilbert's hygiene, theft and suspected drug use. In the next division, the interviewer reads the letter aloud, and Dilbert angrily denies being prone to anger and denial.
punchline: The boss's reference letter is full of insults and accusations, and Dilbert's furious denial of being prone to anger and denial proves the letter's point.
summary: A manager agrees to write a job reference but fills it with slander, and the employee's outburst at the interview seems to confirm the worst of it.

file: 1998/1998-04-16_scavenging_too late_good stuff_pants_computer_technology.gif
title: Scavenging a Departed Coworker's Belongings

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Heh heh. Ed is barely out the door and I got his old computer.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The scavenging was good today.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Alice is going to be miffed that she's too late for the good stuff.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You got his pants?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It wasn't easy. He'd already made it to the bus.

situation: Dilbert and Wally carry off computer equipment belonging to Ed, a coworker who has just left the company, and gloat about their haul. Wally predicts Alice will be too late to get the good stuff, but Alice then appears carrying Ed's pants, which she grabbed as he was boarding the bus.
punchline: Alice outdoes the male scavengers by taking not just Ed's equipment but the actual pants off his back, showing she is the most ruthless scavenger of all.
summary: Two coworkers pick over a departed colleague's leftover gear, only to be upstaged by a third who snatched his trousers at the bus stop.

file: 1998/1998-04-07_jordan preventer of information services_confiscate non standard computer_heavier_disable it.gif
title: Mordac Smashes Non-Standard Computer

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I am Mordac, the Preventer of Information Services. I come to confiscate your non-standard computer.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: You'll give me a new one, right?

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: This is heavier than it looks.

transcript.speaker: Mordac
transcript.text: I'll have to disable it and leave it here.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: The new one is already on its way, right?

situation: Mordac, the head of IT, arrives at an employee's desk to confiscate his non-standard computer. Finding it too heavy to carry away, he raises a hammer to disable it and leave it behind. The employee keeps anxiously asking whether a replacement is coming.
punchline: Mordac cares only about enforcing standards and destroying the computer, not about the employee's ability to work, so the promised replacement is clearly never coming.
summary: An IT enforcer decides it's easier to smash a banned computer on the spot than to haul it away, leaving its owner with nothing.

file: 1998/1998-01-17_ken the skeptic_contents of envelope_charcoal drawing_woodchuck_small orange_little frauf_ink drawing_beaver eating tangerine.gif
title: Skeptic Debunks Psychic's Near-Miss Guess

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ken the Skeptic...

transcript.speaker: Ken
transcript.text: I alone know the contents of this envelope.

transcript.speaker: Psychic Ratbert
transcript.text: It's a charcoal drawing of a woodchuck eating a small orange.

transcript.speaker: Ken
transcript.text: Nice try, you little fraud, but that's a long way from an ink drawing of a beaver eating a tangerine.

setting: A skeptic's testing session, with a yellow psychic on a stool
situation: Ken the Skeptic holds up a sealed envelope and claims only he knows what is inside. A yellow, ratlike psychic on a stool confidently describes a charcoal drawing of a woodchuck eating a small orange. Ken dismisses him as a fraud and reveals the real contents: an ink drawing of a beaver eating a tangerine.
punchline: The psychic's guess is impressively close, with a similar animal, similar fruit and similar medium, yet the skeptic treats the near-miss as total proof of fraud, calling it a 'long way' from the truth.
summary: A doubter quizzes a clairvoyant about a hidden picture and scorns an answer that is almost, but not exactly, right.

file: 1998/1998-08-08_digital archive_greatest art_fixing artists mistakes_funny story_newsletter_dramatically improving_writer.gif
title: Fixing Masterpieces Becomes Dramatically Improving

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm creating a digital archive of the world's greatest art. But my boss insists on "fixing" the artists' mistakes.

transcript.speaker: Newsletter Writer
transcript.text: Hee hee.

transcript.speaker: Newsletter Writer
transcript.text: This is such a funny story for the newsletter!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's a funny story, but change "fixing" to "dramatically improving."

situation: Dilbert tells a newsletter writer that his boss insists on fixing the mistakes of the world's greatest artists while he builds a digital art archive. The writer finds it funny and plans to print it. The Boss, who has apparently heard about it, tells her to keep the story but reword "fixing" as "dramatically improving."
punchline: The Boss isn't bothered that his meddling with masterpieces is absurd; he only wants the newsletter to describe it in more flattering language.
summary: A planned humorous newsletter item about a manager tampering with famous artworks gets spun by that same manager into a flattering rewrite.

file: 1998/1998-08-09_bonus_discontinue_profcits_recorded message_redirect_serve customers better_tech support_evil.gif
title: Cutting Support to Boost Profits

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: We're discontinuing technical support of all our products.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: A recorded message will explain it to the caller this way...

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: "In order to serve customers better, we've discontinued technical support."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How does that serve customers better?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: We'll redirect those resources to other areas.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What other areas?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Profits.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: That makes your bonus larger.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Any other questions?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently I'm engulfed in evil.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: That's the spirit!

situation: A manager announces to Dilbert and other attendees that all technical support is being discontinued. When Dilbert asks how that serves customers, the manager admits the resources are being redirected to profits, which also enlarges Dilbert's bonus.
punchline: Dilbert realizes that his bonus makes him complicit in a cynical decision, and the manager cheerfully approves of his embrace of corporate evil.
summary: A company axes customer help lines under the pretense of improving service, then bribes a skeptical employee with a bigger bonus.

file: 1998/1998-06-04_computer problems_stupid software_code rage_throws computer.gif
title: Code Rage Computer Toss

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stupid software! Won't compile; eh??

transcript.speaker: Police Officer
transcript.text: We call it "code rage." I'm seeing a lot of it lately.

situation: Alice, frustrated that her software won't compile, shakes her computer and then hurls the monitor over the cubicle wall, cursing. A coworker walks past unbothered. A police officer takes notes beside Dilbert and comments that he is seeing a lot of this behavior lately, with broken computer parts on the floor.
punchline: Programmer frustration has become so common that it has earned an official name, 'code rage', and the police are now routinely called in to document it.
summary: After an angry coder throws her monitor over a cubicle wall, a cop calmly explains that such outbursts have become a familiar trend.

file: 1998/1998-08-25_dogbert consults_recommendations_analyis_us dollars_elbonian currency_eye crud.gif
title: Consultant Unaccountable, Recommends Anything Amusing

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: My recommendations are based on an analysis of accountability.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ooh.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: As a consultant, I'm not accountable to your stockholders. So I can recommend anything that amuses me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I recommend that you convert all of your U.S. dollars to Elbonian currency... whatever that is.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The eye-crud.

setting: The Boss's office, across a desk (Dogbert Consults)
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, sits across the desk from the Boss and explains that his advice is based on an analysis of accountability. He admits he isn't accountable to the stockholders, so he can recommend whatever amuses him, then advises converting all the company's U.S. dollars into Elbonian currency. The Boss, impressed, only mutters that Elbonian currency is 'the eye-crud.'
punchline: The consultant openly admits he faces no consequences for bad advice, and the gullible Boss accepts it anyway, even agreeing to a ridiculous recommendation to swap dollars for worthless, unknown currency.
summary: A consultant cheerfully reveals that, since he answers to no one, his advice is whatever entertains him, and the manager nods along as he suggests trading real money for a fictional currency.

file: 1998/1998-03-11_elbonia_deep mud_misogyny_mud weasels_kick people_complimenting_screaming.gif
title: Elbonia Assignment: Mud and Misogyny

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: I'm off to Elbonia, the land of waist-deep mud and misogyny.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: On the plus side, you can kick people and blame it on the mud weasels.

transcript.speaker: Yugi
transcript.text: What's wrong, Yugi? One second you are complimenting this chick, next second screaming.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: Mud weasel.

setting: Conference room, then the muddy fields of Elbonia
situation: Tina, standing at a meeting with Dilbert and the Boss, announces she is being sent to Elbonia, which she describes as a land of deep mud and misogyny. The Boss cheerfully suggests she can kick people and blame it on mud weasels. In Elbonia, Tina is buried waist-deep in mud, and a man who was complimenting her starts screaming after she has apparently kicked him; a bystander asks what is wrong.
punchline: Tina takes the Boss's tongue-in-cheek advice literally, kicking a man who was complimenting her and blaming it on a mud weasel.
summary: A woman facing a dreadful overseas posting is told she can get away with violence by blaming local wildlife, and promptly does exactly that.

file: 1998/1998-09-27_true story_drowning in work_build partition_away from boss.gif
title: Partition Hides Boss From Overworked Carol

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Based on a true story

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: I'm drowning in work!

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: You have to do something.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I could build a partition right here.

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: How will a partition help?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Carol, you shouldn't be afraid to try new things.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If it doesn't work, we'll try something else!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (Two workmen install a partition between Carol's desk and the doorway.)

transcript.speaker: Carol
transcript.text: Are you over there?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It works!

situation: Carol complains to the Boss that she is drowning in work and asks him to do something. He proposes building a partition, and when she questions how that helps, he tells her not to fear trying new things. Workmen install the partition, and the Boss happily realizes it blocks Carol from his view, so he no longer has to see her or hear her complaints.
punchline: The partition doesn't reduce Carol's workload at all; it only solves the Boss's problem by hiding her from view, so he declares it a success.
summary: Instead of easing an employee's overload, a manager walls her off so her complaints are out of sight.

file: 1998/1998-12-30_the sadistic nut_dennis_not cruel_honest_never be married_fun to watch_attacks intern.gif
title: The Sadistic Nut Torments Intern

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Sadistic Nut

transcript.speaker: Sadistic Nut
transcript.text: Hey, it's a little intern!

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Please spare me, Mister Nut.

transcript.speaker: Sadistic Nut
transcript.text: I'm not cruel. I'm honest!

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: No-o-o-o

transcript.speaker: Sadistic Nut
transcript.text: Let me tell you why you'll never be married.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: No-o-o!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have to admit, it's fun to watch.

situation: A bullying coworker known as the Sadistic Nut corners a timid intern and announces he is about to deliver harsh personal criticism. The intern begs for mercy, but the Nut insists he is merely being honest. Meanwhile Dilbert and a coworker peer over their cubicle walls and watch the spectacle.
punchline: Cruelty disguised as honesty becomes entertainment for onlookers who admit it's fun to watch someone else get verbally abused.
summary: A self-proclaimed truth-teller gleefully berates a frightened intern while bystanders enjoy the show from behind their cubicle walls.

file: 1998/1998-10-26_no real purpose_rais eissues_form action plans_urge to stomp_not very professional.gif
title: Meeting With No Purpose Violence

transcript.speaker: Meeting Leader
transcript.text: Thank you all for coming to the meeting that has no real purpose.

transcript.speaker: Meeting Leader
transcript.text: Maybe we could raise issues and then form action plans.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I have an urge to stomp you to death.

transcript.speaker: Meeting Leader
transcript.text: That's not very professional of you.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: A cheerful coworker leading a meeting openly admits it has no real purpose, then suggests the group raise issues and form action plans anyway. Alice, fed up with the pointless exercise, announces she wants to stomp him to death. He responds by scolding her for being unprofessional while Dilbert sits silently by.
punchline: The meeting leader is unfazed by openly wasting everyone's time, yet considers Alice's homicidal urge the real breach of professionalism.
summary: A man hosting an admittedly pointless meeting chides a coworker for threatening violence against him.
